Tafea Province · Vanuatu · formerly the New Hebrides

A Genealogy of the Gospel in Futuna

Compiled by Sero Kalki·1839 – 1935

Futuna is a small, steep, barren island in the far south of Vanuatu — the first island in the western Pacific a missionary ever attempted to reach, and among the last of its neighbours to accept the message. Fifty years passed between the first landfall and the first baptism. This record traces the people — Samoan, Rarotongan, Aneityumese, Scottish and Futunese — through whom the gospel descended on that island, generation by generation, together with the customary life it displaced.

1839John Williams reaches Futuna, 17 November — three days before his death on Eromanga
1853Waihit and Iosefa land: the first native evangelists in the western Pacific
1889The first five Futunese are baptised and a church is formed
1906The last of the heathen come into the church; Futuna is a Christian island

Drawn from the primary mission record: Dr William Gunn’s The Gospel in Futuna (1914) and Heralds of Dawn (1924), and the Rev. Dr J. Graham Miller’s Live. Eighteen pages — use the tabs above, or begin below.

The island and its numbers

FUTUNA · TAFEA PROVINCE · VANUATU

Where this record happens, how few people it concerns, and why that was never an argument against it.

Press / to search

01

The island and its numbers

Futuna lies about seventy kilometres east of Tanna, in the southern group of islands now called Tafea. Dr Gunn, seeing it for the first time on 17 April 1883, called it “this majestic Gibraltar-like mountain”; his wife said only, “How beautiful it is!”

The island is the largest of what Gunn called the “hat” islands of the group, built of both volcanic and coral material and thrust up out of the sea bed. Great precipices rise terrace upon terrace to a plateau some two thousand feet above the water. It is among the most barren islands in Vanuatu; food failed in time of drought, springs were few, and the people planted in small stony plots that islanders elsewhere would not have troubled to dig. There was no sandalwood, so trading vessels rarely called until the labour traffic began. Apart from imported epidemics and consumption the island was healthy: malarial fever, endemic almost everywhere else in the group, was little known there.

Districts

The island was divided tribally into seven districts, joined by difficult tracks along the cliffs. No district lay more than a few miles from the mission house on the north-eastern corner. These district names recur constantly in the record below, and are the closest thing Futuna has to surnames — a person is placed by the district he belongs to.

DistrictPositionPart in the record
IpauNorth-east, at the boat landingHead station of the mission from 1866. Home of the priest Konafia and his son Popoina. Site of the mission house, the printing room, the church of 1892 and the burial ground.
ImoungaNorth-west, by Herald Bay; divided into Upper and LowerWhere the Samoan teachers were landed in 1841 and murdered in 1843. Thereafter the hardest ground in the New Hebrides and the last district to yield, in 1906.
IsiaSouth-east, on a plateau some 500 ft above the seaSite of Gunn’s two-roomed outstation cottage of 1889 and of the first Isia church.
IasoaTwo miles beyond IsiaStation of the Futunese teacher Saula and his wife Teiau; home of Nauiakasi and Forau.
ImatangiSouth-westOne of the two districts where the Aneityumese teachers were settled in 1853. Populous then; nearly empty by Gunn’s time.
IakanaSouth-westThe other 1853 station. Uninhabited for many years before 1914.
IraroAdjoining IpauDistrict of the teacher Anapapo and of Leipanita.

The people

Gunn described the Futunese as a mixture of Polynesian and Melanesian stock, generally slighter in build than the Aneityumese and Tannese, but lighter in colour. Their language, and the names of their places and persons, resemble the speech of Samoa and Tonga. Because the island bears the same name as the other Futuna — Hoorn Island, two hundred miles north-east of Fiji — Gunn thought it probable that some of the earliest inhabitants drifted there by canoe and gave their old home’s name to the new one. Men from Hoorn Island landed from passing vessels were able to converse with the Futunese without difficulty.

Futunese is effectively the same tongue as Aniwan. This single fact governs the whole history that follows. It was because the people of Port Resolution on Tanna could understand Aniwan that John Williams, speaking Samoan and Rarotongan, could make himself understood there in 1839 and settle teachers; and it was through Futunese speech that teachers were afterwards accepted on Aneityum. Futuna was, in Gunn’s phrase, “the gateway of the Light, the key to open the door for the gospel message to the group.”

Population

The demographic collapse is the hard fact behind every page of this record. The labour traffic carried away the young men and brought back imported disease; measles, dysentery and consumption did the rest. The church was planted in a population that was falling by half in a generation.

YearPopulationNote
1866about 1,000At Copeland’s settlement.
1889513Ten births and twelve deaths recorded in the year.
1892480New church opened at Ipau; communicant roll 16.
1893347The dysentery epidemic killed 133 people — nearly one third — in three months.
1898310About 200 counted as regular worshippers.
1904—60 communicant members, 210 regular worshippers, 70 children in day schools.
1917about 300At Dr Gunn’s retirement.
1983over 800Recorded by Miller, who noted that events had vindicated Gunn’s persistence in translation.

Before Gunn: the island in 1880

STEEL · COPELAND · PATON

An earlier and independent witness to Futuna — its formation, its customs, its first teachers and its first Communion — written while the temple ceremonies were still being performed.

Press / to search

On this page
  • The island in 1880
  • What Aniwa said to Futuna
01

The island in 1880

Everything on the custom pages of this record comes from Gunn, who reached Futuna in 1883. But an earlier witness survives. The Rev. Dr Robert Steel of St Stephen’s, Sydney, cruised the group in the mission vessel and published The New Hebrides and Christian Missions in 1880, giving Futuna a chapter of its own. He wrote while Copeland was still the missionary, while the temple ceremonies were still being performed, and before a single Futunese had been baptised. Where he and Gunn agree, the agreement is worth something, because they are independent. Where he adds, the addition is earlier evidence.

The island as Steel described it

SubjectSteel, 1880
FormationA huge rock heaved out of the ocean, showing traces of four or five separate upheavals, the first distinctly marked and the others apparent on close examination, with volcanic rock cropping out on the heights — a bold rocky coast and a broad tableland on the summit about 2,000 feet high.
Position19° 30′ south, 170° 13′ east: the most easterly island of the group.
HealthFever and ague less prevalent than on the other islands, so that some of the missionaries called Futuna the Madeira of the New Hebrides and urged its claims as a sanatorium for those stationed elsewhere. Dysentery, coughs and consumption were common all the same.
The nameCook did not land in 1774 but sighted the island from Tanna and took down both names — Erronan, the Tannese name, which he put on the chart, and Fotuna, which Steel calls the native name. Cook reckoned it about fifteen miles round.
LanguageRelated to the eastern tongues rather than to the usual speech of the group; the same language as Aniwa fifty miles off, and as Fila and Mele in the bay of Pango on Efate, two hundred miles north-west.
ArtsFew, but the people excelled at making bags, which they bartered — chiefly for tobacco — to the few vessels that called. There was no anchorage and the landing places were few and dangerous.
ReligionThey feared the spirits of the dead and offered them a kind of worship; they had their sacred men and made offerings to propitiate the gods; and they had a rude hut for a temple, entered by the sacred men on certain occasions, in which the people’s offerings of food and pigs were deposited.
S 129–131
A custom the later record does not carry

Steel describes the women’s dress with a rule Gunn does not give: the short skirts were made of pandanus leaf or, more often, of bark — and only mothers were allowed to wear the skirt right round the loins. The unmarried and the childless wore it before and behind only, leaving the hips bare. Dress on Futuna therefore stated a woman’s status as plainly as the shell band on a chief’s arm stated his. He also records the men’s hair worked into small cords each wound with plant fibre and displayed at the back of the head and neck, ears loaded with tortoiseshell rings, shells worn on the arms, and bodies often painted — all of which Gunn confirms thirty years later.

S 130

Williams’ own journal, 16–17 November 1839

Steel prints what he calls the last entry ever to come from John Williams’ pen. On the Saturday evening they set apart a special prayer meeting, expecting to make Futuna next morning. Early on the Sabbath they were close in, and saw one large rugged mountain with perpendicular cliffs running to the sea and no lowland anywhere, so that they began to doubt whether the island was inhabited at all — until they made out cultivated patches on the hillsides and low huts among them.

Two canoes came off. The men would not board, for all the looking-glasses, scissors and fish-hooks offered them; so the boat was lowered instead. A man sprang from his canoe into the boat, said he was an ariki — a chief — and asked to go aboard. They put a red shirt on him and fastened a cloth round him, in which he strutted the deck and shouted in admiration of himself, until seasickness, which Williams calls the annihilator of human distinctions, sat him down as quietly as a helpless infant, looking up and crying that he was dead. In smooth water again he recovered and proved an intelligent, communicative man. They found they could exchange ideas tolerably well by a mixture of the Samoan and Rarotongan dialects — the first recorded demonstration that Futuna was a Polynesian island, and the reason Polynesian teachers were sent to it. Asked whether he would have someone placed on his island, he answered that they would give him yams, taro and sugar-cane. On the beach the crowd was entirely unarmed and perfectly civil. Williams left having promised to return with teachers, and wrote that the day’s work had raised such friendly feeling as would let them settle teachers as soon as any could be spared.

He was killed at Erromanga three days later.

S 131–133

The Samoan teachers and the murder of 1843

  • 1841. The Camden came, and the Rev. A. W. Murray settled two Samoan teachers: Apolo of Tutuila and Samuela of Upolu. They were left without wives or children in the first instance; the vessel returned from Aneityum a few days later so that they could be taken off if the people gave no encouragement, and they gave a good report and stayed. Samuela’s wife was brought to him the following year.
  • Early 1843. An epidemic was raging. The people blamed the teachers for causing it and resolved to take their lives — the same reasoning that was still killing accused disease-makers on Futuna forty years later. Apolo and Samuela, with Samuela’s daughter, went one morning to their plantation a little way from home and were waylaid and murdered.
  • The widow. The murderers then went to the mission house. One of them, named by Steel as Nasana, asked the widow — who knew nothing yet of what had happened — to become his wife. She refused with horror and offered him a present to be gone. He raised a shout, his followers came in, and she was killed. The hut was plundered.
  • April 1845. Steel says a full year passed before the John Williams called with Murray and the Rev. G. Turner aboard and the news was learned; the vessel sailed away again without being able to leave anyone to take up the work where it had fallen. Steel’s interval and his date do not agree with each other, and this record notes the discrepancy rather than resolving it.
S 134–135

The Aneityumese, 1853

Nothing could be attempted again until the gospel was succeeding on Aneityum. A Futunese chief with a number of his people had been living there for several months, had seen what was happening, and was favourably disposed. Aneityumese volunteered. Inglis and Geddie chose Waihit and Josefa; the John Williams carried them and the Futunese party home, and landed them on Futuna on 26 October 1853. Steel adds the sentence that gives this record its shape: these two were the first-fruits of the New Hebrides in the work of evangelising other islands. A third Aneityumese followed, with one man from Aitutaki and a second Rarotongan named Kakita. They pioneered without proportionate success, but the footing was kept.

S 135

Copeland’s station

Copeland and his wife settled in 1866 on the north-west side, near the best available boat landing. They lived in temporary premises at first, then built a substantial house plastered with coral lime, about a hundred feet above the sea, with garden and cow paddock fenced in loose coral walls and a very steep zigzag path up from the shore. The first place of worship he had built was burned to the ground by the heathen; a second was raised because a body of people had by then rallied to him and would not let the injury pass — posts interlaced with cane-work, thatched with sugar-cane leaf, floored with coral gravel, small but sufficient for all who came.

The first Communion, June 1871

First

The Rev. John Inglis and his wife were visiting. Inglis baptised Copeland’s child in the forenoon; Copeland administered the Lord’s Supper in the afternoon to the mission families and the native teachers. It was the first observance of the sacrament on Futuna. The afternoon service fell during an eclipse of the sun, and Inglis used it: the heathen wise men professed to make rain and wind, health and sickness, at pleasure, whereas the missionaries’ wise men professed nothing of the sort but could say years beforehand the month, day and hour when the sun or the moon would die — which is the Futunese phrase for an eclipse — because everything God does is exact.

S 136–137

The yams that were planted out of season

Evidence

Copeland had yams planted in his garden before any of the ceremonies had been performed by the sacred man. When they ripened a day was fixed for digging them and a crowd of natives, heathen and Christian, was invited to watch. The Aneityumese teachers opened the mounds and out came yams such as had hardly been seen on Futuna. The Christian party were delighted and the heathen visibly confounded — and the following Sabbath there was not one additional worshipper. The heathen answer, Inglis expected, was that it did well enough for foreigners: the gods of Futuna would not punish a stranger, but they would punish a Futunese.

S 137–138

The temple, and the club

Event

The worshipping party had begun taunting the heathen that their gods were no gods and that the offerings in the temple were eaten by rats. They asked Copeland to go into the temple and preach while they sat round it. He did, and thrust his head out through the thatch as if to defy the gods. The heathen came armed and rushed at him; the Christian party rose and in the end prevailed. Steel records that Mrs Copeland was in the middle of it and by sheer presence of mind talked a furious chief into handing her his club, and that had the thing been done earlier in Copeland’s residence it would have cost him his life.

S 142–143

“It is the price of my life”

The first movement

Steel gives what he says was the first turn in favour of the gospel, and it belongs to a family already in this register. The son of the chief priest of the island lay on his mat cold and apparently lifeless. Copeland got his mouth open and poured in a little brandy; the young man struggled, opened his eyes, and recovered. The people shouted that there was nothing Missi could not do. As soon as he could walk the young man cut a large bunch of bananas and laid it at the mission door, and when asked what should be given in return said only that it was the price of his life.

He learned to read in the evenings, saw the folly of the old practices, and then set himself to bring over his father — who stood at the head of the whole heathen worship, had lived with all the honours of the sacred office, wished to die as he had lived, and had looked forward with pride to his only son inheriting it. Advised not to be too hasty, the son answered that the heathen would get an influence over his father and it would only be harder later. He kept watch lest they take the old man away by force, and in the end brought him to the worship. From that moment the island had two parties, one calling itself Christian and the other content to be called heathen, and it became a point of honour that no one worshipping with the missionary could join the heathen ceremonies.

Steel does not name them. Gunn, writing thirty-four years later, names the priest of Ipau as Konafia and his son, the first Futunese Christian, as Popoina.

S 141–142

The planting tapu, from inside Copeland’s own report

Copeland’s letter, printed by Steel, is the most exact statement of the planting rules that survives, and it is a report of them breaking:

  • Some natives that year planted yams while it was tapu to do so — the penalty for which, by the old belief, was death to the offender.
  • A few also did not abstain from fish and pork during the planting season. The old rule was that a man who ate fish or pork and went straight out to plant would have no crop; he had to wait five days before digging if he wanted one.
  • The ceremonies before the yam planting took four nights that year instead of five weeks the year before — to the mission’s great comfort and undisturbed sleep. Copeland thought the impatience of the Christian party to get on with planting had helped to hurry them.

He adds the state of the work: about 120 at service on the Sabbath, thirty able to read, five schools, no church formed and nobody baptised, clothing becoming more general and a painted face now seldom seen at the principal station on Sabbaths — but not more than half a dozen who regularly wore clothes or cut their hair. He had printed a catechism, Scripture extracts and hymns, and his translation of Mark was printed at Sydney in 1875; Luke and other portions were done but unprinted, because so few could read.

S 138–141

The cost of the years 1871–1879

DateEvent
1871Sixty-six Aniwans with Mr Paton visited Futuna, and between thirty and forty Futunese with Mr Copeland returned the visit. The exchange was kept up for years; the Futunese carried kava to Aniwa, where the plant does not grow.
1871Mrs Copeland lost her infant and made a very precarious recovery.
6 Jan 1873The wreck of the Dayspring cut off the plan of sending her to Sydney.
Sep 1873Copeland brought the whole family to Sydney after seven years’ residence and isolation; he was invalided there with scarlet fever.
Apr 1874He returned alone after nine months. The premises, left with an Aneityumese Christian and his wife, were undisturbed; services had been kept up at every station by the teachers; the attendance had fallen. Twenty-five deaths in a population under eight hundred.
1874Eighteen births and thirty deaths in twelve months. Population down to seven hundred and seventy and falling fast.
Dec 1874To Sydney again; back in April 1875 with his wife and youngest children.
20 Jan 1876Mrs Copeland died. Steel gives the exact date, which the later sources do not.
1876–79Copeland’s own health much impaired; two years in the colonies; in April 1879 he went back to the islands to help settle Mr Lawrie and to visit his station. He refused a station on Aneityum, where the people were all professedly Christian and whose language he already knew, being unwilling to leave Futuna.
The labour trade, counted

Steel gives figures this record has nowhere else. From this one small and almost inaccessible island, one hundred and nine Futunese were taken away in three years by the labour vessels from Fiji and Queensland. Fourteen of them died and twelve were killed while they were away. Twenty-eight were absent in 1874, two of them for seven years by then; eight were taken and six came back in that year alone. Set against a population of seven hundred and seventy and falling, these are not marginal numbers, and they belong beside every figure on the Church page.

S 144
02

What Aniwa said to Futuna

Aniwa is fifty miles from Futuna and speaks the same language. It was evangelised first, and for twenty years the two islands were deliberately shown to each other. John G. Paton recorded one of those meetings, and it is the only surviving report of a Futunese deputation being addressed in their own tongue by islanders who had already made the change.

The Dayspring brought a large deputation from Futuna to Aniwa to see for themselves what the gospel had done. On the Sabbath, after the missionaries had taken the usual service, leading Aniwans spoke to the visitors. Among them was Naswai, a chief, teacher in his own village school and an elder, whose own people Paton calls the worst on the island to manage and the very last to embrace the gospel. He died in 1875, so the meeting is earlier than that.

Naswai to the men of Futuna

He told them that as heathens the Aniwans had quarrelled and killed and eaten one another and had no peace in heart or house or village, and now lived as brethren. When they got home, he said, they would be asked what Christianity is, and they would be able to answer only that it is the thing that changed the people of Aniwa, and that it had given them clothing and blankets, knives and axes and fish-hooks, and had made them stop fighting — but that they could not say what it is, because they had seen its workings and not itself.

Then he turned to the point that matters most for the custom record on these pages. You people of Futuna, he said, think that if you do not dance and sing and pray to your gods you will have no crops. The Aniwans had done the same, sacrificing and doing much abomination to their gods for weeks before the planting season every year; but they had watched Missi merely pray to the invisible Jehovah and plant his yams, and his yams grew fairer than theirs. Every year, he said, you are weak before your hard work in the fields even begins, with your wild conduct to please your gods; we are strong for our work.

He asked Paton whether the great yam the Aniwans had presented to him might be sent back with the men of Futuna, so that their people could see the yams Jehovah grows in answer to prayer.

P II 252–254

He ended with a warning against the errand itself. An inland chief of Erromanga once came down to a feast on the shore, found that every dish was made of coconut, and carried a load of coconuts home to show his people; but he roasted them, and the charred kernels were spat out with the verdict that their own food was far better. The fault was not in the coconuts. So, said Naswai, your attempts to explain Christianity will only spoil it; a man must live as a Christian before he can show others what it is. On their return to Futuna the deputation exhibited the yam and told what had happened at Aniwa — and did not fail, Paton records, to qualify every word of it with the story of the Erromangan chief and the coconuts.

Read this beside the customary year on the Year page. Naswai’s summary of Futunese belief — no ceremonies, no crops — is an outsider’s statement of exactly the rule Copeland was breaking in his garden, and exactly the rule Gunn set down in detail thirty years later: the digging stick cut and hung in the temple, the first yam displayed on the sacred banyan, and no yam dug anywhere on the island until the priest had shown it.

P II 251–255

A Genealogy of the Gospel in Futuna · page 3 of 18

The four streams of transmission

POLYNESIA · ANEITYUM · EUROPE · FUTUNA

The four lines along which the gospel reached and then crossed the island, and the chain of hands that carried it.

Press / to search

On this page
  • The four streams
  • The line of transmission
01

The four streams

The gospel did not reach Futuna along one line. It came down four distinct channels, each with its own homeland, its own losses and its own manner of working. Throughout this record every person carries the colour of the stream he or she belongs to, so that a reader can follow one line through a century at a glance.

Polynesia

Stream I

Samoans and Rarotongans of the London Missionary Society, carried south by John Williams and his successors from 1839. They opened the island and were destroyed on it. Four of them — two men, a woman and a child — were killed at Imounga in 1843, and the district never recovered from the guilt of it. Later Polynesian teachers, Ru and Kakita, worked at Ipau from the late 1850s and, without knowing it, converted the family that would produce the first Futunese Christian.

Aneityum

Stream II

The young church on Aneityum, founded in 1852, sent its first two missionaries to Futuna in 1853 and kept the outreach alive for the better part of fifty years, in the face of apathy and open hostility. Aneityumese teachers held the island alone through the seven years when there was no European missionary at all. The greatest single figure in this record, Pastor Habena, came from that island and is buried in Futuna soil.

Europe

Stream III

The London Missionary Society first; then the Reformed Presbyterian, Free and United Free Churches of Scotland. Two resident missionaries in seventy-five years: Joseph Copeland, who broke the back of heathenism but never baptised a convert, and William Gunn, a medical missionary who arrived in 1883 and lived to see the whole island in the church.

Futuna

Stream IV

The island’s own line, and the only one that continues. It begins with the priest of Ipau and his son, who saved a teacher’s life about 1859 and joined the worship; it takes formal shape in the five baptised in May 1889; it produces its own teachers, deacons and finally, in 1932, its own ordained pastor. Everything in the other three streams exists in order to end in this one.

Plates for this page
  • Saula · John Williams · Popoina · Rev. Joseph Copeland Facing p. 4

The plates themselves, with their narratives, are on the Plates and maps page.

02

The line of transmission

Read left to right. Each strand enters at the year its people first appear on Futuna, breaks where the line was cut, and bends downward where it passed something on to the island’s own people. The three foreign strands end. The Futunese strand does not.

Polynesia Aneityum Europe Futuna × a line cut by death

The line stated in words

Set out as a descent, the transmission runs as follows. Each generation received from the one above it and, in nearly every case, paid for it.

Descent of the gospel in Futuna

John Williams, LMS, makes the first landfall (1839) and promises teachers → Apela and Samuela of Samoa are landed at Imounga (1841) under the protection of the chief Kautiama, who by interpreting at Aneityum opens that island too → the four Samoans are killed (1843) and the line is cut → Bishop Selwyn takes Saliva and Yarai to Auckland (1851), and Dr Geddie brings a chief and fourteen Futunese to see Christian Aneityum → the Aneityum church sends Waihit and Iosefa (1853), then Filipo, Tatavaka, Natuthi and others → Ru of the LMS is settled at Ipau (1859); his life is begged from the people by the priest Konafia and his son Popoina, who then join the worship → Joseph Copeland settles at Ipau (1866), gives the island a Harmony of the Gospels, and leaves without a single baptism (1881) → Tatavaka alone holds the island for seven years → Dr and Mrs Gunn arrive with the teacher Habena (1883) → Popoina, Teiau, Saula, Roroveka and Laku are baptised (May 1889) and a church is formed → Futunese teachers, then Nailo the first deacon, then the five deacons of 1905 → Habena is ordained pastor (1900) and dies in office (1916) → Aresia, teacher to the last heathen district, is ordained pastor of Futuna (1932).

Chronology, 1839–1935

NINETY-SIX YEARS

Every dated event in the record, from John Williams’ landfall to the last of the deaths.

Press / to search

01

Chronology, 1839–1935

Dates given as the sources give them. Where Gunn and Miller differ, both readings are shown.

DateEvent
17 Nov 1839The Camden reaches Futuna on a Sunday morning. Canoes come off but will not board. A Futuna chief leaps into John Williams’ boat and is taken aboard; Williams talks with him using Samoan and Rarotongan words, and the chief promises to look after any teacher settled there. The earliest recorded missionary visit to Futuna, and the first attempt to prepare the way for the gospel anywhere in the New Hebrides.
18 Nov 1839Williams lands three Polynesian teachers at Port Resolution, Tanna — possible only because the people there, being close to Aniwa, could understand him in Aniwan, which is Futunese.
20 Nov 1839Williams and James Harris are killed on Eromanga, three days after leaving Futuna. (Gunn’s introduction gives 1840.)
Mar 1841The Camden returns with the Rev. A. W. Murray aboard and lands the Samoan teachers Apela and Samuela at Herald Bay, in the district of Imounga. The chief Kautiama promises protection and sails on to Aneityum, where he interprets for the missionaries; teachers are accepted on Aneityum in consequence.
Jun 1842The Camden brings Samuela’s wife and daughter to Futuna. The teachers build a place of worship and visit the chiefs throughout the island.
1843An epidemic sweeps the southern islands. Visitors from Tanna advise the Futunese to kill their teachers as the Tannese had done. The people of Upper Imounga attack Apela, Samuela and Samuela’s daughter in their gardens; Nasaua leads. Samuela’s wife is offered her life if she will marry Nasaua and refuses; Kautiama himself takes the club and kills her, to prevent war between Upper and Lower Imounga. The four bodies are cooked, found unpalatable, buried in the sand, and the small bones made into fish-hooks. The house is burned.
Apr 1845The new LMS ship John Williams stands in. Dr George Turner and Mr Murray try to land; armed crowds on the shore, no women or children visible. Told the teachers are busy in their gardens, they sail to Aneityum and learn the truth there. Futuna is closed to the gospel for seven or eight years.
1851Bishop Selwyn takes two Futuna lads, Saliva and Yarai, to his college in Auckland. Brought home at the end of the year, neither returns. In the same year Dr John Geddie of Aneityum visits Futuna; a chief and fourteen men go back with him, are deeply impressed, and renounce heathenism — most resuming their old life once home.
Jan 1852A Futuna man takes refuge on Aneityum from a trading ship and is protected by Geddie’s small Christian band.
13 May 1852The first Christian congregation in western Polynesia is formed at Anelgauhat, Aneityum: thirteen baptised, seven of them women, and two children.
25 Oct 1853The Aneityum church sends out Waihit of Anelgauhat and Iosefa of Aname — the first native evangelists in the western Pacific. The John Williams lands them with their wives at Imatangi and Iakana. Captain Denham of H.M.S. Herald, then surveying Futuna, entertains them on board.
1854A supply boat finds Iosefa gone and all presumed lost. Geddie and Inglis appoint a replacement teacher and wife, carried over by Denham in the Herald. Iosefa in fact drifted five days with the boatman Tom to New Caledonia, went on to the Isle of Pines, and returned after five months. Waihit meanwhile follows the pigs into the bush to eat the roots they dig up.
1856Waihit takes his sick wife home to Aneityum with ten Futunese. Geddie and Inglis walk them four days through the island; some hundred discarded heathen articles are exhibited at a missionary meeting. The visitors declare their own religion wrong — and forget it on returning home.
c.1859Ru is placed at Ipau by the LMS. His chest is stolen and his life threatened. Konafia, the heathen priest of Ipau, and his son Popoina plead for him. Both then join the worship. Popoina becomes the first Futuna man to profess faith in Christ.
1860The Rev. Joseph Copeland visits Futuna for the first time.
1866The Synod at Aneityum appoints Copeland missionary of Futuna. He and Mrs Copeland settle at Ipau, on the north-east, opposite a little bay with a boat landing. Population about 1,000.
1874In Iasoa, a Futunese assistant teacher is shot at night by his own brother Namua, who had returned from Fiji to find his wife taken. The musket is never used again and lies in a cave still.
20 Jan 1876Mrs Copeland dies on Futuna, having returned there to die among the people she had served. She is buried beside her little boy and the graves of the early teachers and their wives. Fifty men cut off their long hair; fifty receive books.
1876–1883No resident missionary. Copeland returns to Sydney broken in health, pays one brief visit in 1879, and resigns; oversight passes to J. H. Lawrie of Aneityum, who manages two visits of a few weeks. One by one the Aneityumese teachers go home until only Tatavaka and his wife Nilumayan remain.
17 Apr 1883Dr William Gunn and Mrs Gunn first sight Futuna. He brings back from the June Synod a new Aneityumese teacher, Habena. About twenty worshipping people are counted.
May 1889The first five Futunese are baptised — Popoina, his wife Teiau, Saula, Roroveka and the young woman Laku — with two infant children of the teachers. In the afternoon the Lord’s Supper is celebrated; twelve communicate, the wine passed round in a plain crystal cup. Fifty years, within a few months, since Williams’ visit.
25 Dec 1889The Gunns occupy the new weatherboard mission house, built with Aneityum timber. The Futunese pay it their highest compliment: “It’s like a house of the gods!”
1890The first Christian marriage on Futuna: the widowed Habena marries Laku, Mrs Gunn’s house-girl. The whole island looks on. Popoina’s verdict: “It has come to stay.” Tatavaka goes home after twenty years’ service and Natuthi after his wife Nanima’s death; Popoina and Saula become the first Futunese teachers.
Early 1890Professor Henry Drummond calls at Futuna in the Dayspring and remarks that what he saw there helped him to understand the Incarnation.
3 Feb 1892The new church at Ipau is opened; it cost £175 and took two years to pay off. Popoina and Habena give the addresses.
Jan–Apr 1893The dysentery epidemic. The labour vessel Empreza lands returning Queensland labourers, among them a woman and a sick half-caste child. Saloki, Popoina’s grand-daughter and the Gunn children’s former nurse, makes herself the child’s nurse and is the first to die. In three months 133 people die — nearly a third of the island. Among them the two Futunese teachers, Popoina and Saula, and the Gunns’ daughters Connie and Madgie. Habena and Laku escape untouched.
1893The first Futunese go out as missionaries to another island, to Ambrym under Dr Lamb.
23 Aug 1893Willie Gunn, the only son, is drowned in shallow water beside the boats on Aneityum. His gravestone reads: Sweet wee Willie landed in Heaven August 23 1893.
1893–1895The Gunns on furlough in Scotland. Habena takes charge at Ipau and settles Mangau as teacher in Isia; Nailo and others assist. Mr Lawrie spends a month and admits several new members; Mr Copeland lands on a visit and preaches in Futunese. Gunn is ordained a minister in 1894.
1895–1898A small printing press is set up in a lean-to eleven feet by five off the church verandah. Almanacs, Jonah, a hymn-book of one hundred hymns, and 230 bound copies of the General Epistles are printed on the island. Type had to be ordered from Scotland: there were not enough letter k’s for a single page of Futunese.
1897Circumcision is banished from the Christian districts and Christian marriage becomes the law. Forau, long blamed as a wind-maker, hands in his sacred stone and is the only new member admitted at the close of the year. In the same year Epeteneto of Aname becomes the first ordained pastor in the islands, the precedent for Habena.
Oct 1899Measles. Yaupa, the oldest man on Futuna and perhaps in the Pacific, dies of it; Gunn reckoned him fully 130 years old. A magic-lantern exhibition at Ipau finally draws the heathen of Imounga down to the mission.
1900A substantial church is built on the sacred marae at Imounga, seventy workers passing the timber up the cliff “like ants”. In September Habena is ordained pastor of Futuna at Ipau by the Rev. William Watt of Tanna and the Rev. G. B. Inglis of New Zealand; the Burns Philp steamer waits offshore four hours for the service. Three pairs of hands are laid on his head.
1901Offered Gunn’s own coat if he will come to church, the chief Sarashi refuses; his elder brother Sengia takes it and follows the party to church, wearing the coat while Gunn preaches without one.
1905Five deacons ordained: Nauni the eldest, Forau of Iasoa, Kavahe, Aresia, and Teitoka the youngest. At the Gunns’ farewell feast the Imoungans appear with scraps of clothing, shake hands, and troop into the Ipau church. “So, after waiting twenty-three years, God in His own good time and way softened their hard hearts.”
1906The last of the heathen come into the church. Futuna is reckoned a Christian island. Severe drought that year; the trees withered and “the land died; the people only lived”. Sarashi never made the break, and died of tuberculosis a heathen.
1907–08Only four men remain outside the worship. A deacon of chiefly rank is elected chief of the whole of Futuna — the first such appointment in some fifty years. Two Futunese teachers are sent out as missionaries to other islands. The chiefs uproot and destroy about two boat-loads of kava.
1912The Epistles from Galatians to Revelation, laid aside after the 1893 epidemic, are printed in Sydney and put into the people’s hands.
1913–14Gunn writes The Gospel in Futuna in 1913; Hodder & Stoughton publish it in London in 1914. Since 1889, 150 people have been admitted to the Lord’s Supper on profession of faith and about 100 children baptised.
1916Pastor Habena dies, aged about sixty-eight, and is buried in the old mission cemetery at Ipau. Synod records a Memorial Minute the following year.
1917A hurricane brings down the mission churches and houses on Aneityum and Futuna. Gunn appoints three new deacons and retires in March after thirty-four years. The southern islands pass to the Rev. Thomson Macmillan of Tanna, who can reach them only rarely.
1924Gunn publishes Heralds of Dawn, a book of portraits of the prominent Futunese of his time.
1931Synod thanks Gunn for completing the New Testament in Futunese — lacking only Romans and 1 and 2 Corinthians.
1932Mrs Gunn dies. Aresia is ordained pastor of Futuna.
9 Jun 1935Dr William Gunn dies on a Sunday at Roseville, Sydney, and is buried the next day. He had been appointed to Futuna fifty-two years before.

The Polynesian teachers

Apela

also Apela of SamoaSamoaMartyr
OriginSamoa
StationImounga, Futuna
On FutunaMarch 1841 – 1843
DiedClubbed to death, 1843

One of the two Samoan teachers of the London Missionary Society landed at Herald Bay by the Camden in March 1841, in fulfilment of John Williams’ promise to the Futuna chief eighteen months earlier. With Samuela he built a place of worship and went round the chiefs of the island urging them to receive “the worship”. For a time all went well.

When an epidemic struck the southern islands late in 1842, the teachers were blamed for making the sickness. Men from Tanna, visiting Futuna, boasted that they had stopped their own epidemic by killing their teachers, and advised the Futunese to do the same. Apela was clubbed to death in the bush garden alongside Samuela.

GF 6–8 · L I 27–28

Samuela

SamoaMartyr
OriginSamoa
StationImounga, Futuna
On FutunaMarch 1841 – 1843
DiedSpeared, then clubbed, 1843

Landed with Apela in March 1841. His wife and daughter were brought out to join him by the Camden in June 1842, and the whole family was killed in 1843. Samuela was transfixed with a spear before being clubbed. The murderers then went on to the teachers’ premises to complete their work, rifled the boxes and burned the house; at their dances afterwards the people decked themselves in the teachers’ clothing.

Family: wife (name not recorded) and one daughter, both killed with him. All four bodies were cooked, found not to suit the Futunese taste, buried in the sand, and the small bones made into fish-hooks. “Thus Futuna was early consecrated by the blood of the martyred teachers.”

GF 6–8 · L I 27–28

Samuela’s wife

name not recordedSamoaMartyr
OriginSamoa
ArrivedJune 1842
DiedClubbed by Kautiama, 1843
RecordName not preserved in any source

Left at the house when the others went to the gardens. The excited warriors found her alone. Nasaua, their leader, offered to spare her if she would become his wife; she recoiled, then held out an axe and other articles for her life, and they were refused. Kautiama and the people of Lower Imounga had wished to protect the Samoans, but to prevent war between the two halves of his district Kautiama took the club from Nasaua’s hand and killed her himself, taking the guilt of the whole affair upon his own head.

GF 7 · L I 28

Samuela’s daughter

name not recordedSamoaMartyr
OriginSamoa
AgeA child
DiedClubbed to death, 1843
NoteAccounts of her death differ slightly

Miller places her in the garden with her father and Apela; Gunn writes that the child was left alone and was not spared, because it was the custom in heathenism to kill everyone related to a disease-maker. The two accounts agree that she was killed and that she was a child. She is the fourth of the Futuna martyrs.

GF 7–8 · L I 28

Ru

Polynesia · LMS
OriginPolynesian teacher of the LMS
StationIpau, north-east Futuna
Placed1859
SignificanceOccasion of the first Futunese conversion

Ru is the pivot of this whole record, though almost nothing is known of him. Settled at Ipau in 1859, he had his chest of personal goods stolen and would have been killed; but Konafia, the heathen priest of Ipau, and his son Popoina pleaded for his life to be spared. The two Futuna men then joined the worship themselves, and Popoina became the first Futuna man to profess faith in Christ. Every Futunese Christian in this record descends, spiritually, from the sparing of Ru.

He was still on the island when Dr Paton passed through on his way to Synod, and pleaded with him to stay: “Me too much love you. Me do anything for you.”

L I 30–31 · GF 15

Kakita

Rarotonga
OriginRarotonga
RoleTeacher on Futuna
PeriodLater Polynesian phase, c.1850s–60s
RecordName only; no station given

Named by Miller as one of the two later Polynesian teachers on Futuna whose names are known, the other being Ru. Nothing further is recorded of his work, his station or his end.

L I 30

Filipo

Origin not stated
OriginNot stated in the sources
StationsIpau, then Upper Imounga
PeriodAfter 1853
IncidentHis house burned over his head

“A teacher who arrived later”, placed first at Ipau — where the mission house afterwards stood — and then in Upper Imounga, the district where the Samoans had been killed. The Futunese burned his house over his head, believing that a friend from Aneityum staying with him was making disease. Both escaped. Gunn names him among the teachers sent in the Aneityumese phase, but does not state his island; his name is Polynesian in form. This record therefore leaves his origin open.

GF 10–11

The Aneityumese teachers and pastors

Aneityum, forty miles to the south-west, was the nursery of the whole Vanuatu church. Its congregation was formed in May 1852, and within eighteen months it was sending missionaries of its own to a hostile island. Teachers there received no wages, only a yearly present of clothing; those serving on other islands were paid five pounds a year from the Native Teachers’ Fund. Between twenty and thirty Aneityumese couples were serving abroad in any given year.

Waihit

of AnelgauhatAneityum
OriginAnelgauhat, south Aneityum
Before conversionChief and sacred man of the sea
Sent25 October 1853
StationsImatangi and Iakana, south-west Futuna

One of the first converts on Aneityum, and before that a sacred man of the sea, fierce and cruel, feared for his power in heathenism. He kept the respect due to his office as a chief, and that gave him a measure of protection on Futuna. With Iosefa he was set apart in 1852 and sent out on 25 October 1853 — a date Miller calls one to be remembered in the Presbyterian Church of the New Hebrides. The two were the Barnabas and Saul of the Aneityum church, and the first native evangelists in the western Pacific.

They were treated as enemies and as slaves. Food planted in their gardens was stolen at night by men and women alike as soon as it was ripe. Refused food outright, Waihit followed the pigs into the bush to eat the roots they dug up, and often tightened his belt to allay the pangs of hunger. When a worshipping chief of Imatangi stayed away long on a visit to Aneityum, Waihit was accused of raising a storm to drown him and was on the point of embarking for home when the mission vessel arrived, bringing the chief back.

He stood against the Futuna custom of human sacrifice in time of famine, and was threatened with death for it. His answer has survived: “Oh, I am not afraid. They may kill my body, but they cannot touch my soul!” In 1856 he took his sick wife home to Aneityum with ten Futunese, whom Geddie and Inglis walked four days through the island to show them what the gospel had done there.

Family: a wife, who went with him to Futuna in 1853 and whose illness brought him home in 1856. Her name is not recorded.

GF 9–12 · L I 93–94

Iosefa

Yosefa · of AnameAneityum
OriginAname, north Aneityum
RankOf a high family
Sent25 October 1853
StationsImatangi and Iakana

Described as a tried, faithful and promising young man; his high birth, like Waihit’s chieftainship, gave him some protection. Starved by the Futunese along with his colleague, he resolved in 1854 to go back to Aneityum for food. The white man Tom, a naturalised Futunese and a good boatman, undertook to take him. A strong wind and heavy sea beat them off; Tom tied the oars in a bundle, made them fast to the bow and let the boat drift. For five days they drifted with a few uncooked yams for food, and made New Caledonia, two hundred miles away. From there they went on to the Isle of Pines, were kindly treated by an English family who had once lived on Aneityum, and after five months a trading vessel landed them back on Futuna.

Meanwhile the boat sent from Aneityum with supplies had returned with the news that Iosefa had left ten days before it arrived. Concluding that all were lost, Geddie and Inglis appointed another teacher and his wife in his place, and Captain Denham carried them across in H.M.S. Herald.

Family: a wife, landed with him in 1853; name not recorded.

GF 9–11 · L I 93

Tatavaka

Aneityum
OriginAneityum
Service on Futunac.1870 – 1890, twenty years
WifeNilumayan
DistinctionHeld the island alone, 1876–1883

The teacher who kept Futuna. When Mrs Copeland died in 1876 and her husband went back to Sydney broken in health, the Aneityumese teachers went home one by one until Tatavaka and his wife Nilumayan were the only couple left. For seven years, with no resident missionary and only two short visits from Mr Lawrie, Tatavaka maintained the Sabbath and week-day services with the help of Popoina and two or three others. It was Tatavaka and Nilumayan who welcomed the Gunns ashore in April 1883.

He was Gunn’s early informant on what was happening among the people, and it was Tatavaka who brought him the news — “The ceremony is to be performed to-morrow on five lads; and Teitoka, the son of Yarai, and heir of Popoina, is one of them.” He returned to Aneityum in 1890, after twenty years of missionary service, once the first Futunese teachers were able to take over two of the four schools.

GF 29, 48, 147 · L IV 162, 170

Nilumayan

Aneityum
OriginAneityum
RoleTeacher’s wife, Futuna
PeriodTo 1890
HusbandTatavaka

Wife of Tatavaka and, with him, the last of the Aneityumese couples on Futuna through the vacant years. Miller records that theirs was the one couple remaining to welcome the Gunns in 1883.

L IV 162

Natuthi

Aneityum
OriginAneityum
RoleTeacher, Futuna
Returned home1890, after his wife’s death
WifeNanima, died on Futuna

One of the Aneityumese teachers of Gunn’s early years. He tried to open meetings with the heathen of Imounga by prayer; when he opened his eyes, his audience had gone. His wife Nanima died on Futuna and is among the teachers’ wives buried there. He went home in 1890 when the first two Futunese teachers were able to relieve him.

Family: wife Nanima, died on Futuna and buried in the mission enclosure at Ipau.

GF 125 · L IV 170

Habena

Pastor of FutunaAneityum
BornAbout 1848, north Aneityum
On Futuna1883 – 1916, thirty-three years
Ordained pastorSeptember 1900, at Ipau
Died1916, aged about 68; buried Ipau

The central figure of this record after Gunn himself, and by Gunn’s own judgement the most devoted and single-hearted native Christian he knew in the New Hebrides.

Birth and early life. His mother threw him out into the bush as an infant and left him to die; his father, hearing of it, went and found the child and saved him. He grew up in north Aneityum under Dr Inglis, and was baptised on the vows of his newly converted father while Joseph Copeland had charge of Aname, between 1860 and 1863 — a link with the first missionary to Futuna that may well have kindled his desire to serve there. In his vigorous youth he joined a whaling station, and later helped to build the mission houses on Eromanga and Tanna, which proved valuable experience afterwards. He was not subject to malaria.

On Futuna. He came over with Dr Gunn in 1883, described then as a tall, strapping, dignified young chief of excellent character and sterling worth, and he never left. He took charge of the school and the Sabbath services at Ipau during the Gunns’ furlough, settled Mangau as teacher in Isia, and gave one of the two addresses at the opening of the new Ipau church in February 1892. He and Laku were among the very few who did not contract the dysentery in 1893. He acted as elder for years before being formally set apart, and directed the teachers, who took their orders from him and obeyed him.

Ordination. Gunn, now missionary of two islands and absent from Futuna for months of every year, conceived the idea of asking Synod to appoint pastors — the first in the history of the Vanuatu church. Epeteneto of Aname was ordained in 1897, and Gunn took Habena with him to that Synod to show him what lay ahead. Synod approved Habena’s ordination in 1900, and it took place at Ipau that September, the Rev. William Watt of Tanna and the Rev. G. B. Inglis of New Zealand taking the service while the Burns Philp ship waited four hours offshore. The usual questions were dispensed with, since pastor-elect and people had already promised before the missionary to help each other; prayer was offered in Futunese and three pairs of hands laid on his head. He conducted marriages, dispensed the sacraments, directed and instructed the teachers, led the evangelism and exercised the discipline.

Health and death. He did not keep good health, and much of his long service was hindered by difficulty in getting about a very steep island; sometimes, unable to walk to church, he would crawl there. Gunn often returned to Futuna to find him so ill he despaired of his life, and after a few weeks’ treatment found him back at work. He never spoke of retirement. Urged by the people of Aneityum to come home and take the position of head chief, he firmly declined; but he returned there for three months in 1908 to steady the work after Epeteneto’s death. He died in 1916, aged about sixty-eight, and was buried in the old mission cemetery at Ipau. His years of service and Dr Gunn’s were almost exactly the same in length.

Family: first wife Annie, an Aneityumese, who died on Futuna. He then married Laku, a Futunese, in 1890 — the first Christian marriage on the island. The Aneityumese were upset that he had not married one of their own. They had five children, brought up, Gunn wrote, with devout care, and all consistent church members. His wife was, Gunn said, a terror to evildoers and easily the most influential woman on the island; when he was too weak to walk to the service she once carried him there on her back and home again.

Habena was the most devoted and single-hearted native Christian I have known in the New Hebrides. He lived for one object — to bring the natives to Christ, and build them up in the faith. His religion was deep and genuine. He grew in grace year by year. Dr William Gunn, Heralds of Dawn, p.56
GF 39, 124, 151–152 · HD 39–56 · L IV 153, 178–181

Annie

Aneityum
OriginAneityum
RoleTeacher’s wife on Futuna
DiedOn Futuna, before 1890
HusbandHabena

Habena’s first wife, who came with him from Aneityum and died on Futuna. Her death made possible the marriage that became the island’s first Christian wedding.

L IV 170

Epeteneto

Pastor of north AneityumAneityum
OriginAname, north Aneityum
Ordained1897 — the first pastor in these islands
Died13 March 1905, aged 71
ServiceTeacher 30 years, pastor over 7

Included here because his ordination was the precedent on which Habena’s rested. Gunn established with the 1897 ordination that a native pastorate was a genuine step forward, and on that basis moved Synod to sanction Habena’s ordination three years later. Epeteneto was head teacher at Anelgauhat for nineteen of his thirty years as a teacher. Shortly before his death Gunn brought elders from Anelgauhat and administered communion in his house; after partaking he said his farewell: “Jesus is with me. He is mine, and I am His. He is in me, and I am in Him.” His people subscribed for a memorial tablet beside the pulpit.

Family: eleven children, none of whom survived him. All died under the age of thirteen or fourteen.

L IV 153, 180

The European missionaries and visitors

Rev. John Williams

the Apostle of the South SeasLondon Missionary Society
SocietyLondon Missionary Society
At FutunaSunday 17 November 1839
KilledEromanga, 20 November 1839
VesselThe Camden

Williams brought twelve Polynesian teachers south on the Camden, writing on the eve of his arrival that the approaching week was to him the most important of his life. Futuna was reached on a Sunday morning. Canoes came off from the rocky island but their occupants would not board; the ship’s boat was lowered, a canoe came alongside, and a Futuna chief leapt into the boat and asked to be taken aboard. There Williams talked with him using Samoan and Rarotongan words, and the chief promised to look after any teacher who might be settled. Williams had none to spare, but gave them to understand he would come back.

He went on to Port Resolution on Tanna, where the people, being near neighbours of Aniwa, could follow him in Aniwan — the same tongue as Futunese — and he landed three teachers. At Eromanga, three days after leaving Futuna, the language was different again; he could not explain his errand, and he and James Harris were killed there. Williams never saw Futuna again, but the LMS leaders remembered his pledge to the Futuna chief and honoured it.

GF 4–6 · L I 26–27

Rev. A. W. Murray

London Missionary Society
SocietyLondon Missionary Society, from Samoa
At FutunaMarch 1841; again April 1845
WroteMissions in Western Polynesia
RoleLanded the first teachers

Aboard the Camden in March 1841 when Apela and Samuela were settled at Imounga, and aboard the John Williams in April 1845 when, with Dr Turner, he tried to land and learn what had become of them. Told the teachers were in their gardens, the two waited hours in vain, then attempted a landing at Ipau; the threatening appearance of the armed natives forced the boat to back out, and with night coming on and a heavy sea they returned to the ship with sad hearts. He had a long association with the New Hebrides Mission and wrote the history of the LMS work in western Polynesia, which Gunn cites.

GF 6, 8 · L I 27–28

Dr George Turner

London Missionary Society
SocietyLondon Missionary Society
At FutunaApril 1845
EarlierTanna, 1842, with Nisbet
NoteGunn’s informant on the 1845 landing

With Murray on the attempted landing of 1845. Gunn adds a correcting footnote of his own: the missionaries were evidently unaware that the teachers had been settled in Imounga, since Dr Turner told him personally that they were stationed at the present mission landing at Ipau.

GF 8 n.1 · L I 34–35

Bishop G. A. Selwyn

Melanesian Mission
MissionMelanesian Mission, Auckland
At Futuna1851
TookSaliva and Yarai to his college
ResultNeither lad returned to Auckland

Visited Futuna during the years when the island was closed to the gospel after the murders, and obtained two lads for his college in Auckland for natives of Melanesia. They were brought home at the end of the year to see their friends and did not care to go back. Yarai, the duller pupil, later sold Copeland the land for the mission house and became the first Futunese to give up an important heathen ceremony.

GF 8–9

Rev. Dr John Geddie

Aneityum
StationAnelgauhat, Aneityum, from 1848
At Futuna1851
FormedThe first church in western Polynesia, 1852
RoleSent Waihit and Iosefa, 1853

Geddie visited Futuna in 1851 and took a chief and fourteen Futunese back to Aneityum to see what the gospel had done there. They were so impressed that they renounced heathenism at once; most resumed their old life on returning home. In January 1852 he sheltered a Futuna man who had taken refuge from a trading ship, hoping this might one day reopen the way. He formed the first congregation at Anelgauhat on 13 May 1852, and with the Aneityum church sent Waihit and Iosefa to Futuna the following year. In 1854, believing Iosefa lost at sea, he and Inglis appointed a replacement.

GF 9–10 · L I 81, 93

Rev. Dr John Inglis

Aneityum
StationAname, Aneityum, 1852–1879
WroteBible Illustrations from the New Hebrides
Role in this recordSent and supervised the Futuna teachers
ConnectionHabena grew up under his ministry

With Geddie he appointed the replacement teacher in 1854 and conducted the four-day tour of Christian Aneityum for the ten Futunese visitors in 1856. Habena grew up in north Aneityum under him. Inglis’s remark on the first Aneityumese converts sets the mission’s whole policy of unhurried admission, which explains why Futuna waited so long for its first baptism: “Our first converts were always our best. They joined us from conviction. Intellectually and morally they were the best men; and they were the longest under instruction.”

GF 6, 11–12 · L I 81–82

Captain Denham

Royal Navy
ShipH.M.S. Herald
At Futuna1853–1854
WorkSurveying the island
ServiceCarried and entertained the teachers

Engaged in surveying Futuna when Waihit and Iosefa were landed in 1853. He took a warm interest in mission work: after the teachers were settled he entertained them on board, and the following year he carried the replacement teacher and his wife across from Aneityum in the Herald. Herald Bay, where the Samoan teachers had been landed in 1841, carries the ship’s name.

GF 9–10

Rev. Joseph Copeland

Reformed Presbyterian Church
Joined the Mission1858
StationsTanna; Aneityum (Aname, 1860–63); Futuna 1866–1881
First visit to Futuna1860
DiedStrathfield, near Sydney, 1908

The first resident missionary on Futuna, and in some ways the most thankless post in the group. He settled with his wife at Ipau in 1866, on the north-east of the island opposite a little bay with a boat landing, in a population of about a thousand. He learned the language and put a Harmony of the Gospels into the people’s hands in Futunese, together with a collection of hymns. He stopped fights, endured constant theft, watched the labour traffic carry off his young men, and saw his church burned.

He never baptised a convert. Under the mission’s policy of unhurried admission — which Miller says may in this case have been carried too far — no church was formed and no one was ready. His own summary of 1875 is characteristically exact: “They are like a house built on the sand, good enough for good weather, but not for a time of storm and trial. Heathenism is not particularly vigorous, but this is not because Christianity is strong.” Yet Gunn judged that when Copeland left, the backbone of heathenism was broken and Christianity would have triumphed in a few more years. The Futunese verdict was simply, “Mr Copeland was wise and clever with us.”

He was a scholar and a missionary; careful and cautious, experienced in the ways of the people and judicious in dealing with them. After resigning he served the Presbyterian Church of New South Wales for years as editor of its weekly periodical, kept up his interest in the group, revisited it several times, and gave Gunn help and advice which Gunn gratefully records. On a visit during Gunn’s furlough he landed at his old station while the people were at school; instead of rushing out to trade they went on with their morning worship, and he addressed them in their own tongue.

Family: married in 1863 the widow of S. F. Johnston. She died on Futuna 20 January 1876. A little son is buried beside her at Ipau. Two children survived, for whose sake he returned to Sydney.

GF 14–30 · L I 31, 81, 190 · L IV 160–162

Mrs Copeland

formerly the widow of S. F. JohnstonScotland
Married Copeland1863
ServedTanna, Aneityum, then Futuna
DiedFutuna, 20 January 1876
BuriedMission enclosure, Ipau

“A true and earnest missionary, first in Tanna and Aneityum, then in Futuna.” Some of her Aneityum pupils were still alive in Gunn’s day and remembered her teaching gratefully. When she learned that recovery was hopeless she returned to Futuna to die among the people for whom she had so long laboured. Her body was laid beside that of her little boy in the enclosure outside the mission premises, near the graves of the teachers and their wives. It was she who described the Futunese in a phrase Gunn kept using: they were “like links in a chain, and they did not want any of the links to fall out” — which is why no one dared to break from heathenism alone.

GF 28–29, 81 · L I 190

Rev. J. H. Lawrie

Free Church of Scotland
StationAneityum, 1879–1892
FutunaIn charge 1879–1883; visits during Gunn’s furloughs
ReceivedAs elder and evangelist; later ordained
NoteBegan annual three-day conferences for church leaders

Given oversight of Futuna from 1879, though effective supervision from Aneityum was out of the question; he managed two useful visits of a few weeks each before the Gunns arrived. During the Gunns’ Scottish furlough he spent a month with the Futunese and admitted several new members. He tried once to read to an Imoungan who had come to barter and the man leaped over the fence as if a musket had been presented at him.

GF 30, 123, 125 · L IV 139, 162

Rev. Dr William Gunn

MissiFree / United Free Church of Scotland
Born1853, Helmsdale, Caithness, Scotland
On Futuna17 April 1883 – March 1917
DistinctionFirst medical missionary of the New Hebrides Mission
DiedSunday 9 June 1935, Roseville, Sydney

Gunn is at once the chief actor and the chief witness of this record; almost everything known about the Futunese named here is known because he wrote it down. A fuller account of his life is given on the authors page.

He arrived a layman — welcomed to the Synod in June 1883 as an elder and appointed to Futuna, not ordained a minister until 1894 while on furlough in Scotland. He found about twenty worshipping people. He was a doctor, a translator, a printer, a builder, a photographer and a cartographer, and from 1893 he carried Aneityum as well as Futuna, spending only four or five months of the year on each. He translated the greater part of the New Testament into Futunese, set up a hand press in a lean-to off the church verandah, produced the mission almanac and the 1904 mission map, and left a photographic record of the islands that is now the principal pictorial source for this period.

The 1893 epidemic cost him two daughters within a week and, later that year, his only son. He stayed twenty-four more years. His summing-up in 1913 was measured rather than triumphant: quarrelling had nearly ceased, the people had become honest and trustworthy, impure language was seldom heard, husbands trusted their wives, and family worship was in almost every house.

Family: married a Miss Matheson. Children: Connie (died of dysentery, Futuna, 1893, aged about eight), Madgie (died six days later, aged six years and eight months), Willie (drowned on Aneityum, 23 August 1893, aged about five years and eight months at the time of his sisters’ deaths), and Ruth, the youngest, who survived the epidemic and had to learn again to sit, stand, crawl and walk. Mrs Gunn died in 1932.

GF, throughout · L IV 160–185

Mrs Gunn

née MathesonScotland
On Futuna1883 – 1917
WorkHouse-girls, women’s classes, day schools
Died1932
NoteSynod recorded its sympathy, 1932

Her first sight of Futuna produced the only recorded verdict on it that was not about its barrenness: “How beautiful it is!” She trained the house-girls — Laku, Saloki, Mou and others — who became the best scholars on the island and afterwards helpers in the schools, and ran a young women’s class that memorised Scripture in Futunese. She promised a new dress to any who could repeat the book of Jonah correctly and had to make twelve of them. Some learned about a hundred pages of Copeland’s Harmony of the Gospels, the General Epistles and parts of Acts with no prize offered at all.

Gunn wrote that the women were harder to help than the men — slower to learn to read, less quick to grasp the message, more wedded to old custom — and that this made the work of the house-girls the more important. It was Mrs Gunn who sat with the dying Popoina and brought back his last testimony.

GF 94–102, 119 · L IV 162, 169–170, 184

Rev. Dr John G. Paton

Tanna and Aniwa

At FutunaVisits, including April 1889
LanguagePreached to the Futunese in Aniwan
FoundedThe Native Teachers’ Fund, 1863

Paton pressed on the Futunese, in their sister dialect of Aniwan, the claims of the gospel; on one such visit in April 1889, storm-bound four days, the newly built church was filled and the largest congregation yet seen on Futuna sat and stood inside and out. It was Paton whom Ru begged to stay on the island. Paton’s 1863 Native Teachers’ Fund paid the five pounds a year that supported island teachers serving away from home. His visit to Wick in the same year made a deep impression on a Scottish boy of ten named William Gunn.

GF 15, 81–82 · L IV 160

The sensitive Drummond was heard to remark that what he saw on Futuna helped him to understand the Incarnation. His impressions are printed in Sir George Adam Smith’s biography.

L IV 169

Rev. William Watt & Rev. G. B. Inglis

Tanna · New Zealand

Watt of Kwamera, Tanna, and G. B. Inglis of New Zealand took the service at which Habena was set apart as pastor of Futuna — only the second such ordination in the history of the church in these islands. Two short addresses were translated from English into Futunese; there was no other transport, so the Burns Philp ship lay off the island until it was done.

GF 151 · L IV 180

Rev. Thomson Macmillan

Presbyterian Church of South Australia
