After Gunn’s retirement Synod placed Aneityum, Futuna and Eromanga under Macmillan, who reached them on the British District Agent’s launch in October 1918. Adequate supervision at such a distance was impossible, and Futuna “sank back into a period of routine Christian life, with little outside encouragement and growing problems” until the island produced its own ordained pastor in 1932.

L IV 156, 183

“Tom”

a naturalised FutuneseEuropean, island unknown
OriginUnknown; mysteriously landed on Futuna
StatusNaturalised Futunese; spoke the language
FeatDrifted five days to New Caledonia with Iosefa, 1854
DiedOn Futuna, of a gun accident

A white man landed on the island some years before 1854 in circumstances no one recorded. He acquired the language, obtained a wife from the Futunese, and lived there for a number of years. He was a good boatman, and it was he who undertook to carry the starving Iosefa back to Aneityum and, when wind and sea beat them off, tied the oars in a bundle to the bow and let the boat drift — five days on a few uncooked yams to New Caledonia. He died as the result of a gun accident.

Family: a Futunese wife and children. Gunn records that one of his family was still alive at the time of writing and had recently been received into the membership of the church — the one part-European line in the Futuna congregation.

GF 10

The Futunese

The heart of the record. Names are given in Gunn’s spelling, with Miller’s variants noted where they differ. Chiefs are marked as such; a chief on Futuna held real authority over his district, and the record shows repeatedly that ordinary people would not enter the church against their chief’s wish.

Kautiama

FutunaChief of Imounga
DistrictImounga, north-west
RankChief; head of Lower Imounga
Period1841 – his death, a heathen
SonsSengia and Sarashi, both head chiefs after him

Kautiama is the most consequential Futunese of the first generation and the most tragic. When the Camden came in March 1841 he received Apela and Samuela and promised to protect their lives. He then sailed with the ship to Aneityum, taking a crowd of his people laden with mats and baskets for trade, and there interpreted the missionaries’ errand to the Aneityumese, who recognised friends aboard and welcomed the teachers. Through Kautiama, a man of Futuna, teachers were accepted on both islands.

Two years later the same man undid it. The people of Lower Imounga, his own, had wished to protect the Samoans; but rather than let war break out between Upper and Lower Imounga he took the club from Nasaua’s hand and killed Samuela’s wife himself, and so took the responsibility for all four murders upon himself. By that act, Gunn writes, he undid all the good he had done, and Imounga became one of the very hardest places in all the New Hebrides to win for Christ. Kautiama lived and died a heathen. Those implicated in the murders all died inveterate heathen, and the guilt of it inhibited every effort in that district for sixty years.

Sons: Sengia, the elder, and Sarashi, the younger and more energetic — joint head chiefs of Imounga in Gunn’s day, and the two men on whom the last resistance of heathen Futuna rested. Sengia entered the church about 1901; Sarashi never did.

GF 6–8, 108, 152–153 · L I 27–28 · L IV 176

Nasaua

Futuna
DistrictUpper Imounga
RoleLeader of the murderers, 1843
ActOffered Samuela’s wife her life for marriage
EndNot recorded; died a heathen

Led the armed party of Upper Imounga that killed the Samoan teachers, and offered Samuela’s wife her life on condition she became his wife. Refused, and refusing her gifts as well, he raised the club — and Kautiama took it out of his hand.

GF 7 · L I 28

Saliva

Futuna
Taken to Auckland1851, by Bishop Selwyn
AttainmentLearned to read and speak a little English
LaterWent to Fiji
DiedKilled in a quarrel, in Fiji

One of the two lads taken by Selwyn to his Auckland college for Melanesians. Brought home at the end of the year to see his friends, he did not care to go back, and stayed on Futuna. He was the abler of the pair and had learned some English, but he afterwards went to Fiji and was killed there in a quarrel.

GF 8–9

Yarai

FutunaChief
DistrictIpau
Taken to Auckland1851, with Saliva
SoldThe mission house land to Copeland
DistinctionFirst Futunese to give up an important heathen ceremony

“A dull pupil” at Selwyn’s college and no scholar afterwards, but two acts make him one of the pivots of this history. When the missionary came, Yarai sold him the land for his house — the ground at Ipau on which everything else was built. And many years later he was the first Futunese to give up an important heathen ceremony, breaking a hold that no argument had shifted.

His course was not straight. Gunn records him as one of the chiefs who swore he had no part in a proposed heathen ceremony while in fact leading it, and who then explained the initiation of his own son with, “Missi, I could not stop it: they stole him from me!” He went about naked except near the mission premises. He was also the man Gunn could rely on to make the arrowroot work happen, and who could be shamed into staying with it.

Sons: Nailo, who became the first deacon ordained on Futuna, and Teitoka, heir of Popoina, deacon of 1905 and the best scholar on the island. Both of Yarai’s sons entered the ministry of the church he had resisted.

GF 8–9, 48–49, 67

Konafia

FutunaPriest of Ipau
DistrictIpau
OfficeHeathen priest — the sacred man of the district
Actc.1859, saved the life of the teacher Ru
AfterJoined the worship

The heathen priest of Ipau. When the people stole Ru’s chest and would have killed him, Konafia and his son Popoina pleaded for the teacher’s life; and having saved him, both men joined the worship. That a district’s sacred man should be the one to protect the Christian teacher, and then follow him, is the hinge on which the Futunese line turns. Konafia is the earliest named ancestor in the Futunese Christian genealogy.

Son: Popoina, the first Futuna man to profess faith in Christ.

L I 30–31

Popoina

FutunaFirst convert · Chief
FatherKonafia, priest of Ipau
DistrictIpau
First professed faithc.1860s, under Copeland
Died1893, in the dysentery epidemic

The first Futuna man to profess faith in Christ. Having with his father begged Ru’s life, he joined the worship and became, in Copeland’s time, the first of his people to profess. He was a chief, and for thirty years the pivot of the Christian party at Ipau; with Tatavaka he kept the services going through the seven vacant years after 1876.

The struggle. His course was long and mixed, and Gunn does not conceal it. He wore a band of shells round his arm and other marks of heathenism to ensure success in fishing; he complained that the missionary had not paid them for worshipping; he was a leader in a heathen ceremony he had denied all part in. Then he changed. He broke from the feasts one at a time, against pressure from Nauni — “Why does Popoina leave us? If we continue feasting, let us all do it” — and he bravely cut down a branch of the sacred banyan himself, and handed Gunn his own sacred fishing stones.

Work. He was Gunn’s most dependable informant in translation, urging brevity and insisting on accuracy of idiom and grammar; the older Futunese orators spoke a kind of parabolic language, and Popoina helped shift the translations into speech everyone could follow. He was one of the first two Futunese teachers, and gave one of the two addresses at the opening of the new church at Ipau on 3 February 1892. Asked what he made of the island’s first Christian wedding, he gave the verdict that Gunn quoted for the rest of his life: “It has come to stay.”

Death. Away in the steamer when his grand-daughter Saloki died, he returned to be stunned by the news, helped in the mission kitchen for some days, and then said, “I must go away, for I am sick myself.” A week later he sent for the Gunns to say goodbye. Asked whether Jesus was near him, he answered: “He is with me. He is leading me by the narrow way to heaven. Tell Missi that I am trusting in Jesus.” Before he died Anapapo came to see him, and Popoina handed him his coat: “I leave my coat to you, as Elijah left his mantle with Elisha. If you obey the Good Word you will be worthy of it.” He was buried beside Saloki, and as they laid him in the grave the breeze carried the sound of “Rock of Ages”, sung in Futunese.

Family: father Konafia; wife Teiau, the first Futunese woman to break from heathenism; daughter Yalima; grand-daughter Saloki, his favourite, who died in the same epidemic weeks before him. His heir was Teitoka, son of Yarai — an inheritance passing outside the direct male line, in the Futunese manner.

GF 48–53, 80–83, 114–119 · L I 31 · L IV 170–176

Teiau

FutunaFirst woman convert
HusbandPopoina
DistrictsIpau; then Iasoa as a teacher
BaptisedMay 1889, one of the first five
DistinctionFirst woman on Futuna to break from heathenism

Teiau was the first woman on Futuna to break from heathenism, and after she and Laku became Christians the number of women members rose at every communion. She relinquished heathenism and wished to serve Jesus, and was baptised with her husband in May 1889. She was a good scholar and took a full share of the teaching at Iasoa, where she and Saula were stationed and where the people were delighted with them both. When Saula died in the 1893 epidemic she returned to Ipau.

GF 82, 108, 119 · L IV 169

Saula

pundit and teacherFutuna
DistrictsIpau; teacher at Iasoa
BaptisedMay 1889, one of the first five
Formed byMr Copeland’s influence
Died1893, in the dysentery epidemic, at Iasoa

Gunn thought Saula’s grasp of sin, saving grace and the new heart clearer even than Popoina’s: “The Christian might commit sin, but hated it, was grieved when he yielded to it, and turned from it.” He was the most consistent of the whole Christian party, kept clear of every form of heathenism including kava, and alone took no part in the ceremony that swept up the rest. Asked whether he would have the courage to join the church if Popoina failed, he answered in the figurative speech of the island: “I will go abroad in my own canoe, with my own paddle, and my own baler.”

In 1886 he and his wife were given a trip to Aniwa in the Dayspring. Aniwa was wholly Christian, and what he saw there he came home and told: that the men who met them on the beach carried no spears or clubs; that at night they did not gather in the marae to drink kava but stayed with their wives and children; that husbands and wives walked together to their gardens and were not jealous of each other as in the time of darkness; that the men had thrown away their sacred fishing stones and caught more fish than when they were heathen; and that they washed their faces and put on clean clothes for church.

He was Gunn’s pundit as well as a teacher, and he was the one man who was making headway with the two heathen head chiefs of Imounga, Sengia and Sarashi, when the epidemic took him. Gunn believed that but for Saula’s death the Imoungans would have begun to worship in 1893 instead of 1906 — “the ripe was taken: the green were spared” — and by then only a remnant was left to receive it. It was the Aneityumese custom to return a dead member’s Testaments to the missionary for reissue; Saula’s widow came to Dr Gunn and said, “I will not give you back my husband’s books; I want to keep them in memory of him.”

Family: a wife, who travelled with him to Aniwa and survived him; her name is not recorded.

GF 54, 81, 108–109, 119 · HD 31–32 · L IV 174

Roroveka

Futuna
BaptisedMay 1889, one of the first five
KinNephew — in Futunese, “son” — Basulu, murdered
Evidence of changeHis answer about the murderer
WorkAssisted at the arrowroot making

Roroveka had already given proof of a change of heart before his baptism, and the proof was this. His nephew Basulu — whom, in the Futunese reckoning of kin, he called his son — had been murdered, and the murderer’s name was not yet known. Roroveka said: “I would like to shake hands with the man who killed my son, and ask him to give up heathenism and help in spreading the ‘Good Word’ in Futuna.” Gunn, who knew exactly what native law demanded in such a case — that every wrong be revenged, and that pardon meant only debts unpaid and insults unavenged — added simply: “Who among us, if in similar circumstances, could do the same?”

GF 82, 67

Laku

FutunaFirst convert · Pastor’s wife
Trained byMrs Gunn, as a house-girl
BaptisedMay 1889; admitted to communion later, for youth
MarriedHabena, 1890 — the first Christian marriage on Futuna
ChildrenFive, all church members

“Laku we regarded as our first convert.” She was one of Mrs Gunn’s house-girls, a trustworthy nurse trained in Bible knowledge, housekeeping and sewing, and the Gunns judged her too young for full communion when she was baptised with the other four in May 1889. Her shame at the foul talk of the men building the Isia cottage, when she carried the missionary’s food over from Ipau, is one of the small human details Gunn kept.

In 1890 the Gunns found her a husband in the widowed teacher Habena, and the whole of Futuna looked on and wondered at the first Christian wedding. She and Habena were among the very few who did not contract dysentery in 1893, and she nursed and buried through that epidemic. In her husband’s declining years she carried a great part of the work: Gunn called her a terror to evildoers and easily the most influential woman on the island, and recorded that when Habena was too weak to walk to the service she put him on her back and carried him there and home again. Of the five baptised in May 1889 she was the last surviving when Gunn wrote in 1913.

Family: husband Habena, pastor of Futuna, died 1916. Five children, all of whom Gunn describes as consistent church members — the first generation born inside the Futuna church, and the point at which the Aneityumese and Futunese streams become one household.

GF 82–83, 116 · HD 56 · L IV 170, 180

Saloki

Futuna
KinFavourite grand-daughter of Popoina
RoleHouse-girl; nurse of the Gunn children
Married1890, the second Christian marriage
DiedJanuary–February 1893, first of the epidemic

One of Mrs Gunn’s house-girls and the former nurse of the Gunn children. When the Empreza landed the returning labourers and the sick half-caste child, Saloki constituted herself the child’s nurse, and so was the first on the island to take the disease. She received all the medical attention the mission could give and grew daily worse. Wishing to go outside to eat some food Mrs Gunn had sent her, she was supported by her mother; at the door she stumbled and fell, and when her mother looked at her face she was dead. Her grandfather Popoina was away in the steamer, and the people said, “Popoina will not see her.” She was buried in the mission ground near the grave of Mrs Copeland; Popoina was buried beside her a few weeks later.

Family: grandfather Popoina; a mother, present at her death, name not recorded; a husband, married in 1890. Gunn notes that the couple often quarrelled and blamed this for the two-and-a-half-year gap before the next Christian marriage.

GF 113–115, 119 · L IV 170

Mou

Futuna
RoleHouse-girl at the mission
BrotherTafaroi, of Isia
PhotographedWith Connie Gunn, 1893
1893Taken away ill by her friends

It was Mou who ran into the schoolroom in agitation to ask whether the doctor would come and see if Saloki was dead — the moment at which the lessons stopped and the epidemic began. The Gunns kept her from the children as long as they could; when she fell ill herself they sent for her brother Tafaroi to take her away, and she asked first to see the children, saying goodbye to them “now thin, pale, and suffering”. She appears with Connie in one of Gunn’s photographs.

GF 114–116

Nailo

FutunaFirst deacon
FatherYarai
BrotherTeitoka
OrdainedThe first deacon of the Futuna church
PortraitPhotographed by Gunn, published 1914

Son of the chief Yarai, and in his youth a disappointment: Gunn had expected better things of him and found him dressing his hair in the heathen fashion, refusing to give it up, promising only to cut it before it grew long. He came right, and was ordained the first deacon on the island, with Mangau added afterwards.

Two acts stand out. In the epidemic of 1893 he brought his father-in-law and brother-in-law by canoe from Isia and nursed them back to health after his mother-in-law and three children of that household had died; and in those same weeks, when the mission house was left without native help and the whole family lay ill, Nailo now and again laid a breadfruit inside the door, thinking they might be hungry. Later it was Nailo who came to Gunn before a feast at Ipau and said: “Come to the square for the weekly meeting to-day, and read the Book to the heathen. They have heard us preaching and praying; but they do not know the Book.”

Family: father Yarai; brother Teitoka. A wife, with a father, brother and mother in Isia; her name is not recorded, and her mother and three of the household died in the epidemic.

GF 48–49, 115, 120, 133–137

Teitoka

FutunaDeacon, 1905
FatherYarai · Heir of Popoina
As a boyTaken for the heathen ceremony against Gunn’s effort
LaterChurch member and the best scholar on the island
Ordained deacon1905, the youngest of the five

Teitoka’s life runs the whole distance of this record in one span. Tatavaka came to Gunn by night: “The ceremony is to be performed to-morrow on five lads; and Teitoka, the son of Yarai, and heir of Popoina, is one of them.” The five boys were led into the public square with great show and took their places with the men, and months passed before the people came back to church.

He grew up to be the best scholar on Futuna. Asked one day to take Gunn’s place in church while the missionary went to Imounga, and given the substance of an address by Mrs Gunn, he did not stick closely to it but spoke well and made a good confession: “Listen to the words of Jesus. I have listened to His voice, and obeyed it.” He prepared his addresses at home, speaking them aloud as if to a congregation, and became a very good, energetic preacher. He was ordained deacon in 1905, the youngest of the five, and it was Teitoka who wrote to Scotland about the drought of 1906: “The trees — the cocoanuts, bread-fruit, and chestnuts — withered. The land died; the people only lived; and if it were not that God took care of us, we should have died too.” Miller records that he lapsed for a time.

Family: father Yarai; brother Nailo, first deacon. Heir of Popoina — an inheritance of chiefly position passing, as Futunese custom allowed, outside the direct male line.

GF 48, 154, 157–158 · L IV 182

Mangau

FutunaDeacon

StationTeacher at Isia, from 1893

Mangau appears first as one of the ten young men who slipped away to Aneityum in a labour boat — his wife knew nothing of his intention until she saw him aboard, clung weeping to the gunwale and was forced away. He came back. As the mission goat-herd he brought milk in large quantities to the mission house during the 1893 epidemic, when the family lay ill and alone. Habena settled him as teacher in Isia during the Gunns’ furlough, and he was ordained deacon after Nailo.

GF 67, 115, 124, 133

Anapapo

Futuna
DistrictsIraro; teacher to Iraro and Imatangi
Brought backTo church through Saula’s efforts

PortraitPhotographed by Gunn, published 1914

Dragged back to church in Iraro through Saula’s efforts and afterwards a willing member of the candidates’ class. Appointed teacher to Iraro and Imatangi, he was accused of helping in the ceremonies to make the breadfruit grow; the people said, “This is a bad servant, remove him.” He angrily repelled the charge and induced the sacred man to bring the sacred stones to the mission house. Habena and Gunn met the two districts and discussed it for hours, and it was decided he should hand the work to another for a time. He was brought back and became a reliable preacher, giving evidence, Gunn writes, that he was a true Christian.

He came to see the dying Popoina, who handed him his coat with the words about Elijah’s mantle. He was also the man who, of his own accord, went and shook hands with Saula Sore on his return, though he had cause to fear him.

GF 119, 133–136

Forau

A young man who had gained some notoriety as a wind-maker because his guardian had been one; whenever there was a high wind or a heavy swell on the shore, Forau was blamed. He resolved to end the talk. Early one morning the Gunns saw him waiting outside with something wrapped in a handkerchief — the sacred stone used by the wind-makers, about the size of a child’s head and pierced with a number of holes, into which the sacred man stuffed leaves, leaving one or two empty to represent the wind he wanted to blow. He handed it over saying, “Tell the people that I have given you this.” Gunn told them, and Forau was charged no more with wind-making. He was the only new member admitted at the communion at the close of 1897, and was ordained deacon in 1905.

GF 133–134, 157

Aresia

FutunaPastor of Futuna, 1932
Ordained deacon1905
Teacher to ImoungaFrom 1904
Ordained pastor of Futuna1932
SignificanceThe first Futunese pastor of Futuna

Aresia is the terminus of this genealogy: the first man of the island to hold the office that Habena of Aneityum had held before him. Stationed as teacher to the heathen district of Imounga in 1904, he did good work there and the new chief joined the worship. Gunn described the preaching of that generation of teachers as vigorous, intelligent and practical, showing a knowledge of the translated Epistles beyond his expectations.

Two moments show his method. Cooking breadfruit at Ipau one day, he saw the sacred man approaching who was about to inaugurate the ceremonies that made it lawful to eat breadfruit; Aresia handed him a cooked one and said, “Here, eat this before you go.” Taken off his guard, the sacred man ate it. The story went round the island, the worshippers laughed at him, the heathen began to see the ceremonies were foolish, and before long they were given up. On another day, noticing three chiefs asleep in church, Aresia stopped in the middle of his address and said, “As Sengia, Kaipapa, and Napau are asleep, we will wait until they are awake.” All three started up, and he continued his sermon.

His summary of what the gospel had done for Futuna is the plainest in the whole record: “When heathenism was great, people could not sleep at night; they were not safe. Now, with the worship, we can go to our plantations, work all day, come back at night, and sleep in peace.”

GF 130, 153, 157 · L IV 181–184, 428

Nauni

FutunaDeacon, 1905
DistrictIpau
Early stanceResisted Popoina’s breaking from the feasts
LaterProposed removing the sacred stones from the marae
Ordained deacon1905, the eldest of the five

Nauni’s protest when Popoina began to leave the feasts is the clearest statement of the Futunese social difficulty: “Why does Popoina leave us? If we continue feasting, let us all do it; if we give it up, let us all do it, and not leave one at a time.” It was afterwards Nauni, with Meiri, who suggested to Gunn that the sacred stones be dug out of the marae and the sacred banyan burned, since so long as these remained “the root of heathenism was untouched”. He was the eldest of the five deacons ordained in 1905.

GF 52, 67, 81, 157

Kavahe

KaveheFutunaDeacon, 1905
Early years“For so many years had troubled us”
LaterTeacher and preacher
Ordained deacon1905
SpellingMiller gives Kavehe

Gunn’s single sentence about him is the whole biography and enough: “Kavahe, who for so many years had troubled us, was now a teacher and preacher.” Ordained deacon with the other four in 1905.

GF 154, 157 · L IV 182

Meiri

Meiri IpauFutuna
DistrictIpau
With NauniProposed clearing the marae
OfferedLand at Imounga for the new church
EarlierNamed among those leading a heathen ceremony

One of the two men of Ipau who put it to Gunn that the sacred stones and the sacred banyan must go. He is also named, with Popoina and Yarai, among the men who solemnly denied any part in a proposed heathen ceremony while in fact leading it. Later he offered land for the new church at Imounga; Sarashi refused the site, and another had to be bought.

GF 48, 52, 149, 151

Nauiakasi

FutunaChief and orator
DistrictIasoa
Formed bySaula’s class
OfferHis own land in the public square for the Imounga church
NoteFriends in Imounga wanted a feast before his baptism

An orator, and one of the chief persons in Saula’s class — fruit of a man already dead. When his friends in Imounga heard he was to be baptised they complained, “Why did you not tell us? We wanted to make a feast for him before his baptism”; the Gunns were glad they had not the chance. On his reception into the church they said, “They need not continue longer in heathenism, after their chief had left them.” When the old Isia church was falling down and Gunn proposed one larger church for the three districts, it was Nauiakasi who demanded, “Build in Imounga — on my land, in the public square!” The site proved too small, but the offer broke the ground.

GF 111, 128, 149 · L IV 177–178

Sengia

FutunaHead chief of Imounga
FatherKautiama
BrotherSarashi, the younger
DistrictImounga
Entered the church1901

The elder of the two sons of the chief who killed the Samoan teacher’s wife, and joint head chief of the district that killed her. He had often visited Saula at Ipau, and Saula brought him to the mission house for fish-hooks and began to tell him the gospel and to press him to give up heathenism. “But what about that ceremony?” Sengia asked. “Give it up,” said Saula. “Oh, dear!” sighed Sengia. The epidemic ended those conferences and Saula and his heathen friends never met again.

Eight years later Gunn offered Sarashi his own coat to come to church; Sarashi hesitated, then pointed to his older brother: “My brother here will take the coat.” Sengia followed the party to church wearing it while Gunn preached without one, and attended regularly afterwards — though Gunn adds candidly that his influence was small, and that elderly men like him rarely became satisfactory worshippers, sometimes settling in a corner of the church and going to sleep.

Family: father Kautiama, chief of Imounga in 1841–43; brother Sarashi. The two brothers inherited both the chiefship and the guilt of the district.

GF 108, 152–153

Sarashi

SarajiFutunaHead chief of Imounga
FatherKautiama
BrotherSengia, the elder
PositionThe last stronghold of heathenism on Futuna
DiedOf tuberculosis, a heathen

The younger and, Gunn says, the more energetic of Kautiama’s two sons, and for twenty years the single obstacle between the mission and the last heathen district in Futuna. As long as he stayed outside the church the majority stayed with him.

He was not implacable. He was beguiled into the church to see the pictures and the printing press, and let Gunn read to him from the Book so that he might know it was not so dreadful. “Let those who want to sew come and sew,” he told the girls when Mrs Gunn offered to make them dresses — though they were too afraid to come. Of an extraordinary crop of chestnuts he said, “It is the work of God.” He objected to the church being built on Meiri’s land, then agreed to a site by the public path near the marae — and was paid about £3 for it, with a further £2 10s. given by the worshippers of the whole island to stop the Imoungans grumbling. He and his people helped occasionally with the building and brought the workers food.

Offered Gunn’s coat in 1901 he said, “I have no clothes”, and then handed the excuse and the coat to his brother. He never made the break. He died of tuberculosis, a heathen still, while the rest of his district came into the church in 1906.

GF 136, 149–153, 130 · L IV 178–179

Yaupa

FutunaThe oldest man in the Pacific
Age at deathBy Gunn’s reckoning, fully 130 years
DiedOctober 1899, of measles
EarlierA worshipper, then a heathen, then a worshipper again
EvidenceToo old for a sham fight in 1843

Gunn set out his reasoning carefully, since no ages were recorded in the New Hebrides. Yaupa’s contemporaries on Aneityum had all died seventy or eighty years before him, some of them at seventy or eighty; Aneityumese remembered seeing him in 1860 as a very old man with a staff; and when the Samoan teachers were killed in 1843 he was already too old to take part even in a sham fight. Gunn concluded he was fully a hundred and thirty. He remembered hiding in the bush as a child during a famine that followed drought, lest he should be killed and eaten.

He had been a worshipper before the Gunns came, took offence at some trifle, and was a heathen through their first two or three years. Finding the weekly meeting thinly attended one day, Gunn went out to look for people and found Yaupa in the marae. “Where are you going to, Missi?” “I am looking for people to come to church. Go on before me while I look for others.” When Gunn came back Yaupa was in church, and from that day until his last illness he never missed. He was active in all his movements to the end, kept his bush gardens, and Gunn says he died a Christian. After escaping for nearly a century and a half all the ills that flesh is heir to, he died of a child’s disease.

GF 52, 146–148 · L IV 176

Tabau

Futuna
DistrictImounga
DescriptionAn old white-haired heathen
ActBlocked the removal of the church timber
ThenAmong the first to worship in the new church

When Sarashi’s opposition looked final and Gunn had told the Christians to carry the timber back to Ipau, it was old Tabau, a white-haired heathen, who said flatly: “The timber will not be taken away.” Another Imoungan seconded him. He was afterwards one of the first who worshipped in the church that timber built.

GF 149–152

Namua

Futuna
DistrictIasoa
ActShot his own brother, a Futunese assistant teacher
LaterReceived into the church with his wife
ChildrenTwo died in the 1893 epidemic; one spared

Returning from Fiji, Namua found that his brother — an assistant teacher at Iasoa — had taken his wife. He crept to the house at night with a loaded musket, rested it lightly on the woman lying near the door, and fired, killing the man instantly. The musket was never used again; it was put into a cave nearby, where Gunn says it still remained.

He and his wife afterwards both gave up heathenism and wanted to cling to the gospel, and he was among the members received before the Gunns left in 1893 — one of three men in a communicant roll of thirty who had been murderers. Two of their children died in the epidemic; one, they said, had been spared through persevering prayer.

GF 27–28, 111–112

Narua

FutunaChief of Isia
DistrictIsia
WivesTen — more than any man on Futuna
ActShot his own sister; barred the church with a musket
PeriodCopeland’s time

Gunn’s harshest portrait: a man who combined in himself all the bad qualities of the Futunese, none more covetous or grasping, none more clamorous for a trip in the mission vessel. His ten wives were his slaves, subject to his fierce and changing passions. In a fit of anger he shot his own sister dead, to be “quits” with a couple whose son had died abroad and so silence their mourning, since he too was now a mourner. Seeking the missionary’s favour he attended church for a time; then, offended at being reproved for clinging to heathen customs, he stood outside the church one Sabbath with a loaded musket and prevented anyone from entering. The worship in Isia lapsed for a season, and when Narua’s “anger was finished” the people slowly came back.

GF 27–28

Tafune-tatai

“The woman-of-the-sea”Futuna
DistrictImounga
NameTafune-tatai, the woman-of-the-sea
ActFirst Imoungan to ask for cloth and make a dress
EndFell ill; last seen resting in Imatangi

A pretty, dainty woman of Imounga who came occasionally to the mission house for fish-hooks. One day she brought a bunch of bananas and wanted print for it. Asked what she meant to do with it, she answered brightly, “Wear it when I come to Ipau” — a new thing for an Imoungan to say, when the usual covering was a grass skirt, some bright leaves and paint. Next time she came with the print sewn into a dress and her long hair cut short. She would have come to church long before, Gunn believed, but dared not against the will of the chiefs. Her visits grew less frequent and she did not look well; he found her one day lying in the shade of a great rock in Imatangi, thin and tired, talked with her a little, prayed, and left her.

Of Isia, and one of the few who asked outright for more teaching: “Missi, do not rest, but come often and speak to us.” Gunn read it as a man who knew his people were ignorant and needed instruction. He came for his sister Mou when the dysentery took her.

When the mission family lay ill and alone, and even friends kept away, Nakki went about praying with the sick, burying the dead, and was one of the few who came to see them.

Recorded for what the epidemic cost one household: Fatapa lost about ten relatives altogether, his mother-in-law and his son on a single day.

Daughter of Popoina. When the water ran dirty during the arrowroot work and men were sent up the hill to find out why, two boys saw a woman stirring the mud with a stick; Roroveka went up and found it was Yalima. She fled. The day’s work was lost, and Gunn had the people called out to work by moonlight instead. She is one of the few Futunese women of the first Christian generation whose name and parentage are both recorded.

Family: father Popoina; mother Teiau.

Named only in the account of his uncle’s forgiveness, which is nonetheless one of the turning points in the moral history of the island. In Futunese reckoning Roroveka was his father, not his uncle — a point of kinship on which the whole force of the story depends.

On his return his friends wished a feast; he would take none, but wanted Anapapo to come and “place his hand in his”. Anapapo went of his own accord and shook hands with him, though for a time uneasy, fearing Saula Sore might attempt revenge. There was no trouble, and he lived peacefully in his own district until the measles took him.

Having come back from Fiji, Nalau tried to renew a ceremony the Christian people had banned. Their opposition was so strong — and their threat to burn the house so credible — that he went off to Imounga, where he was not hindered. This was the last attempt to perform the ceremony in the Christian districts.

When the sacred stones were being dug from the marae at Ipau, the two most active helpers were heathen — Wotu and old Yaupa. They were glad to remove the signs of the gods’ presence, hoping to take away their power to do them harm.

01

Family trees and houses

Only a handful of Futunese pedigrees survive, because no one was writing them down; the missionaries recorded kinship only when it explained something. What follows is every documented family connection in the sources, set out as trees. Dashed boxes mark people the record mentions but does not name.

Tree 1 · The Futunese line

The house of Konafia, priest of Ipau

The oldest recorded Christian pedigree on the island, and the one from which the whole Futunese church descends. Konafia was the district’s heathen priest; his son became its first believer.

      • Yalimadaughter
      • a childname not recorded
        • Salokid. Jan–Feb 1893

Heir: Popoina’s heir was Teitoka, son of the chief Yarai and no blood descendant — succession on Futuna did not run through the male line only.

Yarai sold the mission its ground and was the first Futunese to abandon a major heathen ceremony — and was also caught leading one. Both his sons became office-bearers of the church.

02

How descent was reckoned

A genealogy of Futuna cannot be read with European assumptions. Gunn set down the island’s system of relationship in some detail, and without it several entries above make no sense — not least Roroveka calling his nephew his son, and Teitoka inheriting from a man who was not his father.

Chiefship

Chiefs did not descend through the male line only. The successor was often the son of the sister or the niece of the late chief. This is why Popoina’s heir was Teitoka, son of Yarai, and why Miller could record in 1908 that a deacon of chiefly rank was elected chief of the whole of Futuna — the first island-wide chief in some fifty years.

Brothers and sisters

The male and female children of two or more brothers, or of two or more sisters, were called brothers and sisters. It was therefore against native law for them to intermarry, and the prohibition extended to their grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Children called their father’s brothers “father” and their mother’s sisters “mother”, and those so-called parents called them “my son” and “my daughter”.

Cousins and betrothal

The children of a brother and a sister — cross-cousins — were cousins in the European sense and were eligible to marry. They called their mother’s brothers “uncle” and their father’s sisters “aunt”, as we do. Such cousins of opposite sex were betrothed from birth: a boy called his female cousin “my wife” while still a child, and she called him “my husband”. If on growing up he did not want her, his friends found him another wife — but no one could take his first betrothed without his sanction or without paying him for her in full.

Husbands and wives

A husband called each of his wife’s sisters “my wife”; they stood in the same relation to him as his own wife, and if she died he took one of her unmarried sisters. A wife spoke of her husband’s brothers as “my husbands”. A father called his daughter’s husband his “nephew” and his son’s wife his “niece” — and, when the marriage followed native law, they really were.

Foster kin and respect

Two boys brought up together fell into calling each other “my brother”, two girls “sister”, and their children to the second and third generation were called brothers and sisters likewise. The old were addressed as “grandfather” and “grandmother” as a title of respect. In Futuna, unlike most of the group, children usually did call their real parents “father” and “mother”; elsewhere they used the personal names for their real parents and the kin-terms for more distant relatives.

Why it matters here

Gunn notes that the real father was he who begat the children and the real mother she who bore them — the distinction existed, but it was not the one that governed daily speech. So when Roroveka says “the man who killed my son”, he means his nephew; and when the sources call someone a chief’s son, the relation may be classificatory rather than biological. Every kin statement in the register above is given as the source gives it, with this caution standing.

01

The rolls of the church

The first communion roll, May 1889

Baptised one Sabbath morning in May 1889, with two infant children of the teachers; the Lord’s Supper was celebrated the same afternoon. Twelve people sat down — the Aneityumese teachers, four Futunese, and the Gunns — and the wine was passed round in a plain crystal cup. It was within a few months of fifty years since John Williams had brought the message to Futuna. When Gunn wrote in 1913, of these five only Laku remained.

TeiauIpau, then IasoaWife of Popoina; had relinquished heathenism and wished to serve Jesus.Died before 1913
RorovekaNot statedHad already given proof of a change of heart, in his words about his nephew’s murderer.Died before 1913
LakuIpauRegarded by the Gunns as their first convert; withheld from full communion for youth.Survived all four

The deacons

There were never any elders on Futuna. The pastor effectively ruled the church with the help of the deacons and teachers — a pattern fairly general in the mission at that period.

02

Milestones

Miller drew up a table of the steps by which the church was planted in each of the southern islands. Futuna’s row is set out here in full.

StepFutunaNote
First Polynesian teachers1841Apela and Samuela, at Imounga.
First Aneityumese teachers1853Waihit and Iosefa, at Imatangi and Iakana.
First European missionary1866Joseph Copeland, at Ipau.
First Christian marriage1890Habena and Laku.
Church planted1889Five baptised in May; a church formed.
First Ni-Vanuatu missionaries sent out1893Futunese to Ambrym, under Dr Lamb.
First pastor ordained1900Habena — only the second in the whole church.
A Christian island1906The last of the heathen came into the church.
New Testament in the language1931Completed by Gunn in retirement, lacking Romans and 1 and 2 Corinthians.
First elders appointednoneFutuna never appointed elders; the pastor governed with deacons and teachers.

For comparison, Aneityum planted its church in 1852–53 and had its New Testament by 1860; Aniwa planted its church in 1869 and was reckoned a Christian island in 1874. Futuna, first visited of all of them, was last.

The wider mission, 1797–1980

SHIPS · MONEY · SELF-GOVERNMENT

The machinery that carried the gospel to Futuna and the church that grew out of it, from the first mission ship to an independent national church.

Press / to search

On this page
  • Ships, money and the shape of the mission
  • From mission to independent church
01

Ships, money and the shape of the mission

Futuna had no harbour, no anchorage, no money and almost no soil. Everything that reached it — teachers, timber, printing paper, the mail, the missionary’s family — came by an organisation that had to be built first. This section sets out that machinery, because the dates on the Chronology page only work if the ships are understood.

The vessels

VesselService
Duff, 1797The first London Missionary Society ship, just under 300 tons, which landed the first Protestant missionaries at Tahiti.
Messenger of PeaceBuilt by John Williams himself, a sixty-foot schooner. He arrived in the group in 1817 and would not be held up for want of a ship.
CamdenWilliams’ vessel on his last voyage, which brought him to Futuna in November 1839 and to Erromanga three days later. She landed the first Polynesian teachers on Futuna, Aniwa, Aneityum and Erromanga.
John Williams, 1845A barque of 296 tons named for the dead missionary, with a figurehead showing him holding an open Bible. She carried the news of the Futuna murders in 1845 and the Aneityumese teachers to Futuna in 1853, and served twenty years until wrecked on Niue in May 1864.
John Knox, 1861A schooner of only twelve tons, bought with money raised in Glasgow. Too small for the growing work, but the first vessel the Presbyterian mission owned.
Dayspring I, 1863A barquentine of 115 tons built at New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, largely on money raised by John G. Paton from Sabbath-school children, dedicated 22 October 1863 and sailed from Halifax on 7 November. Ten years’ service; wrecked in the hurricane at Anelgauhat Harbour, Aneityum, on 6 January 1873. No lives lost.
Dayspring IIFormerly the schooner Paragon, 159 tons, bought in Sydney; the longest-lived of the ships, twenty-three years without a single life lost by drowning.
Dayspring III, 1895An auxiliary steamship, the biggest and best of them, reached Melbourne from Scotland — and on her fourth voyage struck an uncharted rock north of New Caledonia and was a total loss with all her cargo.
LaunchesBy 1910 every isolated missionary felt he needed a motor launch; by 1913 there were sixteen in the service of the mission. The Mary Milne memorial launch was photographed at Vila in 1909 with Peter Milne aboard.

The name Dayspring is from the Benedictus in Luke 1 — the dayspring from on high visiting those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. A mission flag designed by Mrs J. G. Paton and approved by Synod in 1889 flew from the masthead of every mission vessel: a white St Andrew’s cross on Presbyterian blue, with the letters N.H.P.M. in red on the four arms.

L III 126–138

Money in an island with none

  • There was no money. Trade goods — tobacco, matches, cloth — did the work of currency. A young Aneityumese named Williamu who wanted to help pay for the translations was sold four silver dollars’ worth of prized shells by a trader; those four dollars were the first money Williamu ever owned, and he gave them to the Bible Society.
  • Nobody was paid in cash. Work on a church, a school or a teacher’s house was done by the whole village and paid for in food and community feasts. Teachers were supported from a Teachers’ Fund and given clothing at the year’s end.
  • Arrowroot was the cash crop. The LMS missionaries introduced it. Grating, washing, sifting and casking arrowroot was a long and careful process, and for nearly a century it covered most of the cost of Bible translation and printing. A small island like Futuna would produce as much as a ton of arrowroot in a year — which is how a people with no money paid for their own Scriptures.
  • Cash offerings began late. The first reference to them seems to be in the 1891 report; a collection was set apart by the Aniwa session on 14 October 1891 for John G. Paton’s home church, to be used in sending the gospel to the people of the New Hebrides who were still in darkness.
L III 151–154

The map that divided the group

In 1880 the Presbyterian Synod asked Bishop J. R. Selwyn to agree the terms of his father’s plan of 1853, that the whole of the New Hebrides should be recognised as the Presbyterian field and the whole of the Banks and Torres as the Melanesian. Selwyn replied on 7 July 1880 and 23 April 1881, withdrawing the two Anglican missions from Emae and drawing a boundary between the two missions which left the whole of the New Hebrides to the Presbyterians except Oba, Aurora, Pentecost, and the Banks and Torres. The Presbyterian Synod acquiesced in 1881, and Futuna, at the far south-eastern corner of the map, lay well inside the Presbyterian field for the whole of the period this record covers.

L III 144–146

The roots of the church

Miller draws the Presbyterian Church of the New Hebrides as a coconut palm with many roots, and lists the sending bodies in the order they arrived: the London Missionary Society and its daughter churches in Polynesia from 1839; the Presbyterian Church of the Lower Provinces of British North America, which sent Geddie and most of the Canadians, from 1846; the Reformed Presbyterian Church of Scotland, which sent Inglis and others from 1852 to 1875; the Presbyterian Church of Victoria, which appointed J. G. Paton and J. Cosh in 1866; the Presbyterian Church of New South Wales, which appointed J. D. Gordon in 1868; the Presbyterian Church of New Zealand, which appointed William Watt in 1868 and Peter Milne in 1869; the Presbyterian Church of England; the Canadian Maritime church; the Presbyterian Church of South Australia, which sent William Gray in 1882; the two Presbyterian churches in Tasmania, which sent R. M. Fraser in 1882; and the John G. Paton Mission Fund, established in 1890, which for some years was the largest supporting body of all.

L III 146–150
02

From mission to independent church

This record closes in 1935. The church it describes did not. This section carries the line forward to the point where the Futunese congregation became part of a self-governing national church — because the ordination of Habena in 1900, which is one of the milestones on the Church page, is the first move in that story.

The ordination of islanders

  • 1897 — Epeteneto. Of Aneityum, ordained in May 1897 during the Synod meetings at Aneityum: the first ordained pastor of the New Hebrides Presbyterian Church. Miller describes him as a man of superior intelligence, a true Christian, devoted to his master’s work and Dr Gunn’s close friend. He died in 1905 at about seventy-one.
  • 1900 — Habena. Of Futuna, the second. Gunn moved Synod to sanction the ordination, having first established that Epeteneto’s had been a truly forward step. He died about 1917.
  • 1917 — the Synod minute. Synod recorded Gunn’s tribute: that for about seventeen years Habena was teacher on Futuna and for nearly the same period its pastor; that the Futunese trusted him; and that the teachers took their orders from him and obeyed him. That minute is the formal end of the line this record traces.
  • 1920 onward. The idea of more pastors had germinated. Synod “sat in committee to consider the ordination of certain teachers as pastors”, and approved Sopi of Efate, Judah of Onua, Malekula, and Winzi of Malo. Four more men were ordained in 1934 at Hog Harbour — well-tried leaders drawn from the first generation of converts.
L III 121–124

Elders, sessions and Synod

The pattern was older than the ordinations. Geddie had seven men nominated for the office of ruling elder on Aneityum by October 1860, and wrote that he expected to ordain them the next week — the first eldership in the group, and the beginning of self-government in the church. The Synod itself began as a council of missionaries: Inglis wrote that the missionaries found it convenient in 1872 to apply the name Synod to their annual business meeting, and that no native elders sat as members. Under the Mission Constitution of 1892 the missionaries held Synodical powers over the entire mission in all its areas and activities, and made no further mention of representation from the New Hebrides church. Miller calls the resulting drift a tragedy for the church.

L III 116–120

The line to independence

DateEvent
1941Synod resolved to open the way for growth into self-government within the church. World War II then prevented Synod meeting.
1 Jul 1948The Presbyterian Church of the New Hebrides was inaugurated. The Rev. Fred J. Paton, MBE, the oldest missionary present, died shortly afterwards.
1948–The Tangoa Training Institute, already long at work, took on fresh importance as the leadership training college. Rev. Graham Miller — the author of Live, and one of the principal sources of this record — and from 1958 Rev. Paddy Jansen were the key principals of the period.
2 Aug 1949The first General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church of the New Hebrides. Pastor Moses Manasakau of Tongoa asked the moderator, on the day the mainland gained its freedom, whether that was the day “we gain our freedom”.
1953The New Zealand Assembly reported that the era of foreign mission had ended and that what was now being done was not maintaining a mission but sharing in inter-church aid.
May 1973The 25th General Assembly, meeting at Tanna — Futuna’s nearest neighbour — declared that representing more than half the population of the New Hebrides, it confidently looked towards the goal of responsible self-government of the New Hebrides people as a nation.
1975The Assembly set church leaders apart for political service, leaving gaps in the church’s own leadership that younger men and some women filled.
Jul 1980Independence. The New Hebrides became Vanuatu, and Futuna a part of Tafea Province.
TodayThe Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu is the largest denomination in the country, with membership equalling some 38 per cent of the population, wholly autonomous and wholly indigenous in its leadership. Pastor training is at the Talua Ministry Training Centre.
L III 124–125 · W 1–2
Why this belongs in a genealogy

A genealogy of the gospel is not finished when the last heathen enters the church. The Futunese who took their orders from Habena, and whose grandchildren appear in the “third generation” plate, are the same line that produced the elders, deacons and pastors of a national church. The seventy-two names in the register are the first six or seven links of a chain that has not stopped.

The old religion of Futuna

GODS · TEMPLE · SPIRITS

The gods, the temple of the eight pillars, the priest and the two sacred girls, the worship of the dead, and the world to come.

Press / to search

01

The old religion of Futuna

Nothing in the record that follows is intelligible without the religion the gospel displaced. Gunn set it down deliberately, and at length, because he could see it going: the men who had performed the ceremonies were dying, and their sons already knew only fragments. “We do not know the religious customs,” the old man Tatavaka told him. “It was the people of long ago who knew the root; we know only the branches.” What is gathered here is the root, as far as it could still be recovered in the 1880s and 1890s.

On the word “heathen”

The nineteenth-century sources call the old religion heathenism and its adherents the heathen, and this record keeps those words where it is reporting the sources, because to soften them would be to misreport what the writers meant and what the Futunese themselves came to mean by them — on Futuna the division between “the worship” and “heathenism” was a real and public one, and people chose sides. Where this record speaks in its own voice it uses custom or the old religion. In modern Vanuatu the whole inheritance is called kastom, and it is not a term of reproach.

The gods

The Futunese were polytheists. They believed in many gods, great and small, each with his own sphere and independent of the others. The chief of them was Amoshishiki — the same figure known as Moitikitiki on Aneityum and at Weasisi, and as Maui-tikitiki and Ma‘ui‑ti‘iti‘ across Polynesia. He was said to have fished the land up out of the sea, raising one headland after another. The Futunese could still point out the place where his foot slipped as he hauled up the last part of the island, and a row of stones that stands for his broken fishing line.

Beneath the great gods were gods inhabiting particular trees and stones, so that the religion descended into fetishism; and beneath these again the innumerable sacred stones, held by chiefs and commoners alike, which acted on the things they resembled — a stone for breadfruit shaped almost exactly like the fruit, stones for yams, stones for catching fish, love charms for obtaining a wife or a husband, stones to steady the aim of a spear or ward off an enemy’s blow. The sorcerers used them for making disease; the sacred men used them for making drought, hurricane and rain.

GF 217 · 221–222

How the world and death began

TraditionAs the Futunese told it
The raising of the islandAmoshishiki fished the land up from the sea bed, headland by headland. His footprint and the row of stones marking his broken line were shown on Futuna as proof.
The origin of manTwo yams were laid on the ground. Next morning one had become a man; the following day a woman stood beside him.
The origin of deathTold across the group; the Aneityum form is that an old man used to take off his skin before working in his garden and so looked young again, until his two grandchildren found the folded skin and pricked it full of holes. Putting it on again he shivered, saw the holes, and said that because of what they had done all would now die.
Yawia and the whaleA man named Yawia in the Futunese telling was swallowed by a whale and came out alive. Versions are found through the New Hebrides and the wider Pacific. Gunn translated the book of Jonah early, precisely because the story was already at home on the island; it made little appeal, and ended up as a school reader.
Traces of a floodGunn records faint resemblances to the account of the Flood in other Futunese folk-lore, without pressing the point.
GF 217–218 · L IV 176

Sun, moon and the altars

South of Efate, where Polynesian influence was thinner, there were traces of sun and moon worship. On Aneityum the sun and his wife Sina, the moon, held the power of life and death, and were asked for life and health while the lesser gods were asked for lesser things. Feasts were held at new moon. On Futuna as on Aneityum the people built altars in which the two tallest posts stood for the sun and the moon. Children were held to be the gift of the moon.

The belief that the phases of the moon govern the weather, the sea and the planting and harvesting of crops long outlived the old religion. It was still universal in Vanuatu in the 1980s. Dr Gunn was asked from 1893 to prepare the annual mission almanac showing the phases of the moon, and it was eagerly sought after by islanders wanting an auspicious time of the month for a sea journey. The almanac is still produced, much enlarged, by the Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu.

GF 218 · L IV 162

The temple of Amoshishiki

Futuna had a temple — the house of Amoshishiki — and unlike an ordinary Futunese hut, which was simply a roof set down on the ground, it was built with high walls and gable ends. It was last rebuilt in 1859. Inside stood a row of eight pillars representing the eight principal deities, each with branches for arms, and shorter posts for the minor deities: the temple was, in Gunn’s word, the pantheon of Futuna. When the pillars rotted they were not replaced, and the roof settled down onto the ground. It was in this building that the struggle took place which ended the ceremonies conducted in it.

GF 219

Who performed the ceremonies

The priest

Office

Distinct from the ruling chiefs and subject to them. He prayed over the catch, presented the fish to the god, cut and hung up the digging stick at the close of the season, dug and displayed the first ripe yam of the sacred plantation, and named the gods over the food before a feast was given out. Konafia, the priest of Ipau — the man who saved the teacher Ru and whose son Popoina became the first Futunese Christian — held this office.

GF 201 · 219–221

The two sacred girls

Officethe priestesses

Two young women served through the ceremonial season. Every evening one of them cooked the sacred taro — the smallest they had was what was given to the gods — lit the sacred fire for the fishers, and fetched the water for their kava, part of which was poured out to the god and part drunk by the men. The second priestess led the procession of the catch, a garland round her head and her face painted red on one side and black on the other.

Basiva, the wife of Yarai and mother of Saloki and Teitoka, was one of these sacred girls in her youth — a direct link between the temple ceremonial and the first generation of the Futunese church.

GF 219–220

The sacred men

Office

Specialists whose power lay over one thing: the sea, the wind, the rain, drought, hurricane, the breadfruit. They worked through sacred stones and were under food and behaviour restrictions while their ceremonies ran. Their public surrender of the stones is the single commonest sign of conversion in this whole record. If a sacred man had no son or relative to inherit his stones he would destroy them rather than let them leave the family.

GF 221–222 · 255

The chiefs and the people

Participants

The chiefs, and the common people, men and women together, took part — the chiefs shouting over the food, the people answering “Ho!”, which Gunn calls their Amen. The chiefs also fixed the district to which the ceremonial catch was to be carried.

GF 219–221

Worship of the dead

The chief worship of the Futunese, however, was not directed to the gods at all but to the spirits of the dead. Friends loved in life, and wives ill-used in life, became objects of worship once dead. A Futunese was overheard addressing his dead wife by name and promising her food if she would not be angry with him. Food was laid on the graves of relatives or hung beside them in baskets, and this continued on Futuna for years. If the offerings lapsed through the passage of time, then whenever misfortune came — sickness, accident, an unfruitful season, want of rain — it was set down to the anger of the spirits, and the offerings began again.

Most of the ceremonial and most of the feasting existed to appease these spirits, so that the living might have abundance of food, freedom from disease and long life: which were, Gunn observed, the essentials of happiness as the Futunese understood it.

GF 222

The soul, and how it wandered

The body was held to be the principal part of a man; the soul was only his shadow. The spirit had a separate existence from the body — temporarily during life, permanently after death. In sleep it left the body and wandered where it liked, and it was its return that woke the sleeper. A disease-maker worked by driving the spirit out, and the body then sickened. When a person fainted the spirit had gone, and only a few people had the power of recalling it, which they did by calling the name over and over, rapidly, instead of using any restorative.

When the sick sank towards death and lost consciousness the spirit was said to have gone finally. It was called back all the same, but now as a cry of grief. A child dying near the mission premises was mourned in this way by almost every woman in the district, one after another taking up the lament and calling her by name to come back out of space.

The spirit also left the body at an accident. A boy of seven or eight fell from a coconut tree at Futuna and, though hardly hurt, lay in bed for some days. At night the people gathered under the tree and called his name, telling the spirit to return. A burning stick was laid at the foot of the tree with a small white shell over it; two men watched, and when the stick went out they said the spirit had put out the fire and entered the shell. The shell was carried carefully and laid on the boy, so that his spirit might come out of it and re-enter him. The boy objected that his spirit could hardly fit into so small a shell, and had to be persuaded. His mother settled it: this was the custom long ago.

GF 222–224

Spirits, and words that could not be spoken

Prohibition or fearWhat was believed
Going out alone at nightThe air was peopled with spirits that came abroad after dark. A rustle in the bush — wind, a pig, a bird — was a spirit. In company they would risk it; asked to go anywhere alone, a Futunese would answer with a question: who is to go with me?
Naming a baby’s teethMothers asked how many teeth their babies had looked frightened. To refer to the teeth by name was to stop them growing.
Looking at the setting sunTo look at the sun and its rays as they went down meant death or sickness to the one who looked.
The banyan over the dancing groundSpecially sacred. No one would dare strike it or cut off a branch. In 1886 two men of Ipau told Gunn that the sacred stones in the marae and the sacred banyan were “the root of heathenism” and should be destroyed — and it was done.
Certain words in certain seasonsWords could be tapu — sacred, forbidden, ominous — at particular times of the year.
Unpierced earsA god living in, or represented by, a great stone in the sea off the beach kept the entrance of the spirit-land, and rolled a stone over those who had not pierced their ears. See the note below.
GF 193–194 · 224 · L IV 165–166
The man who fought the door-keeper

One Futunese refused to conform to the ear-piercing custom and told his friends to bind a club to his arm at death, to fight the god with. His body was thrown into the sea, as was usual, near the guardian stone. The waves carried it towards the stone, and those on shore heard blow after blow as the breakers dashed the club against it. The body came back to the beach with the club still on the arm, broken and useless. The door-keeper of the spirit-land had smashed it, the people said, and the law-breaker was beaten. After that the young were afraid to leave their ears unpierced. The practice was given up once Christianity became dominant.

GF 194

The world to come

Belief in a future world was universal, but on Futuna the immortality was a limited one. The shades went down to the lower world and passed a miserable existence there with only refuse for food. Those wounded or killed in war carried their wounds down with them. The spirits were no longer thinking, conscious beings; they could neither enjoy nor suffer. After a time they sank to a lower stage, and at last became dead shells. Infant spirits were nursed by their friends. Stillborn babies became gods, with endless happiness.

The feasts made by the living were to quiet the spirits, which wandered restlessly until all the ceremonies were finished; when these were done the restless activity — and perhaps the existence — of the spirit came to an end. There was no distinction between good and bad: all alike went down through the descending stages, and the feasts and good things of earth were gone for ever.

The only sins recognised were greed, and neglect of disfiguring the face. There was no punishment for those who wronged, murdered or dishonoured a neighbour. Prayers were made to the spirits, but never for forgiveness — the object was to be indulged, and the spirits were paid in food. The old worship did not teach reverence for the aged, nor obedience to parents, nor love of neighbour. It was, in Gunn’s summary, a religion of fear and of self-interest. He adds, fairly, that the existence in it of sacrifice, of prayer, and of belief in a world to come helped the Futunese to understand those things afterwards under Christianity.

GF 224–226

The customary year and its fixed dates

OCTOBER TO MARCH

The ceremonial round, season by season, with the rule or tapu attaching to each.

Press / to search

01

The customary year and its fixed dates

Futunese time was not counted in years but in seasons, and the seasons were marked by ceremonies. The ceremonial year ran from about October to March and had two objects only: plenty of fish, and a good harvest. Everything else — the feasting, the dancing, the exchanges, the tapus on food — hung on those two. What follows is the round of the year as Gunn recorded it, together with the occasions that fell whenever they fell.

The round of the year

SeasonWhat was doneRule or tapu attaching to it
Aug–Sep Clearing and planting. The land was cleared for yams and hedged round with trees or a neat reed fence to keep the pigs out. Deep pits were dug some yards apart and the earth heaped, finely powdered, into mounds; upright reeds were set as supports for the climbing sprouts, which then spread over a network of reeds between the mounds. At this stage the gardens were models of neatness — in striking contrast, Gunn thought, to the general disorder of the premises. While new gardens were being made it was tapu to eat pork, lest the yams should fail. When the Gunns killed a pig for the men who had built the first church, the builders threw their portions away or gave them to the Aneityumese.
Oct–Mar The ceremonial season. The temple ceremonies were carried on through these months, conducted by the priest with the chiefs, the people and the two sacred girls. The ceremonial was tedious and full of detail, and concerned with food only; but they were most careful to omit nothing in offering, prayer or thanksgiving.
Summer The flying-fish season. On moonless nights the men paddled to and fro with blazing torches of withered coconut leaves twined together like a pole, sometimes twelve or fifteen feet long. The flying fish leapt at the light and were caught in small circular nets on ten-foot poles. Torchlight fishing for flying fish was confined to Futuna and Aniwa. Before going out on a dark night each man took a sacred taro and, going out one by one, threw it down beside the sacred stones for the gods’ food. The fishers ate no bananas during the season, lest the fishing be spoiled. Sugar-cane and taro were taken from the altar, part being left to the gods.
At dawn,
after a catch		 The procession of the fish. The catch was carried up in glad procession to the temple, the baskets of gear hung on a pronged pole with the flying fish above them. Men and women danced their thanks to the god. The priest then took the fish down, handed some to the second priestess, and she — garlanded, her face painted red on one side and black on the other — headed a procession of women, then girls, then men carrying the fish, to a district fixed by the chiefs. Further ceremonies were performed there, a return feast made, and all went home. The priest prayed to the god and presented the fish to it before any of it was carried away.
End of
summer		 The closing of the fishing. When the flying fish disappeared, men and women made a ceremonial feast — separately. Next morning the priest cut down the tako, the digging stick, and hung it up in the temple. The two feasts were kept apart by sex. This is the one point in the Futunese year at which the separation of men’s and women’s ritual is explicit in the record.
Evening of
the same day		 The first yam. The priest dug up the first ripe yam in the sacred plantation and exposed it on the sacred banyan for all to see and praise. Only then was it lawful for everyone to dig their yams. When the first yam had been cooked a feast was made: part of it was given to the gods and part eaten by the priest and the chiefs. Before the food was given out the priest named the gods who had cared for the yams; a chief gave a loud shout; and all the people assented together, calling “Ho!” — which was their Amen. That was their prayer, and then the feast was distributed.
Mar First digging. The earliest yams were dug in March; the rest two or three months later. No yam could be dug before the priest had shown the first one on the banyan.
When the
yams ripened		 The great feasts. The principal feasts of the year. Preparation ran for months: people stinted themselves so that their best yams and fattest pigs would be there for all to praise. The marae was cleared of weeds and houses were built to receive guests from distant districts. On the day the yams, taro and bananas were piled in the square five or six feet high and many yards long, and the great black pigs, lashed to poles, were carried in on men’s shoulders — ten, twenty, thirty of them — and laid down grunting and struggling. See Customary law for the law of exchange that governed all of this. Where all ate together in the public square, the remnants were thrown into a basket set in front and tipped over a cliff into an inaccessible place, to keep the fragments out of the hands of the disease-makers.
Later in
the year		 The small feast. When yams were few and planting had begun again, bananas and coconuts with a pig or two made up the feast. The obligation to return an equal feast still held, whatever its size.
New moon Feasts at the new moon, in the islands where sun and moon worship survived. Children were held to be the gift of the moon. Sea journeys, planting and harvesting were timed by the moon’s phases — a belief that long outlasted the old religion.
Every
evening		 The public square. The men ate the chief meal of the day in the square while the boys prepared the kava. After drinking they often sank into a heavy sleep; towards midnight, on Futuna, they went out to fish or went home. No woman dared appear in sight while the kava was being brewed. The men spat out the first mouthful, calling to the spirits.
All year Work and idleness. On fertile islands the people were at regular labour only about four months in the year; where nature was less kind, eight or ten. The rest of the time went in feasting, talking in the public square, or war. Futuna was among the most barren islands in the group. —
GF 39 · 197–198 · 203 · 209–211 · 218–222

The occasional feasts

Besides the seasonal round there were feasts for every important occasion. Gunn’s list is worth giving whole, because it shows how little of Futunese life stood outside the obligation to feast: at a birth; before a death; at a burial; at the end of mourning; on a girl’s reaching womanhood; at a marriage; at a house-warming; at the reconciliation of friends; at murders; at peace-making. When disputes led to quarrelling and fighting, the price of peace was more feasting still.

So nearly the whole year went. In a few weeks the guests became the hosts and the feast was returned in another district with the same number of pigs, yams, bananas and puddings, and the same scenes took place. With the coming of the flying-fish season, big fish caught at night were carried to other districts seeking an exchange of food. And so, round almost the whole year, the Futunese feasted.

GF 208 · 211
What the feasting cost

By the late 1880s the burden had become visible. Some were tired of carrying food and heavy pigs over dangerous cliff tracks; some fell ill through the protracted labour of it, and consumption followed. Others left the island rather than refuse to help. Men were “dead with the work of the canoe”, as Saula Sore said of Yarai. Looking back, the Christian people concluded that they had been wasting food and injuring themselves. Ten members were still under discipline in 1904 for offences mainly connected with heathen customs.

GF 62 · 70 · L IV 182

Mourning periods

PlaceReckoning of the mourning
Futuna and TannaThe mourners bathed after a burial and did not go near the sea again for several days. Grave-diggers carried coconut cloth for months afterwards, into which friends put their food. All ended with a feast, at which the signs of mourning were put off.
AneityumThe body was set in a sitting posture in a few inches of earth, and food was placed before it day by day for the spirit; when much decomposed it was covered over.
NgunaPigs and fowls killed beside the grave; feasts every fifth day until the hundredth day, to placate the spirit. Sometimes the mourning ran to a thousand days, with rites of worship paid to the dead.
Big Bay, SantoThe body laid on a raised bamboo bed in a house open at both ends, cooking utensils beside it, the widow keeping a smouldering fire underneath and living there for ten or a hundred days until the mourning ended.
GF 214–216

The Sabbath, before it was kept

Even before the island was Christian the seventh day was observed after a fashion. The people seldom did any work on the Sabbath; but to the heathen it was the lazy day, and they idled or slept through it. The women wove baskets and mats; the young men dressed their hair. Feasts continued to fall on it, which was a constant grief to the mission — at Iasoa Gunn once found a crowd sitting round a feast on a Sunday and asked why they were feasting on God’s Day. They answered that they were not making a feast: the feast had been made the day before, and they were only dividing it.

GF 40 · 128 · L IV 164
