A Genealogy of the Gospel in Futuna · page 11 of 18

Customary law, rule and rank

CHIEFS · TAPU · EXCHANGE

Chiefs and rank, the law of land, the law of exchange, tapu, sorcery, revenge, and the cutting and carrying of the canoe.

Press / to search

01

Customary law, rule and rank

There was no king in the New Hebrides and no code. What governed Futunese life was a body of custom about rank, land, exchange, prohibition and revenge, enforced by the chiefs, the sacred men and the fear of sorcery. Gunn, who sat in the island courts when mission questions were involved, set these rules down carefully. They are given here as rules, because that is what they were: breaking them carried consequences, and in several cases the consequence was death.

Chiefs, priests and rank

RuleHow it worked
No kingThe people were broken into many independent tribes, each with its own chiefs. The authority even of the highest chief was small, limited to his tribe, district or village. An energetic chief might gain more influence than the man above him.
Chieftainship hereditary in the southIn the southern islands, including Futuna, the office passed by descent; in the north it was usually acquired.
Succession not only through menChildren, especially males, became the property of the tribe to which the mother belonged. Chiefs did not descend through the male line only: the successor was often the son of the late chief’s sister or niece.
The priesthood separate and subordinateThe priest was distinct from the ruling chiefs and subject to them.
Rank acquired by killing pigsTen pigs, sometimes a hundred. By this order of merit a man rose from one grade to the next, and with the grade rose his social position and his influence.
Caste (north of Efate, not Futuna)In Malo eleven grades, in south Santo twenty. Men cooked on the fireplace of their own grade in the eating-house, and to eat food prepared on a higher fire was death. Women stood outside caste altogether and could never eat with their husbands. Futuna had no caste system.
GF 201–203 · 205 · 94 · L IV 169

The law of land

The Futunese owned the soil. They were landed proprietors who had inherited from their forefathers, and the rules were exact:

  • Every child had its own plot of ground and its own fruit-trees, inherited from father, mother, uncles or aunts, or given by the friend who named it.
  • The ground was owned apart from the trees growing on it. A man therefore often possessed coconut and other fruit-trees, planted by himself or his forefathers, standing on land far from his own and belonging to somebody else.
  • Daughters were rarely allowed to marry outside their own district or tribe, and when they were, a woman was sent in exchange. Marriages were arranged so that the land should stay in the family — so that, as Gunn put it, quoting Numbers, they might enjoy the inheritance of their fathers.
  • The fruit-trees of a dead man were cut down after burial. When a young man died at Ipau the people of Imatangi and Isia crowded into the district and felled fifty or a hundred coconut trees. Gunn tried in vain to stop it; some of the Ipau people pleaded for the trees too, and the headman of Imatangi, seeing their displeasure, promised it would not happen again. With small exceptions, it did not.
GF 202 · 215 · 275

The law of exchange

The governing rule of Futunese economics

Every feast had to be paid for by an equal quantity of food: yam for yam, pig for pig, banana for banana. The same principle ran through every transaction; every article had to be paid for, and every service was repaid in kind or by a feast. When food was distributed a portion was set aside for each village or premises and subdivided until everyone had a share.

Behind the rule lay a belief: the Futunese held that if they ate the food they themselves had planted, or the fish they themselves had caught, they would die. So they exchanged with their neighbours. A man who did not share his food was accused of greed — greed being one of the only two sins the old religion recognised.

Gunn describes one such exchange at length, and it is worth recording because it is so unlike a European feast. A heap of food was laid in the public square and word sent to another district that it was waiting. Next day the guests filed in one by one, each carrying a yam, a sweet potato or a bunch of bananas. The hosts sat about, looking on. The guests quietly piled up their food until a heap of equal size stood beside the first. Then, whispering among themselves, they broke down the heap assigned to them, each man taking a yam, a bundle of sweet potatoes or a bunch of bananas in return for his own. That done, they stepped out one behind the other, without a look at their hosts, and went home. Not a word had passed between givers and guests.

The same etiquette governed small things. Given food by the missionary, a Futunese would eat it if alone; if two stragglers were near he gave it to them — so to be sure the right person got it, one had to hand it to them, since by native etiquette they would pass it on to him. No stranger went to another’s house without a present, though it might be only a few coconuts or a stick of sugar-cane. And because every service was repaid, a man whose house burned down was often left to rebuild it alone: to offer help was read as a mild suggestion that one wanted a feast, and he would rather work alone than part with his food.

GF 208–209 · 255 · 276

Tapu

Tapu — sacred, and therefore forbidden — was the main instrument of prohibition, and it belonged largely to the chiefs. Anything good that the chiefs did not want the common people to have or use was made tapu, that is, reserved to themselves: good fishing places, good springs of water. Coconuts were made tapu so that they might multiply for the feasts, the owner binding leaves round the trunks to prevent theft.

Kind of tapuEffect
On a food or a treeWhoever broke through it became sick. Illness was often put down to a broken tapu. Only the owner of the trees — or sometimes a specialist — could cure that sickness.
On landForbidding a man to cultivate certain ground.
On a placeForbidding a man to enter it.
Of expulsionOn Futuna, a tapu could order a man to leave the district altogether.
SeasonalPork was tapu while new gardens were being made; bananas were tapu to the fishers through the flying-fish season; the sacred men who had power over the breadfruit could not touch water during their ceremonies and had to abstain from certain foods.
PenaltyWhoever disregarded a tapu, native or foreigner, did so at his peril: the penalty was death. With Christianity the tapus were given up.

Shortly after the mission goat-house was burned in February 1888, a tapu was noticed at the mission premises — a signal that the Gunns were ordered to leave the island. Gunn pulled out the reeds in front of the people and threw them away. When it became known across the island that a tapu had been set before the mission, many of the Futunese were angry; the people of Iasoa came saying, “Missi, don’t leave us, stay to teach us” — one of the most encouraging things that had yet been said to them. Who set the tapu was never learned, though Gunn suspected Saula Sore.

GF 39 · 66 · 213–214 · 222

Sorcery, and the law of death

The whole system of justice rested on a single premise: no one died a natural death except in extreme old age. Everyone who died before then, apart from those killed in war, had died through sorcery. The disease-makers were believed to work by secretly picking up scraps of the victim’s food, hairs from his head, or the earth from under his feet, and burning them with incantations. The person who had dropped the food or shed the hair then sickened and died.

  • When someone fell ill, his friends sent presents to the witch-doctors to stop the process; if some fragments were saved from the burning, the sick recovered. Such was the terror of the disease-makers that large presents were given to stop the sorceries.
  • When the sick died, the sorcerer was blamed — and their crimes gave rise to war. On Futuna the body was left half-buried in the grave while the friends looked for the disease-maker, so that he might be killed in revenge.
  • The belief itself became one of the chief obstacles to the gospel: people said that gathering for worship gave the disease-makers their opportunity to pick up scraps of food and hair.
  • The fear only broke when the disease-makers themselves gave up the art and threw away their sacred stones. The common people, who had lived in terror of them, then lost their fear altogether. “The Good Word,” they said, destroys their power.
GF 212–213 · 214 · 254 · 259

Cutting the canoe, and carrying it

Tavaka — the canoe

To “cut a canoe” meant, in the figurative speech of the island, that someone should be put to death to remove a disease and placate the gods. The heathen understood it plainly as a sacrifice, and told Gunn afterwards that it had been effective in securing plenty of food. To “carry the canoe” meant that the whole island, including those made outcasts by the killing, must unite in feasting as a pledge of keeping the peace and preventing further disease-making.

This is not an antiquarian note. It happened in Gunn’s first years. In 1886 the sacred stones and the sacred banyan at Ipau were destroyed; the Imatangi people, who refused to give up theirs, predicted that judgment would fall on Ipau for it. Influenza then raged through Futuna and the talk of cutting a canoe began. For weeks groups of Futunese discussed tavaka, even inside the mission enclosure. Then the talk stopped, and the sick began to recover.

One night in May 1887 a rifle went off close to the mission house. Gunn found Basulu — a handsome, strong, dignified man, brother of Saula Sore — lying dead in the kava-house with a jagged wound in his back. The men had been sitting at a feast a few yards from the mission premises when the shot rang out and the bullet passed Popoina’s face. Asked what it meant, Popoina answered with one word: Tavaka. Basulu had boasted of originating the influenza and had disregarded the talk of the canoe. His own father had ordered him shot, and was obeyed. The killer was Anapapo — a young man raised in the worship, taught to pray by his great-grandmother, once asked to pray over the food at a feast because so few could, and charged by Mr Copeland to help lead the services at Iraro.

At the burial next day about two hundred people came in from every district, all armed with loaded muskets, clubs, killing stones and spears, some covered with the dust of years. Boys of ten and twelve carried clubs or bows and arrows. Black paint, the sign of war, was on their faces; Kavahe and his brother Tafa were painted ebony black to the eyes. Gunn’s cry that no second person should be shot — called out without his knowing why — stopped Saula Sore, who was at that moment taking aim inside the kava-house at a relative of Kavahe. He learned of it only eighteen months afterwards.

The killing did not banish the sickness; the influenza lingered. Then the island had to carry the canoe. Kavahe and others brought food again and again as a bait, with threats if it were refused, and the food was left untouched. Highways were blocked, and after dark men were posted to throw stones at anyone crossing the barrier. Ipau at last gave way; Yarai was appointed leader and director of the feasting, and was, by his own account, “so angry about carrying the canoe” that he could have killed someone. Saula, Gunn’s pundit, alone took no part in it. In the end there was more stealing, more immorality, more fear of disease-making and more rumour of war than before the murder; the sick died through neglect; and heathenism, in Gunn’s judgement, had been put on trial and had failed.

GF 54–63 · 70 · L IV 166

Revenge, and the settling of disputes

RuleApplication on Futuna
An eye for an eyeIn heathen times every injury, great or small, done to person or property — and every hard word — was avenged. If a man of one tribe killed or wounded another, the dead man’s friends killed or wounded someone of that tribe. If a father scolded his son, the son ran away to his friends in revenge. If a husband was unfaithful, the wife revenged herself by being unfaithful too.
Brothers defend their sistersBrothers were the special defenders of a sister’s good name, and not infrequently put to death those who dishonoured her.
The duty of burialSons and daughters were bound by native law to bury their parents, and few would willingly leave it undone. Men wanting to go abroad were often held back by being reminded of it; when they went anyway, their friends asked Gunn to write and beg them to come home and bury their parents.
The brother takes the widowWhen a man died leaving a wife, with or without children, his brother took her to be his wife. Saula Sore took Namuli in this way.
Blocking the roadsIn time of war the highways were blocked to keep the enemy back, and travellers went by the byways.
Reconcile before sunsetWhen two parties quarrelled, a third sometimes came between them saying that the sun had not yet set, and they should be reconciled while it was day. Gunn notes this and one other maxim — “take up your trouble and carry it; do not run away from it” — as rules of conduct existing among the Futunese independently of Christianity, and before it.
The pillar as witnessWhen the people near the mission broke a promise not to attend a distant heathen dance, a young man set up a pillar in the public square as a witness against them — and then went himself; whereupon another young man set up a second pillar beside the first, as witness of his fickleness.
The oathOn Aneityum and Efate, placing the hand under the thigh was a way of making a solemn declaration — a form of oath.
Finding a thiefA coconut-shell drinking vessel was set on the ground and turned by a stick pushed into the opening, with a small shell laid on top. As the performer turned it he named the suspects rapidly, and the shell stuck fast to the nut as the guilty one was named. Gunn suspected a juice rubbed on the nut.
GF 214 · 275–280

The palaver: how public business was done

The native parliaments, or palavers, were chiefly harangues by the island orators on witchcraft, wind-making and drought-making, followed by a small feast. The men always came armed, and sometimes a fight broke out; Gunn therefore opposed the continuing of them, and they were given up. In ordinary courts the figurative language was set aside, and where mission questions were involved he sat with the chiefs to advise them.

The speech of the palavers was itself a barrier. Only a man well versed in the parabolic style of Futunese oratory could follow the speakers; young men told Gunn that the allusions and parables of the orators were often unintelligible to them. This was not accidental. It allowed men to talk openly about their plans while covering the meaning — plots hatched in private stayed hidden until the appointed day, friend and enemy meeting on the paths and in the square with apparent friendliness in the meantime. The name of a chief was used for his whole tribe, so that go thou abroad, said by one chief to another in war, meant that his people were to leave the island; and the crime will be found with Nauiakasi meant that one of his tribe was guilty.

When the palavers ceased the parabolic style began to decline with them, and the people came to understand that God’s Word and the missionary’s message were not parables either. The older Futunese speakers in church still used figurative language: asked to denounce a proposal to revive the heathen dancing, Nauni preached vigorously about a wild beast that was abroad and would eat them if they let it into their houses. The young men understood him at once. The children had no idea what he meant.

GF 161 · 164–165 · 211 · 250 · 277

Food rules

Gunn, writing for a church readership, noticed that Futunese food custom ran directly opposite to the Levitical law at almost every point, and the list is a useful record of what was actually eaten and how:

Futunese practiceNote
Blood was cooked and eaten with relishPigs were sometimes strangled rather than clubbed, precisely to prevent the blood escaping.
Pigs were prized everywhereThey were the currency of rank, of bride-payment, of feasting and of peace-making.
Fish without scales were valued above others—
Anything that died of itself was readily eaten—
CookingGreat pits formed the ovens. The dismembered pigs were wrapped in leaves and laid in with puddings, yams and bananas; stones heated almost red hot were scattered among them, lifted with tongs made of a stick split three-quarters of its length; leaves, mats and earth were spread over, and the mound left to steam for hours or all night. Opened, the food was well cooked and the juices kept in.
GF 210 · 280–281

A Genealogy of the Gospel in Futuna · page 12 of 18

The life course: birth to burial

BIRTH · NAME · MARRIAGE · DEATH

Every stage of a Futunese life, and the ceremony and rule attaching to it.

Press / to search

01

The life course: birth, name, marriage, death

Every stage of a Futunese life was marked by a ceremony and governed by a rule. This section follows the course from the halloo that greeted a birth to the feast that ended the mourning. It is placed here because the register that follows — who was whose son, who was betrothed to whom, who was named by whom, who buried whom — only makes sense against it.

Birth

The birth of a boy

Custom

The women attending the mother gave a joyful halloo announcing the birth. The men in the public square heard it and rushed out in frantic joy for their clubs, to celebrate the event with a sham fight. A feast was made at a birth, as at every other important occasion.

GF 204 · 208

The birth of a girl

Custom

No sound of gladness greeted the birth of girls. Sometimes the unwelcome baby escaped with her life only narrowly: the friends, or the mother, threw her into the bush, and she might be saved by someone willing to adopt her. Infanticide, though not general, was common in the islands. The reason Gunn gives is labour — the work of caring for an infant, digging the gardens, preparing food and feeding the pigs was too great; so the child was sacrificed and the pigs were tended for the coming feast.

Two of the principal figures in this record survived that custom. Habena, who became the first pastor of Futuna, was thrown out into the bush by his mother on Aneityum and searched for and saved by his father. The wife of the late pastor of Aneityum was cast out in the same way, and her father likewise saved her life.

GF 204 · L IV 179

Naming

A name was given soon after birth by the father, the mother, or a relative. The rules attaching to it were substantial and economic, not merely sentimental:

  • The one who named the child set apart land and fruit-trees for its use, and the child, when grown, was expected to visit and work for that relative. A name was therefore a property settlement.
  • If the baby cried habitually the name was changed, because — they said — either the child, or the spirit of the person it was called after, objected to it.
  • If a growing child showed bad traits the name was changed again, on the reasoning that he was becoming like some bad person of the same name; changing the name was believed to alter the child’s nature.

The same instinct survives in the Christian record. When Roroveka fell off his seat asleep during the night’s translation work, just as Gunn read the passage about Eutychus falling from the window, the incident was retailed in the public square and Roroveka was called Eutychus for years afterwards.

GF 62 · 204

Childhood and the passage to manhood

StageWhat happened
Ear-piercingThe ear was pierced in childhood and the hole enlarged until a circular piece of wood an inch and a quarter across could be put in; some preferred tortoise shell cut in strips or made into chains. Unlike most of the ornament customs, this one was religious, not decorative — the door-keeper of the spirit-land rolled a stone over those who came to him with unpierced ears.
BelongingChildren, males especially, became the property of the tribe to which the mother belonged.
Before circumcisionBoys lived with their mothers and went naked.
CircumcisionPerformed in many of the islands in childhood or early youth; in the south at the age of eight or ten. A lad was set apart to attend the boy and put his food into his mouth. At the end of a month he was led to the marae with great acclamation. He was then clothed with the belt and pendant of the men and took his place among them at work and in the ceremonies. It was both a religious and a social rite: until it was done the boys were children; after it they were young men.
GamesSpinning tops made of shells and of a hard fruit; whips for cracking, made from the bark of a tree; swings from strong creepers; foot races, canoe races and tug-of-war; tig; hide and seek; throwing the reed; and guessing games.
Why circumcision matters to this record

On some islands the missionaries left the rite alone. On Futuna it was an issue from Mr Copeland’s time, because the ceremonial surrounding it involved the whole tribe. Early in 1885 Gunn learned that five youths were to be circumcised. The ceremony was kept in total secrecy and his best leaders were involved and deceived him; only Saula stood out. A total reversion to heathenism followed, months passed before any of those involved came back to worship, old vices resurfaced, and heathen dancing at Isia drew the whole population, the dancers disguised in leaves, mats, baskets and calico. It went on for weeks. That was the last heathen fling on Futuna.

Yarai was the first Futunese to break it. He had complained that they “stole” his elder son for the ceremony; he promised that no heathen ceremony would be performed on his second son, and kept the promise. Others imitated him, and within a few years the custom had died in the Christian districts. In 1897 Gunn could report that the ceremony had been banished from five of the six districts. Miller records the same event from the other end: Yarai, one of the two lads taken to New Zealand by Bishop Selwyn in 1851, was the first Futuna man to give up an important heathen ceremony.

GF 92–93 · 207 · 279 · L I 30 · L IV 165 · 177

Betrothal and marriage

RuleHow it worked
Betrothal from birthCousins of the opposite sex — the children of a brother and a sister — were betrothed from birth. A boy, while still a child, called his female cousin “my wife”, and she called him “my husband”.
Release from betrothalIf the boy on growing up did not want his betrothed, his friends found him another wife. But no one could take his first betrothed without his sanction, or without paying him for her in full.
Marriage a business transactionThe parties were betrothed in infancy, or an agreement was made between the parents without consulting the girl. Payment was made in pigs for a wife, or more rarely by a feast to the wife’s friends.
AgeExcept in the islands where there was child marriage, girls were married when they reached womanhood. Futuna had no child marriage.
Etiquette of silenceBrothers were not supposed to know the arrangements for their sisters’ marriages; to speak of it to them in the presence of others was a breach of etiquette, though it could be done privately.
The sister-wives ruleA husband called each of his wife’s sisters “my wife”; if his wife died he took one of her unmarried sisters. A wife spoke of her husband’s brothers as “my husbands”.
PolygamyCommon, especially among chiefs. On Futuna many chiefs had two wives and a few had three; elsewhere in the group some had ten or more. Peace was rare where there was more than one wife. Where there were several, one usually held the position of wife and the others were concubines or slaves.
The reproach of the unmarriedTo be unmarried was a reproach. If a girl refused several offers, the men of Futuna — with the approval of the chiefs — sometimes bound themselves not to marry her, so that she should be ashamed and her unmarried state be a reproach to her.
Marrying above one’s rankCommon people were sometimes unwilling to marry the daughter or sister of a chief, since a high price was expected and the husband became the chief’s servant. “It is not a light thing to marry the sister of the chief,” a poor man would say; “I have not a pig to give him.”
ElopementAfter the great feasts it would be found that a girl, the belle of the district, had disappeared, and days later she was seen in another part of the island, having eloped with a young chief. It was well if war did not follow. Sometimes the girl was sent back, or a compromise made by sending another in exchange.
GF 205–207 · 211 · 250 · 277 · L IV 169

The married state

In heathenism, Gunn writes, the marriage bond was the weakest of all and the most easily broken. The wife was the mother of her husband’s children; otherwise she was his property. The husband owned his gardens apart from her and she had no share in his possessions. What she brought with her from her parents was her own, and sometimes what she afterwards earned; but she had to dig for him and weave mats and baskets, the price of which he claimed, occasionally favouring her with a part of it. She was his servant and often his slave. The husband might be unfaithful with impunity; the wife, if she proved untrue, might be beaten or cast adrift.

Futuna, however, was not the worst case in the group, and the record should say so plainly. There was no caste and no child marriage. Widows were not strangled, as they were in heathen times on Aneityum, where women wore a marriage rope round the neck instead of a ring and were strangled with it at their husband’s death so that their spirits might wait on him in the lower world. The number of women on Futuna was equal to or greater than the number of men, so polygamy pressed less heavily on the common people. There were wife-beaters, but they had no public sympathy.

What the Futunese women did instead, when accused of unfaithfulness or in jealousy or anger, was to kill themselves — commonly by leaping over the rocks. Teiau, the wife of Saula and the first Futunese woman to break from heathenism, limped all her life and bore the effects of a broken jaw from a leap off a cliff as a young wife. Quarrels among the women themselves were frequent and violent; the men would sometimes settle a dispute peaceably, but a woman would bring a club and incite her son or a relative to fight. In thirty years, Gunn says, he never once saw a woman try to stop a fight.

GF 94–95 · 202–203 · 250 · L IV 169 · 174

Sickness and the native doctors

PracticeMethod
MedicineThe native doctors were specialists who professed to cure only a few complaints each. The juice of certain leaves formed their medicines. Foreign drugs were quickly preferred once known.
FracturesThey set fractures and used splints, but held a wrong principle of healing: a simple fracture was converted into a compound one by cutting an opening near the break to let out the bad. Suppuration often followed and the bone took months to heal. They were careless about rest, and limbs failed to unite properly.
TrepanningPerformed in several islands when the skull was broken in warfare. The bone was laid bare by cutting through skin and flesh and scraped a little each day with a shell, as much as the patient could bear, until it was all removed; the wound was then let heal. When glass became available it replaced the shell and the work went faster. One man on Futuna who had undergone the operation about 1883 was still alive thirty years later.
Incisions and venesectionCutting over the seat of pain to let the pain out was the commonest remedy. Bleeding at the elbow vein, introduced by the Samoans, spread through the group.
Counter-irritantsHeated stones, leaves warmed at the fire, or the scrapings of a certain root which blistered more powerfully than mustard.
GF 211–212

Death and burial

  • Who was buried and who was not. In the southern islands the chiefs were usually buried; the common people were thrown into the sea. In inland districts the dead were laid in caves. The burying-ground was usually in or near the premises.
  • Burial at sea. The bodies committed to the sea were generally weighted with stone and hurled over a precipice.
  • The half-burial. On Futuna the body was left half buried in the grave while the friends searched for the disease-maker, so that he might be killed in revenge.
  • The fire for the spirit. On both Aneityum and Futuna a fire was lit at which the spirit might warm itself before going down to the lower world; while it burned, the friends of the dead made their escape from him. If the fire were neglected, the spirit would visit them at night, lay a cold clammy hand on them and call out in a shrill unearthly voice for fire.
  • The trees. After the burial the fruit-trees belonging to the dead were cut down — see Customary law.
  • The words. When a Futunese died the phrase used was that he had been gathered to his people: his spirit had gone to the land of spirits, to be with the friends who died before him.

The signs of mourning

The men

Mourning

They bathed after a burial and did not go near the sea again for several days. They cut off their long hair — the great labour of the Futunese male toilet, three to five hundred bound locks — as the sign of grief, and wore old ornaments.

When Mrs Copeland was buried on Futuna in January 1876, having come back to the island to die among the people she had served, fifty men cut off their long hair; and fifty received books.

GF 216 · 280

The grave-diggers

Mourning

Those who dug the grave did not touch food with their hands, believing that their teeth would fall out if they did, and did not dig their gardens, lest the fruit should not grow. For months after the burial they carried a piece of coconut cloth into which friends placed their food.

GF 216

The women

Mourning

They put away their ornaments, hung long strings of old worn shells round their necks, and put on old tattered skirts. The wailing for the dying — the calling of the name into space, to bring the spirit back — was women’s work.

GF 216 · 223

The end of it

Mourning

All ended with a feast, at which the signs of mourning were put off. The ceremonial for the dead showed, Gunn observes, that the Futunese recognised a future; and that they were trying to please the shades of dead friends who had now become angry, malicious spirits.

GF 215–216

A Genealogy of the Gospel in Futuna · page 13 of 18

What men, women and children did and did not do

THE ORDINARY CONDUCT OF LIFE

Who did what work, who wore what, who ate where — and what each was forbidden to do.

Press / to search

01

What men, women and children did and did not do

This section sets out the ordinary conduct of life on Futuna before the island became Christian — who did what work, who wore what, who ate where, and, just as importantly, what each was forbidden to do. The prohibitions are the more revealing half. Many of them carried no penalty but shame or sickness; several carried death. Everything here is drawn from Gunn, who lived among the people for thirty-four years and set it down while the last of the men who had kept these rules were still alive.

How to read the tables

Where a rule belonged to the whole New Hebrides rather than to Futuna in particular, it is marked (group). Where Futuna differed from its neighbours — and it differed in several important respects, generally to the advantage of its women — the difference is stated. Gunn uses the past tense for customs given up and the present for customs still practised in 1913; that distinction is preserved here.

The men

What the men didDetail
Worked in seasons, not steadilyIn times of peace they were employed in house-building, planting, fence-making, fishing and feasting. On fertile islands they were at regular labour only four months in the year; where nature was less kind, eight or ten. Futuna was among the most barren islands in the group, and the people planted in small stony plots that islanders elsewhere would not have troubled to dig.
Ate the chief meal apart, in the public squareAt evening the men ate in the square while the boys prepared the kava. This was the fixed daily rhythm of male life.
Drank kavaThey spat out the first mouthful, calling to the spirits, and after drinking the rest often sank down into a heavy, stupefied sleep. Towards midnight, on Futuna, they went out to fish or returned to their premises. Nearly every night in Ipau in the 1880s men — worshippers and heathen alike — were intoxicated with it.
Sang and danced through the nightAt the first sound of the native drum after dark, men and women flocked to the night-singing and kept it up till morning. At feasts they ranged themselves in the square on either side of a log, struck it with a slow regular beat, and sang and shouted until dawn. Dances were rehearsed in private for weeks until each man knew his part.
Dressed their hairIn the four southern islands the men divided the hair into three to five hundred locks, wound each with a white fibre and bound the whole with pandanus leaf — a style Gunn thought like Assyrian sculpture. The Futunese let it grow almost to the waist, forming a sort of queue.
Painted and ornamented themselvesFaces painted red, black, and sometimes yellow, in stripes or stars; black was the sign of mourning in the south, and also the sign of war. Long plumes of feathers and bright leaves in the hair; rings and beads at the neck; pendants cut from pearl shell or a disc of greenstone; armlets of coconut shell with variegated leaves stuck into them — and, once tobacco came, their pipes.
Advertised their standing at a feastA man bringing a pig to a feast on Futuna wore a bright-coloured dracaena in his armlet, so that onlookers might say: look, he has a pig at the feast.
Rose in rank by killing pigsTen, sometimes a hundred. Rank raised a man’s social position and with it his influence.
Went armedWhile heathenism was strong men never went unarmed into another district. They came armed even to the palavers, and sometimes a fight resulted. When they came to barter at the mission station there were so many muskets, clubs and bows that a stranger would have thought a battle was gathering; Gunn frequently failed to get them to leave loaded muskets outside the fence.
Made canoes, weapons and toolsAxes and adzes ground from hard volcanic stone and lashed into sockets with coconut-fibre sinnet, taken out each night and sharpened; gouges of shell. Futunese bows were five or six feet long; the killing stones, cut from the coral and about two feet long, were deadly at twenty yards. Fire was never used in hollowing out a canoe.
Fished by torchlightCatching flying fish by torch was confined to Futuna and Aniwa. The Futunese were the most assiduous fishers of the group along with the Aneityumese and Aniwans.
Smeared their chins with sootThe young men of Futuna did this to hasten the growth of their beards, and could not understand why a white man with such an easy beard should shave it off. Both sexes plucked out the first grey hairs; bald men covered their heads; and they would hardly allow a decayed tooth to be drawn, lest people should mock them as toothless with age.
What a man might not doReason or penalty
Eat pork while new gardens were being madeTapu — the yams would not grow. The builders of the first church threw away the pork the Gunns gave them, or passed it to the Aneityumese.
Eat bananas during the flying-fish seasonIt would spoil the fishing.
Touch water or eat certain foods (sacred men)Binding on the sacred men whose power was over the breadfruit, for the duration of their ceremonies.
Marry within the forbidden degreesThe children of two or more brothers, or of two or more sisters, were called brothers and sisters in the language, and it was against native law for them to intermarry. The prohibition extended to their grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
Take another man’s betrothedNot without his sanction, or without paying him for her in full.
Speak of a sister’s marriage arrangements before othersA breach of etiquette; brothers were not supposed to know. It could be done privately.
Appear before a sister in deshabille, or talk indecently within her hearingHighly improper in most, if not all, the islands. Gunn cites it as evidence of a real modesty among people the sources otherwise call savages.
Strike or cut the sacred banyanThe tree overhanging the dancing ground was specially sacred; no one dared touch it.
Look at the setting sun and its raysOn Futuna it meant death or sickness to the onlooker.
Go out of his premises alone at nightNot a prohibition but a fear — the air was full of spirits. Asked to go anywhere alone, a man would ask who was going with him.
Leave a parent unburiedSons and daughters were bound by native law to bury their parents. It was the standing excuse for refusing to go abroad as a teacher or servant.
Break a tapu of any kindSickness at least; and for the tapus forbidding cultivation, entry, or continued residence in a district, the penalty was death — for foreigner as well as islander.
Eat from a higher caste fire (group, north)Death. Futuna had no caste system; this applied in Malo, Malekula and Santo.
Keep food to himselfNot a law but an accusation: a man who did not share was charged with greed — one of the only two sins the old religion recognised.
GF 39 · 40 · 162 · 192–198 · 201–208 · 210–214 · 222 · 224 · 250 · 256 · 258 · 278

The women

Futuna was not the worst place in the group to be a woman

Gunn is blunt about the general position — across the New Hebrides the women were the slaves, valued for their strength and their ability to work, bought and sold like pigs, regarded as inferior beings and beaten for faults real or imaginary. But he is equally clear that on Futuna their lot was comparatively easy. There was no caste, no child marriage, and no strangling of widows. The number of women equalled or exceeded the number of men, so polygamy pressed less heavily on the common people. Husbands and wives lived in the same house except at certain seasons and worked together in their gardens. There were wife-beaters, but they had no public sympathy.

GF 94 · 202–203 · L IV 169
What the women didDetail
Carried the greater part of the food workIn heathen days the largest share of the labour of keeping the family in food fell on them: digging the gardens, preparing the food, feeding the pigs, caring for the infants.
WoveMats, baskets and fans from dried pandanus leaf. The chief basket-makers of a plain kind in the group were the Futunese. A wife had to weave for her husband, and he claimed the price of what she made, occasionally giving her part of it.
Fished with rod and lineAn explicit Futunese difference: in Futuna women as well as men used the rod and line.
Dressed better than the menUnder heathenism the women were the better clad. In the southern islands other than Erromanga and Tanna their skirts reached the knees; the men wore only a narrow belt with a pendant.
Wore flowers and shellBright flowers, and sometimes feathers, in the hair; rings or beads at the neck; on Futuna, pendants cut from pearl shell or a disc of greenstone.
Served in the templeTwo young women served as the sacred girls, or priestesses, through the ceremonial season — cooking the sacred taro each evening, lighting the sacred fire for the fishers, fetching the water for the men’s kava, and leading the procession of the catch with a garland and a face painted red on one side and black on the other. Basiva, mother of Saloki and Teitoka, had been one of them as a girl.
Took part in the ceremonies and dancesMen and women together danced their thanks to the god when the flying fish were brought up to the temple, and in some of the dances both sexes took part. The women made their own ceremonial feast, separately from the men, at the close of the fishing season.
Wailed for the dyingThe calling of the spirit back — naming the dying person and crying to them to return out of space — was women’s work. Almost every woman in a district would take up the lament in turn.
Quarrelled and foughtFights among the women were common; screaming would be heard, then the rattle of stones, and unless one party retreated it ended in bloodshed. A woman would bring a club and incite her son or a relative to fight. Gunn never once saw a woman try to stop a fight.
Killed themselvesWhen accused of unfaithfulness, or in jealousy or rage, Futunese women not infrequently committed suicide by leaping over the rocks. Teiau, the first Futunese woman to break from heathenism, survived such a leap as a young wife and carried a limp and a broken jaw for the rest of her life.
What a woman might not doReason or penalty
Appear in sight while the kava was brewedNo woman dared. The evening kava of the public square was closed to them absolutely.
Enter the amil (group, north)Death. No woman might appear in the northern marae, where the ten-foot painted figures stood. The equivalent southern ground, the marae under the banyan, was not closed to women in the same way — women took part in the Futunese ceremonies.
Eat with her husband (group, north)Women were outside caste and could never eat with their husbands. In the north they lived mostly apart from the men, in huts only four or five feet high with a hole two feet by three to crawl through. In the south — Futuna included — husbands and wives lived in the same house except at certain seasons.
Dress her hair in the men’s styleThere is a tradition that the women of Futuna once wore the long bound locks as the men did, and that the jealousy of the men forced them to give it up.
Be unfaithfulThe husband might be unfaithful with impunity; the wife, if she proved untrue, might be beaten or cast adrift — or would take her own life.
Own a share in her husband’s propertyHe owned his gardens apart from her. What she brought from her parents was her own, and sometimes what she afterwards earned; the rest, including the price of her weaving, was his.
Choose her own husbandBetrothed in infancy, or married by an agreement between the parents without being consulted.
Refuse offers of marriage without costIf a girl refused several offers, the men — with the chiefs’ approval — sometimes bound themselves not to marry her, so that being unmarried should be a reproach to her.
Survive her husband (group, Aneityum)On Aneityum a wife wore a marriage rope round the neck instead of a ring, and was strangled with it at her husband’s death so that her spirit might wait on him below; where there were several wives, one was sacrificed. The custom was imitated on Tanna and practised in Santo, and in the middle of the group chiefs’ wives were buried with them. On Futuna widows were not strangled.
Kneel before men (group, Ambrim)In Ambrim the women crawled on their knees before men; a party of them dropped to their knees at the sight of the Gunns’ small boy. Not a Futunese custom.

Gunn adds a note that belongs here. It was harder to raise the women than the men: they were slower to learn to read, less quick to grasp the teaching, and more wedded to the old customs. When the men had given up their ceremonies before the advance of Christianity, the women clung to theirs, and it was only through the stern determination of chiefs and teachers that the women gave them up.

GF 94–96 · 192–195 · 197–198 · 202–203 · 220 · 223 · 250 · 277 · L IV 169 · 174

The children

What the children didDetail
Inherited land at birthEvery child had its own plot of ground and its own fruit-trees, inherited from father, mother, uncles or aunts, or given by the friend who named it.
Worked for the one who named themWhen the child grew up he or she was expected to visit and work for that relative, who had set apart land and fruit-trees at the naming.
Belonged to the mother’s tribeMales especially. Chiefly succession often passed to the son of the late chief’s sister or niece.
Were betrothed from birthCousins of the opposite sex — children of a brother and a sister — called each other “my wife” and “my husband” while still children.
Had their ears piercedIn childhood, the hole enlarged until a wooden disc an inch and a quarter across could be worn. A religious custom, not an ornamental one.
Boys lived with their mothers, naked, until circumcisionAt eight or ten in the southern islands they were circumcised, attended for a month by a lad who put their food into their mouths, then led to the marae with great acclamation and clothed with the belt and pendant of the men.
PlayedSpinning tops of shell and of a hard fruit; whips for cracking made from the bark of a tree; swings from strong creepers; foot races, canoe races and tug-of-war; tig; hide and seek; throwing the reed; guessing games. They laughed and shouted at their games as if they were the happiest people alive.
Carried weapons when the island was armedAt Basulu’s burial in 1887 boys of ten and twelve carried clubs, or bows and arrows, among the two hundred armed men who came in.
Prepared the kavaThe boys made it ready in the public square each evening while the men ate.
Were cruel to animalsGunn records it as an everyday sight: it was the greatest amusement to mutilate and torture birds and insects, and it was never supposed that the lower creation felt pain. Pigs and fowls were maimed to stop them roaming, and fowls sometimes plucked alive before cooking.
Learned the natural world thoroughlyAgainst that, the faculty of observation was highly cultivated. Even the most unlettered could name most of the trees and plants, describe the habits of insects and birds, classify the shells, and name the chief constellations — the Pleiades, the Great Bear, Orion, the Milky Way — by which their fathers had steered canoes to other islands.
What was not done to, or by, childrenReason or consequence
They were seldom chastisedThey might be scolded, but were rarely punished. The parents excused their leniency by saying the children would retaliate when they reached maturity. Not infrequently they grew up idle and dependent; when hungry they would sometimes stone their parents, who were afraid to check them lest they run away to their friends.
They ran away when crossedAnd stayed with relatives until, in the Futunese phrase, their anger was finished, or until their parents fetched them back. Gunn saw children throw themselves down in fits of rage, strike their heads on the ground and scream for hours.
A girl’s birth was not welcomedNo halloo, no sham fight; and sometimes the child was thrown into the bush to die, or to be picked up by whoever would adopt her.
They might not marry those called brother and sisterThe children of two brothers, or of two sisters, however distant — the prohibition ran to the third and fourth remove.
Brothers and sisters kept a strict reserveIt was highly improper for them to appear before each other in deshabille, or to speak indecently within each other’s hearing.
Books were feared before they were prizedIn the early mission years the children were afraid to take their books home; they left them at school or hung them in baskets on a tree. Their books, like the fetishes, were feared: to keep them in the house while heathen ceremonies were being performed would be death. Within a few years the books were their treasures — the first thing, with the clothing, they ran to save from a fire.
GF 57 · 93 · 193 · 202–208 · 250–253 · 258

The household and its premises

The Futunese hut was simply the roof of a house set down on the ground, the doorway usually at the end and closed with coconut matting, and about six feet high. Its contents under heathenism were spears, clubs, bows and arrows; perhaps a digging stick; paddles; coconut drinking vessels; sleeping mats, native pillows and baskets; a few yams, a bunch of bananas, and quite possibly a pig or two. The premises were fenced, often screened with coconut leaves for privacy.

Attached to every village was a public square, in which the kava-house stood: the place where the men sat, held their palavers, made their feasts and drank their kava. The kava-house was large, and in some islands grimly ornamented with the skulls of enemies taken in war, though generally with the jawbones of pigs killed at feasts. The marae lay under a spreading banyan and was the ground for ceremonies, for dancing, and sometimes for a fight; in the south it held an altar, with sacred stones scattered round it representing the gods.

Gunn notes what changed. With the spread of Christianity houses became larger and stronger, with walls and a wooden door; in many Christian villages people were building lime houses with a raised platform for a bed, perhaps a table and chairs, yam spades, a basket of books, and a box or two holding the family’s clothing and valuables. On Futuna itself the huts remained poor — the sites, on so precipitous an island, were cramped, stony and uneven, and there was a great lack of durable building timber.

GF 163 · 194–196

The character the sources describe

Gunn devotes a chapter to Futunese character, and it is a hard one; it should be read with his own qualification, which he supplies at the end of it and which this record keeps. He describes people who were clannish and would rush for their weapons to help a kinsman; who could not keep a secret, so that a whisper of sorcery passed from mouth to mouth until the supposed sorcerer was killed or the talk was ended by a feast; who nevertheless concealed a plot perfectly until the appointed day; who counted honour to lie in gaining an object rather than in gaining it fairly, and preferred treachery to risk; who were envious of a neighbour’s possessions and shared out prizes for the sake of peace; who were fulsome in flattery and rare in gratitude; who were industrious at planting time and lay till noon at others.

He also records the other side, and insists on it: that they tended the sick carefully and crowded round a bedside in sympathy; that they had their own etiquette and marks of respect and could be courteous and deferential; that they were as trustful as children, which is what made them easy prey to the recruiters of the labour trade; that there was a real modesty among them; that they saw through a joke quickly and told jokes against each other; and that behind the cold Futunese exterior lay a deep feeling that rarely surfaced. Told that his stepson had died, Popoina said only “Indeed!” — and was afterwards seen to have been cut to the heart. Saula Sore, asked whether he missed his murdered brother Basulu, answered that when he walked along the path he remembered that they two used to walk together, and when he went to his plantation he remembered that they always went together, and that he thought of him wherever he went.

Gunn’s own conclusion is that both descriptions are partly true and neither alone is honest; that the dark picture was mainly the character formed by heathenism; and that vanity, cruelty to animals, carelessness, ingratitude and superstition are common to human nature everywhere, and that it was the gospel which liberated his own forefathers from the same.

GF 248–260

A Genealogy of the Gospel in Futuna · page 14 of 18

The passing of the customs, 1866–1913

A DATED REGISTER

Which custom went, when, and on whose initiative — and what survived.

Press / to search

01

The passing of the customs, 1866–1913

The old religion did not fall at a stroke. Gunn’s own phrase is that heathenism rarely dropped off at once; in most converts it “died by inches”. This section is a dated register of the inches — which custom went, when, and on whose initiative. It is the hinge between the customary sections above and the chronology of the mission below, and it is the part of the record most worth checking against the memory of families still living on the island.

DateCustomWhat happened
1859The temple of AmoshishikiRebuilt for the last time, with its row of eight pillars for the eight principal deities. When the pillars rotted they were not replaced and the roof settled down onto the ground. Gunn found the struggle that ended the ceremonies conducted there already belonging to Mr Copeland’s period.
1866–76Ceremonies in the templeAbandoned during Copeland’s residence. Gunn records that when Copeland left in 1876 the back of heathenism had been broken, though no convert had yet been baptised and no church formed.
Jan 1876Mourning by cutting the hairAt the burial of Mrs Copeland, who had come back to Futuna to die among her people, fifty men cut off their long hair in the customary sign of mourning; and fifty received books. The old sign and the new thing arrived on the same day.
Early 1885Circumcision (first crisis)Five youths were circumcised in total secrecy; Gunn’s best leaders took part and deceived him, and only Saula stood clear. A general reversion followed. Heathen dancing at Isia drew the whole population, the dancers disguised in leaves, mats, baskets and calico, and it ran on for weeks. Miller calls it the last heathen fling.
1886The sacred stones and the sacred banyan at IpauTwo men of the mission village told Gunn he should get rid of the stones in the marae and burn the banyan, as these were “the root of heathenism”. The desire to root them out spread and was acted on. Saula and Popoina handed over the stones they used for success in fishing. Habena failed to persuade the Imatangi people to give up theirs, and they predicted that judgment would fall on Ipau for what had been done.
May 1887Human sacrifice — “cutting the canoe”Influenza followed the burning of the fetishes and the talk of tavaka began. Basulu was shot dead in the kava-house at Ipau on the order of his own father. This is the last recorded sacrifice on Futuna. The influenza did not stop.
1887–88“Carrying the canoe”The island-wide reconciliation feasting that followed a killing. Ipau resisted, then gave way; Yarai was made director of the feasting and hated it; Saula alone took no part. It produced more stealing, more fear and more rumour of war than before, and men left the island rather than carry it on. The last such cycle on Futuna.
Feb 1888The tapu of expulsionA tapu was set at the mission premises ordering the Gunns to leave the island. Gunn pulled out the reeds in front of the people and threw them away, and the island’s reaction was anger at whoever had placed it. The last attempt to use a tapu against the mission.
c.1888Felling the dead man’s treesAfter a young man died at Ipau, people from Imatangi and Isia felled fifty or a hundred coconut trees. The Ipau people themselves objected, and the headman of Imatangi promised it would not happen again. Gunn records this as the last time, with small exceptions, that the custom was heard of.
1889–90Circumcision (first refusal)Yarai promised that no heathen ceremony would be performed on his second son, having complained that his elder son had been “stolen” for it. He kept the promise; others imitated him; and within a few years the custom had died in the Christian districts. Miller records Yarai as the first Futuna man to give up an important heathen ceremony.
1890Custom marriageThe first Christian marriage on Futuna: the widowed Habena married Laku, and the whole island looked on and wondered. Popoina’s verdict — “It has come to stay”. A second followed the same year. Then two and a half years passed before another was asked for.
1891Rain-making, and heathen feastingThe Gunns returned from furlough to find that heathen feasting had been given up by the Christian population, and that three rain-makers had come forward, publicly handed over their sacred stones and joined the communicants’ class. The stones were put in a pit in the public square to be burned at the weekly meeting; asked who would light them, Nauiakasi stepped forward at once.
1891–92Dressing the hairMen who had revived the long bound locks were barred from working on the new church — “it is tapu for you to work at the house of God when you are bringing back heathenism”. Tafa sat idle for a day, then cut his hair and became one of the best workmen; others followed, one borrowing Mrs Gunn’s scissors to do it. The custom was eradicated in Ipau and Isia.
c.1892Heathen dancingGunn records that the native dances could not be separated from the immorality that went with them, and that the Christians gave them up of their own accord — not by missionary prohibition. When some young men proposed reviving the dancing, Nauni was asked to denounce it in church and did so in parable, as a wild beast abroad.
1890sThe palaversThe armed public assemblies with their harangues on witchcraft, wind-making and drought-making were opposed by Gunn because men came armed and fights broke out, and they were given up. With them the parabolic style of oratory began to decline — and, Gunn thought, the assumption that the missionary’s message was itself only a parable.
1897Circumcision, formally; custom marriageGunn reported that the heathen ceremony of circumcision had been banished from the five Christian districts, and that Christian marriage was now the law, though the chiefs were not always able to enforce it. A sacred man with power over the breadfruit gave up his stones. Of Imounga he wrote that even on their own confession they were forgetting their heathen customs.
1899The isolation of ImoungaThe heathen stronghold held out until a magic-lantern exhibition at Ipau, which they could not resist. They came down, asked for more, and heard the gospel. Measles carried off many of their old men the same year, including Yaupa, whom Gunn reckoned about 130 and who had remembered the arrival of the Samoans in 1840.
1900The marae itselfA substantial church was built at Imounga on the public marae, ground sacred to the old gods — the timber hauled up the cliffs piece by piece. Nauiakasi of Iasoa had demanded that it be built in Imounga, on his land, in the public square. Many were still afraid of such a building standing among them.
1904What was leftThe church had 60 members, 210 regular worshippers and 70 children in the day schools; nine marriages were celebrated in the year. Ten members were under discipline for offences mainly connected with heathen customs — a fair measure of how much custom was still alive inside the church.
1905The last separationAt the Gunns’ farewell feast — made according to island custom, and inviting the whole island — the Imoungans came, with scraps of clothing to make them acceptable and big leaves for their share, shook hands and trooped into the Ipau church. Twenty-three years of waiting ended.
1906Heathenism as a public partyThe last of the heathen came into the church. Futuna was reckoned a Christian island. Saraji, the chief who had blocked the Imounga church for the sake of the land price, never made the break and died of tuberculosis a heathen; those implicated in the murder of the Samoans in 1843 all died heathen.
1907Dressing the hair (extinct)Gunn reported that the elaborate heathen dressing of the hair was now extinct, that only four men remained outside the worship, and that only three or four children were not at school.
1908KavaAll church members abstained, though some were still planting it. The chiefs decided to take it away: they uprooted about two boat-loads in two districts and destroyed it, the rest to be removed before Christmas. In the same year a deacon of chiefly rank was elected chief of the whole of Futuna — the first such appointment for some fifty years.
1913Gunn’s summaryWriting his book, he recorded that the arguments never had to be made: polygamy, heathen dancing, kava-drinking and the other customs disappeared, and died before the gospel light. Quarrelling had almost ceased; men no longer went armed; tapus had been given up; ear-piercing had been given up; and the young were growing up ignorant of the customs and beliefs of their fathers and mothers. Asked whether any of the old people still “whished” the gods out of their premises, a girl present laughed aloud: she had never heard of it.
GF 92–93 · 102–105 · 157 · 161–164 · 194 · 210–215 · 219 · L IV 165–166 · 170–171 · 177–183
What survived, and what has returned

This record ends its dated register in 1913 because that is where its primary source ends. It should not be read as saying that Futunese custom ended there. Several of the things described in the sections above outlived the mission period entirely — the reckoning of planting, harvest and sea journeys by the phases of the moon; the land law by which trees are owned apart from the ground they stand on; the naming of a child by a relative who then sets aside land for it; the obligation of exchange. Futuna today is known within Vanuatu for the strength of its custom dance, performed at weddings, church events and national occasions, and the island’s oral literature — the cycle of the culture hero Majihjiki, who is Gunn’s Amoshishiki under a modern spelling — was recorded in Futunese and English by Janet Dixon Keller and Takaronga Kuautonga of the Vanuatu Cultural Centre and published in 2007. Their work, and Arthur Capell’s of 1958, are listed in the references, and a reader who wants the Futunese account of these matters rather than the missionary’s should begin there.

01

Plates and maps

The complete illustration record of Gunn’s The Gospel in Futuna — twenty-three printed plate pages carrying thirty photographs and two maps — with a narrative under each. Several are portraits of people named in the register, and for some of them these are the only likenesses that survive.

Provenance and handling

The plates were extracted from the file Images.docx, which holds twenty-three page captures of the 1914 edition. Nothing in any photograph has been altered. Two mechanical steps were applied and no others: the surrounding screen and reader interface was cropped away so that only the printed page remains, and the plates that were printed landscape — and therefore captured on their side — were rotated upright. There has been no retouching, no cropping into the images themselves, no adjustment of tone, contrast or colour, and no reconstruction of damaged areas. The printed captions and page numbers are left in place, as part of the plate.

Resolution is limited by the captures, which were taken at screen size; each plate is shown at the largest size the source allows rather than enlarged. Click or tap a plate to open it at full size in a new tab.

The wider mission archive — how these pictures were used

02

How these plates were made and used

The plates above are evidence, but they are not neutral evidence, and a record that reproduces them owes the reader an account of what they were for. This section follows Lamont Lindstrom’s study of New Hebrides mission imagery, which treats Gunn’s own photographs as part of a very large publishing enterprise.

The trade

  • Mission pictures dominated the market. From the 1880s to the 1930s, images made by Presbyterian missionaries and their supporters swamped the world supply of views of the southwest Pacific, and of the New Hebrides in particular. Until the airfields and the cruise ships came after the Pacific War, they largely determined how island life was pictured abroad.
  • The same picture had several lives. One negative might appear as a book plate, a magic lantern slide and a picture postcard, recaptioned each time. Photographers in Sydney and Hobart — Henry King, J. W. Lindt, J. W. Beattie — converted mission negatives into slides and cards; Beattie alone produced some eight hundred New Hebrides postcards from one 1906 visit, and missionaries went into the postcard business themselves.
  • The pictures paid for the work. Missionaries on furlough toured Australia, New Zealand, Scotland and North America, lecturing with lantern slides and selling images to congregations who thereby came to know the Pacific at second hand. A contemporary guide to running a successful lantern evening advised borrowing postcard stands of the sort used on railway platforms.
  • The lantern worked both ways. On the islands the same apparatus showed Scripture slides. On Futuna it was a magic-lantern exhibition in 1899 that finally brought the Imoungans down from the district that had held out for twenty-three years.
  • Not all of it was drawn from life. Illustrators who had never met an islander supplied generic figures; the same engravings of a village “under heathenism” and “under Christianity” were lifted from a Cook Islands book of 1876 into a New Hebrides book of 1890 without anyone objecting.
LX 36–41 · 44 · 49 · L IV 177

The conventions, and where Futuna sits in them

ConventionWhat it didIn this record
Darkness and lightThe governing metaphor, taken from Scripture and used everywhere; white clothing in the illustrations carried both a spiritual and a racial charge.The mission ships were all named Dayspring; the jubilee history was called Light in Dark Isles; and Gunn’s own second book is Heralds of Dawn.
Before and afterPaired views of the same village, or the same kind of person, heathen and Christian.Gunn attempted it with two women, and it did not come off: his subject dressed for the camera. Plate 24.
SupplantingThe new building shown replacing the old — church and school against temple and kava house.The postcard at plate 27, against the Futunese fact: a church built on the public marae at Imounga in 1900, and two boat-loads of kava uprooted by the chiefs in 1908.
The passing of the oldOld men among broken idols, with a scrubbed Christian generation coming up behind.Plate 28 — and the “third generation” plate at plate 31 is the same argument made from Futuna.
RecaptioningOne photograph serving different purposes in different books.Plate 29: a photograph credited to Gunn, printed once as “the murderer of Gordon” and once with the man’s own name.
The Book as the missionary’s weaponA stock composition set the unarmed missionary, holding only the Bible, against a ring of islanders carrying clubs and muskets — the Book cast as the one weapon that would win where powder could not. Two of the most reproduced examples are Oscar Michelsen’s Cannibals Won for Christ (1893) and a plate in Paton’s Story.The trope had a literal counterpart on Futuna, but reversed: here it was the heathen who feared the Book. When Gunn first opened it among the Imoungans, saying they would worship God, they fled as though a bomb had been thrown among them; the disarming that actually took place was of the island — sacred fishing-stones handed in, the sacred banyan cut, and two boat-loads of kava uprooted by the chiefs in 1908.
Islanders as childrenFollowing Nicholas Thomas, Lindstrom notes that mission pictures reached more often for metaphors of age than of gender: the islander was a child, but a child who could grow up — be schooled, clothed and matured into an adult believer, an ultimate “sibling child of God” — where the colonial administrator’s imagery tended instead to fix the islander as permanently weak and in need of endless tutelage.The same parent-and-child language runs through the Futuna record from the other side: the people called the missionary and his wife father and mother, and the old addressed the young as my grandchild — kin-terms of the island’s own, onto which the mission’s picture of growth was laid.
LX 42–49 · 44 (the Book as weapon) · 47 (age metaphor, after Thomas) · GF 130–131, 153
What follows for this compilation

None of this makes the plates false. The people in them existed, the houses stood where they are shown, and several of the portraits are the only likenesses of persons in the register that survive anywhere. What it means is that a printed caption is an argument and not a label, and that the narratives on this page try to say what is in the picture before saying what the picture was for. Where a caption names somebody — Aresia, Manjau, Kavahé, Nauni, Teitoka, Yaupa, Laku, Mou — that naming is the most valuable thing in it, and this record treats it as the primary content of the plate.
