01

Dictionary

Words needed to read this record: Futunese terms recorded by Gunn, the vocabulary of the island world, and the offices of the mission church. Futunese is a Polynesian language, effectively the same as Aniwan, and unlike the Melanesian languages of its neighbours.

Futunese words and idioms

makiFutunese · verb

To be sick. The abstract noun is formed with a suffix: makinga, sickness. Gunn notes the same pattern across the group — mertaingina, goodness, in Santo; namarian, death, in Epi.

maraePolynesian · noun

Sacred ground: the open place under a spreading banyan where the people gathered for heathen ceremonies, dancing and sometimes fighting. In southern Vanuatu the marae held an altar and scattered sacred stones representing the gods. The Melanesian equivalent is the nakamal or amil. The church at Imounga was deliberately built on the marae — the headquarters of the gods.

tapuPolynesian · adjective

Sacred, and therefore forbidden. When the Gunns killed a pig for the men who built the first church, the men threw their portions away or gave them to the Aneityumese: they were making new gardens, and it was tapu to eat pork lest the yams should fail.

tiana / tionaFutunese · possessive

Two words for “his” or “her”. Tiana is used when the thing possessed is the owner’s special care; tiona when it is not. Thus tiana fine, his wife, and tiana pakasi, his pig — from which Gunn drew the dry conclusion that pigs, like wives, were objects of special care.

tano hiveFutunese · kin term

His sister, or her brother — used when the person owned is of the opposite sex to the possessor. The contrasting term is tano soa, his brother or her sister, where both are of the same sex. Many Melanesian languages make the same distinction; Aneityumese does it differently again, with natamaing iran, “the male of her”, for her brother.

teku nuane matuaFutunese · idiom

Literally “my old man”: my husband, or my lover. Its counterpart is tiaku fine matua, “my old woman”: my wife, or my sweetheart. As in English these are words of endearment; unlike English, Gunn notes, they were not used in public.

tafonu / tafonufonuFutunese · reduplication

A turtle; and an insect resembling a turtle. Reduplication runs through Melanesian and Polynesian languages and is used to intensify, belittle, magnify or multiply the root sense. Other examples Gunn gives: nongarue, to move, and nongaruerue, to move gently; kosashina, to forbid him, and kosasashina, to forbid them.

MissiFutunese and general · title

The missionary. Spelt also Misi; Misisi was used for his wife, or for a single woman missionary. It is the commonest word in this record after the personal names.

“the worship”Translation · noun

Christianity itself — not an act of worship but the whole new religion. To “take the worship” or to “come to the worship” was to become a Christian. In the northern islands the equivalent word was “school”, which stood at once for Christianity, the local church and the building it met in.

“the Book”Translation · noun

The Scriptures. The heathen of Imounga were in absolute terror of it, believing it could cause their death; when Gunn opened his book in their midst saying “We shall worship God”, they fled as though he had thrown a bomb among them.

The island world

kavaNoun

The drink prepared from the root of Piper methysticum and drunk by the men in the public square at evening. Abstaining from it was one of the sharpest tests of a Futunese convert; Saula kept clear of it entirely. By 1908 the chiefs had uprooted and destroyed about two boat-loads of kava plants across two districts.

kanakaNoun · labour trade

An islander of the western Pacific recruited for work abroad, chiefly on the Queensland sugar plantations. Those who came home were called “returns”. The labour traffic drained Futuna of its young men — often, Gunn lamented, his most promising candidates — and the ship that brought the returns in January 1893 brought the dysentery with them.

customNoun · regional English

Everything belonging to the old culture: custom dress, custom medicine, custom marriage. In the mission sources of this period the word used is usually the blunter heathenism.

arrowrootNoun · economy

The one cash crop by which the Futunese paid for their Scriptures and their church buildings. Made communally, shipped to Scotland, and sold there. The arrowroot of 1899 yielded £50, and even the heathen Imoungans shared in producing it — at first for a small present, later for nothing.

sacred manOffice · heathen

The priest of a district or of a particular power — of the sea, of the wind, of rain, of the breadfruit. Waihit had been a sacred man of the sea on Aneityum before his conversion; Konafia was the sacred man of Ipau; Forau was reputed a wind-maker because his guardian had been one. Their surrender of the sacred stones is the recurring sign of conversion in this record.

sacred stonesObjects · heathen

Stones representing the gods, kept in the marae and in private hands and used to secure success in fishing, planting, rain or wind. Forau’s wind-stone was about the size of a child’s head and pierced with holes, into which the sacred man stuffed leaves, leaving one or two empty to represent the wind he wanted to blow.

consumptionNoun · medical

Pulmonary tuberculosis, introduced from outside and spreading on Futuna from the 1870s. It killed the chief Sarashi, and it cut short the service of more than one missionary in the group.

DayspringShip

The mission vessel of the New Hebrides Mission, and the name of its annual printed reports, which are one of the standing sources for this period. Other vessels in this record: the Camden and the John Williams of the London Missionary Society, H.M.S. Herald, and the labour vessel Empreza.

Ni-VanuatuNoun

The people of Vanuatu. A modern term, used by Miller writing in the 1980s, and used here in preference to the language of the older sources wherever this record speaks in its own voice.

The offices of the church

teacherOffice

The working missionary of this whole story: an islander, usually married, settled in a district to hold school and Sabbath services. Aneityumese teachers received no wages at home, only a yearly present of clothing; serving on another island they were paid five pounds a year from the Native Teachers’ Fund founded by John G. Paton in 1863.

candidates’ classInstitution

Also the communicants’ or catechumens’ class. The mission required a year’s catechetical instruction before admission, to give converts a broad knowledge of the facts and time to show a changed life. Futuna’s first class produced the five of May 1889.

deaconOffice

An ordained office-bearer under the pastor. Nailo was the first ordained on Futuna; five more followed in 1905 and three in 1917.

pastorOffice

An ordained islander with charge of a congregation — a step beyond teacher, and new to these islands in Gunn’s day. Epeteneto of Aneityum was the first, in 1897; Habena of Futuna the second, in 1900; and then no further ordination anywhere in the church until 1920.

SynodInstitution

The annual meeting of the missionaries of the New Hebrides Mission, held on a different island each year. It appointed missionaries to stations, sanctioned ordinations, and recorded memorial minutes for the dead — including Habena’s in 1917.

furloughPractice

Extended home leave, generally in Scotland or Australia, taken every several years. Futuna was left in the hands of Habena and the teachers during the Gunns’ furloughs of 1890–91, 1893–95 and 1905–07 — and the record shows that the work went forward in their absence.

The old religion and custom

tavakaFutunese · noun

A canoe; and, in the figurative speech of the island, a killing. To cut a canoe was to doom someone to death in order to remove a disease and placate the gods — understood by the heathen as a sacrifice. To carry the canoe was the island-wide feasting that followed, in which every district, including the outcast relatives of the dead man, had to join as a pledge of peace. The last cutting was the shooting of Basulu in May 1887; the last carrying ran through 1887 and 1888. See Customary law.

AmoshishikiFutunese · deity

The principal god of Futuna, who fished the island up out of the sea bed headland by headland. The Futunese pointed out where his foot slipped as he hauled up the last part, and a row of stones standing for his broken fishing line. The same figure is Moitikitiki on Aneityum and at Weasisi, and Maui-tikitiki through Polynesia. The temple at Futuna was his house. In modern Futunese orthography he is Majihjiki, and the cycle of stories about him was recorded in the language by Keller and Kuautonga in 2007.

takoFutunese · noun

The digging stick. At the close of the flying-fish season the priest cut down the tako and hung it up in the temple; that evening he dug the first ripe yam in the sacred plantation and displayed it on the sacred banyan, after which it was lawful for everyone to dig.

amilMelanesian · noun

The northern equivalent of the marae, also called the nakamal. In the middle and northern islands it held figures ten feet high with ugly human faces painted red, green and yellow, and upright hollowed-log drums for beating signals for war or feasts. No woman might appear in the amil under pain of death — a restriction that did not apply to the Futunese marae, where women took part in the ceremonies. Gunn saw forty figures in one amil in Malekula; seven years later there were four.

“Ho!”Futunese · response

The people’s assent, called out together after the priest had named the gods who cared for the yams and a chief had given a loud shout. Gunn calls it their Amen. It was their prayer, and the feast was then distributed.

the shadesTranslation · noun

The spirits of the dead in the lower world. On Futuna the immortality was limited: the shades had refuse for food, carried the wounds they died with, could neither enjoy nor suffer, sank through descending stages and at last became dead shells. Stillborn babies, by contrast, became gods with endless happiness.

disease-makerOffice · heathen

The sorcerer. He was believed to work by secretly gathering scraps of a person’s food, hairs, or the earth from under his feet, and burning them with incantations. Because no one was held to die naturally except in extreme old age, almost every death was laid at a disease-maker’s door, and the accusation was the commonest cause of war and of judicial killing on the island.

“whishing”Translation · verb

Driving the spirits out of a household or district by shouting at them. Gunn watched the old witch Tamanu do it at Ipau, calling in a tremendous voice on the spirits to leave and sweeping them out. By 1913, when he asked whether any of the old people still whished the gods out of their premises, a girl present laughed: she had never heard of it.

killing stoneObject · weapon

A ground stone nearly two feet long, shaped in Tanna from volcanic rock and in Futuna cut from the coral. Thrown from about twenty yards it was a deadly weapon. Killing stones were among the arms carried by the two hundred people who came to Basulu’s burial in 1887, some of them covered with the dust of years.

sinnetMaterial · noun

Twine made from coconut husk fibre, used to lash stone axe and adze heads into their sockets, to sew the raised side-planks of a canoe, and to bind the twin logs of the larger Futunese canoes together. The Futunese canoes used in Gunn’s day for catching flying fish had been the island’s ships in earlier times, raised with two rows of planks for voyages to other islands.

kastomBislama · noun

The modern Vanuatu term for the whole inherited body of custom — land tenure, kinship, ceremony, dance, song, medicine, chiefly title. It is not a term of reproach, and it is the word under which the material on the custom pages is discussed in Vanuatu today. Futuna is known within the country for the strength of its custom dance.

References and sigla

Every statement in this record rests on one of the works below. Short sigla are used in the register: GF, HD, L I, L IV. Page numbers follow the editions cited.

Primary sources

  1. The Gospel in Futuna, with Chapters on Grammar and Native Customs
    Gunn, Rev. William, M.D. London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1914. Written 1913. Siglum: GF

    The indispensable source. Gunn’s own narrative of his thirty years on the island, with a second part on the islands, the people, native customs, religious beliefs, the languages of the New Hebrides, folk-lore, and the decrease of population. Almost every Futunese name in this record comes from it.

  2. Heralds of Dawn
    Gunn, Rev. Dr William. 1924. Siglum: HD

    A book of portraits of the prominent Futunese of Gunn’s time — unique in the literature of the mission for being about the islanders rather than the missionaries. The fullest account of Pastor Habena is here, at pp. 39–56.

  3. Live: A History of Church Planting in the New Hebrides to 1880, Book One
    Miller, Rev. Dr J. Graham. Sydney: Committees on Christian Education and Overseas Missions, General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church of Australia. ISBN 0 909503 33 8. Siglum: L I

    Chapter 9, “Futuna, the First Martyrs”, and chapter 22, “The Church Reaches Out From Aneityum”, cover the period to 1880. Miller supplies details Gunn omits — notably Konafia and Popoina’s rescue of the teacher Ru, which is the origin of the Futunese Christian line.

  4. Live: A History of Church Planting in the Republic of Vanuatu, Book Four, 1881–1920
    Miller, Rev. Dr J. Graham. Port Vila: The Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu, 1986. Printed by Mission Publications of Australia, Lawson, NSW. ISBN 0 949197 05 X. Siglum: L IV

    Chapter 12, “Futuna: The Conversion of the Island, 1881–1920”, at pp. 160–185. Miller worked from the Synod minutes, the Dayspring reports, the New Hebrides Magazine and the Quarterly Jottings, and gives the statistics and dates that Gunn’s narrative leaves out. The appendix contains the roll of missionaries and the comparative table of steps in the planting of the church.

  5. Live: A History of Church Planting in the Republic of Vanuatu, Book Six, The Northern Islands 1881–1948
    Miller, Rev. Dr J. Graham. Port Vila: The Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu, 1989. Siglum: L VI

    Consulted for context on the wider mission, the glossary of terms, and the northern islands to which Futunese teachers were afterwards sent.

Works cited within the primary sources

  1. Missions in Western Polynesia
    Murray, Rev. A. W. (LMS).

    Cited by Gunn at p. 23 for the landing of the Samoan teachers and the part played by Kautiama at Aneityum. Murray was aboard the Camden in 1841.

  2. Bible Illustrations from the New Hebrides
    Inglis, Rev. Dr John.

    Cited by Gunn at pp. 223 and 246 for the acceptance of teachers on both islands and for the 1856 tour of Aneityum. Inglis also supplies the mission’s rule on unhurried admission of converts.

  3. Memoirs of the Rev. John Williams
    Prout, Ebenezer.

    Quoted by Miller at pp. 381–383 for Williams’s own journal of the approach to Futuna on 17 November 1839 and his promise to return with teachers.

  4. Misi Gete: John Geddie’s Journal
    Geddie, Rev. Dr John.

    Quoted by Miller at p. 123 for the forming of the first church in western Polynesia at Anelgauhat on 13 May 1852 — the congregation that sent Waihit and Iosefa to Futuna.

  5. The Life of Henry Drummond
    Smith, Sir George Adam.

    Cited by Miller at pp. 376–377 for Drummond’s impressions of Futuna in 1890.

  6. Peter Milne of Nguna
    Don, Rev. Alexander.

    Cited by Miller at p. 240 for the Aneityumese teachers serving on other islands.

  7. The Dayspring reports; the New Hebrides Magazine; the Quarterly Jottings of the John G. Paton Mission Fund; the Minutes of the Mission Synod

    The serial record of the mission, from which Miller draws almost all the statistics quoted in this document. The photographic record is largely Gunn’s own; some plates are held by the Mitchell Library, Sydney.

A note on names and spellings

Futunese names are given in Gunn’s spelling, since he learned and printed the language. Where Miller differs the variant is noted in the entry — Sarashi / Saraji, Kavahe / Kavehe, Iosefa / Yosefa, Soia / Swaea, Anatato / Natato. Some names in the sources are titles or descriptions rather than personal names, and several people — four of the martyrs’ household, the teachers’ wives, Habena’s five children — are recorded without names at all. They are entered here as the sources leave them, because a genealogy that invents its missing generations is worth nothing.

Further sources added to this record

These five were supplied after the first compilation and are cited by the sigla shown. Between them they carry the record back before Gunn and forward past 1935.

  1. The New Hebrides and Christian Missions, with a Sketch of the Labour Traffic
    Steel, Rev. Dr Robert. London: James Nisbet & Co., 1880. Cited as S.

    Chapter VI is given wholly to Futuna, pp. 129–145. Written while Copeland was still resident, before any Futunese had been baptised, and containing John Williams’ own journal of 16–17 November 1839, the naming of the Samoan teachers and their murderer, the landing date of the Aneityumese in 1853, the first Communion of June 1871, Mrs Copeland’s death on 20 January 1876, and the labour-trade figures. The scan consulted carries no text layer and was read by optical character recognition; readings have been checked against the page images, and where the OCR is uncertain this record paraphrases rather than quotes.

  2. John G. Paton, Missionary to the New Hebrides: Second Part
    Paton, John G., edited by his brother. London: Hodder and Stoughton. Cited as P II.

    The Aniwa volume. Used here for the pen-portrait of Naswai and his address to the Futunese deputation, pp. 251–255 — the only surviving report of Futunese being addressed in their own language about their own planting ceremonies by islanders who had already given them up.

  3. Live: A History of Church Planting in the New Hebrides — Book Three
    Miller, Rev. Dr J. Graham. Cited as L III.

    Part Four, Topical Surveys, chapters 24–31: the birth of a literature, education, the seeds of self-government, the mission ships, the Roman Catholic and Anglican missions, the roots of the church, and money in the young church. It supplies the portraits of Epeteneto and Habena, the Synod minute of 1917, the attribution and dating of Gunn’s Aneityum rock-carving photographs to about 1902, and the note that a small island like Futuna would produce as much as a ton of arrowroot in a year.

  4. “Darkness and Light in Black and White: Travelling Mission Imagery from the New Hebrides”
    Lindstrom, Lamont. In Kalissa Alexeyeff and John Taylor (eds), Touring Pacific Cultures, chapter 3, pp. 33–53. Canberra: ANU Press, 2016. Open access. Cited as LX.

    The scholarly account of how mission pictures were made, captioned, sold and recaptioned. It discusses Gunn twice by name: as the photographer credited with the Erromanga portrait that was printed under two different captions, and as the maker of the “heathen and Christian” pair in Heralds of Dawn. The plate reproduced here at plate 24 comes from this chapter.

  5. A Brief History of the Work of the Church in Vanuatu
    Whimp, Rev. Neal, missionary in Vanuatu 1969–1980. Cited as W.

    A short survey by a participant, used here only for the twentieth-century frame: the growth from 11 to 46 missionaries between 1901 and 1930, the founding of the Presbyterian Church of the New Hebrides in 1948, the Tangoa and Talua training institutions, the church’s part in the move to independence in 1980, and the present standing of the Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu.

A note on the sigla

The short forms used throughout this record are: GF Gunn, The Gospel in Futuna (1914); HD Gunn, Heralds of Dawn (1924); L I, L III, L IV Miller, Live, Books One, Three and Four; S Steel (1880); P II Paton, Second Part; LX Lindstrom (2016); W Whimp. A number after the siglum is a page number in that work.

02

Sources for the custom record

Modern and external sources on Futunese custom

The sections on the old religion, the customary year, customary law, the life course and the conduct of men, women and children rest on Gunn’s own ethnographic chapters, written on the island between 1883 and 1913. Gunn was a missionary and not a trained ethnographer, and he wrote of the customs as things to be replaced. The works below are the scholarly and Futunese-authored record of the same island, and a reader who wants the culture described from inside rather than from the mission house should go to them. Web addresses are given as they were consulted.

  1. Nokonofo Kitea (We Keep on Living This Way): Myths and Music of Futuna, Vanuatu
    Keller, Janet Dixon, and Takaronga Kuautonga. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2007. ISBN 978‑0‑8248‑3113‑4. uhpress.hawaii.edu/title/nokonofo-kitea-we-keep-on-living-this-way-myths-and-music-of-futuna-vanuatu/

    The principal modern source, and the only one co-authored by a Futunese: Takaronga Kuautonga is a fieldworker of the Vanuatu Cultural Centre. The stories and songs are given in Futunese and in English. The cycle of the culture hero Majihjiki — Gunn’s Amoshishiki — accounts for the rocks, reefs and landscape features of the island, and the collection also treats gender, marriage, residence, exchange and alliance, and encodes the disquiet of the early evangelistic period in metaphor.

  2. Myths and Music of Futuna, Vanuatu: Past and Present in Dialogue
    Keller, Janet Dixon, and Takaronga Kuautonga. In John Taylor and Nick Thieberger (eds), Working Together in Vanuatu: Research Histories, Collaborations, Projects and Reflections, chapter 10, pp. 115–122. Canberra: ANU Press, 2011. Open access. press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p146521/html/ · jstor.org/stable/j.ctt24h3dg.20

    The authors’ account of how the 2007 collection was made, in a volume opened by Ralph Regenvanu as Director of the Vanuatu Cultural Centre and National Cultural Council, and containing William Mohns on the Centre’s digital archive and catalogues.

  3. The Culture and Language of Futuna and Aniwa, New Hebrides
    Capell, Arthur. Oceania Linguistic Monographs No. 5. Sydney: University of Sydney, 1958. OLAC listing: language-archives.org/language/fut

    The standing scholarly description of the two islands and the language they share. Capell also worked over Gunn’s own linguistic papers; the Pacific and Regional Archive for Digital Sources in Endangered Cultures (PARADISEC) holds his Aniwa–Futuna word and phrase notes compiled with Gunn, and a file described as papers for Doctor Gunn in very poor condition.

  4. West Futuna-Aniwa: An Introduction to a Polynesian Outlier Language
    Dougherty, Janet W. D. University of California Publications in Linguistics, vol. 102. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1983.

    The modern grammar and dictionary. Futuna-Aniwa is an Austronesian, Polynesian outlier language of Tafea Province with roughly 1,500 speakers, unusual among Polynesian languages in distinguishing trial from plural number. It is called West Futunan to distinguish it from the unrelated East Futunan of Wallis and Futuna — a distinction this record is careful to keep.

  5. Stones in Motion: monuments and chiefly title histories in central Vanuatu
    Ballard, Chris. Archaeology in Oceania, 2023. onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/arco.5283

    Cited here for its summary of Keller and Kuautonga’s account of the mythological genesis of the Futunese landscape — its rock and reef features largely created by the culture hero Majihjiki, with further features attributed to other ancestral figures. It is the scholarly frame for what Gunn recorded as the footprint and the row of stones.

  6. The Gospel in Futuna — digitised copy
    Gunn, William. Internet Archive, from the British Empire Collection, gift of the Church of Scotland. archive.org/details/gospelinfutunawi00gunniala

    The scan from which the page references in this record were checked. A print-on-demand reissue also exists under ISBN 978‑1‑330‑60490‑8.

  7. Pacific Manuscripts Bureau photographic catalogue
    Australian National University, Canberra; records supplied by the Presbyterian Research Centre, Knox College. asiapacific.anu.edu.au/pambu/catalogue/

    Holds Gunn’s photographic record of Futuna, including the new mission house of 1889 with Mrs Gunn and the four children — two of whom died in the dysentery epidemic of 1893 and one by drowning on Aneityum in the same year.

  8. Trove and the National Library of Australia
    In Memoriam: Mrs Margaret Mathieson Gunn, late of Aneityum and Futuna, New Hebrides, Roseville, N.S.W., 1932. nla.gov.au/nla.obj-364182946

    Gives Mrs Gunn’s dates — born 16 March 1854, died 18 January 1932 — which the mission sources leave vague.

  9. Ethnobotany of Breadfruit in Vanuatu: Review and Prospects
    Ethnobiology Letters, 2016. ojs.ethnobiology.org/index.php/ebl/article/view/582

    Consulted for the standing of Gunn 1914 and Capell 1958 in the modern ethnobotanical literature, and for context on the breadfruit — the crop over which the Futunese sacred men held their particular power.

  10. “Feeling at home in Vanuatu”: Integration of newcomers from the East during the last millennium
    PLOS ONE, 2023. journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0290465

    Context for the Polynesian outlier status of Futuna and Aniwa, and for the argument that Polynesian arrivals were well integrated into local Vanuatu societies rather than held apart — which is what Gunn was describing, in the language of his day, when he wrote of a people mixed of two stocks whose women preserved the older tongue.

A note on the customary sections

The six custom pages report the old religion and custom of Futuna as the mission sources describe them, and they carry that source’s judgements as well as its facts. Gunn was an honest and unusually observant witness — he recorded the Futunese view of the future world, the exact procedure of the temple ceremonies, the names of the priestesses, and the arguments the people made against him — but he was not a neutral one, and where he passes verdicts on Futunese character this record says so rather than repeating them as findings. Nothing here should be taken as displacing the account Futunese families give of their own past. Where the two differ, the family is the better authority, and this record would be glad to be corrected.

02

The two principal authors

Between them these two men produced everything of substance that is known about the people of Futuna in the mission century. Gunn wrote as a participant, from inside the house; Miller wrote seventy years later, from the archive, and could see what Gunn could not.

Rev. Dr William Gunn

1853–1935 · “Missi”Scotland
Born1853, Helmsdale, Caithness, Scotland
Sent byFree Church of Scotland; from 1900 the United Free Church
StationsFutuna 1883–1917; Aneityum from 1893; Eromanga from 1915
DistinctionFirst medical missionary of the New Hebrides Mission
Ordained1894, on furlough in Scotland
DiedSunday 9 June 1935, Roseville, Sydney

Origin and formation

Gunn was born in 1853 in Helmsdale, a fishing village on the Caithness and Sutherland coast in the far north of Scotland. He was a boy of ten in 1863 when John G. Paton, home from Tanna, visited Wick; Paton’s life and words made a deep impression on him, and the sensation the visit caused in that Scottish town stayed with him for the rest of his life. Forty-one years later, at the Mission Synod at Nguna in 1904, it was Gunn who seconded the motion congratulating the veteran Dr Paton on his eightieth birthday, and who recalled that memory aloud.

When William was fifteen his parents moved to Edinburgh. He spent a few years in business, then decided to train as a teacher. In 1873 the Moody and Sankey mission profoundly influenced Scotland; Gunn was converted in it, and threw himself at once into evangelistic work among young people. He hoped the way would open for him to take medical training, and it did.

Appointment

In March 1883 two missionaries from the Free Church of Scotland were introduced to the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church of New South Wales in Sydney. One was W. B. Murray, ordained for Ambrym, whose service was cut short by tuberculosis and who died in 1885. The other was Gunn, sent out by his church as a medical missionary — the first the New Hebrides Mission had. In June he was welcomed to Synod as an elder and appointed to Futuna, succeeding Joseph Copeland. He was not ordained a minister until 1894, while on furlough in Scotland; for his first eleven years on the island he was a layman.

The work

He was, in practice, several men. As a doctor he carried the mission’s first medical work through measles, dysentery and consumption epidemics, and treated a population in steep decline. As a translator he put the greater part of the New Testament into Futunese, working with Popoina and later informants, and completed the task in retirement; Synod thanked him for the finished New Testament in 1931 and for the Psalms in 1924. As a printer he set up a hand press in a lean-to eleven feet by five off the church verandah, and printed almanacs, Jonah, a hymn-book of a hundred hymns and 230 bound copies of the General Epistles on the island itself. As a cartographer he prepared the first edition of the mission map of the islands in 1904, which forty years later still held pride of place in stores and government offices, British and French alike. As a photographer he was expert, developing his own plates on Futuna, and left a pictorial record of the islands, the people, the early church leaders and important events that is now the principal visual source for the period; many of his photographs appeared in the New Hebrides Magazine and the Quarterly Jottings, and some are deposited with the Mitchell Library, Sydney.

From 1893 he had charge of Aneityum as well as Futuna, with three homes — Futuna, Anelgauhat and Aname — and a family, he said, forever on the move between them. He learned Aneityumese with the help of Pastor Epeteneto and translated a Scripture Treasury and additional hymns into it.

Family

He married a Miss Matheson. They had four children on the island: Connie, Madgie, Willie and Ruth. In 1893 the dysentery brought ashore by the labour vessel Empreza killed Connie and, six days later, Madgie; Ruth barely survived and had to learn again to sit, stand, crawl and walk; Gunn made her coffin at the same time as Madgie’s, fearing he would be too weak later. In August of the same year Willie, the only son, was drowned in shallow water beside the boats on Aneityum. Gunn stayed another twenty-four years. Mrs Gunn died in 1932; Synod recorded its sympathy that year.

Retirement and death

He resigned from the United Free Church of Scotland’s Foreign Missions Committee in 1915, judging that the reduced populations of Aneityum and Futuna no longer warranted a missionary of their own and that the three southern islands could be worked together by a vigorous younger man. At the urgent request of the John G. Paton Mission Fund he stayed on in charge of Aneityum, Futuna and Eromanga until March 1917 — the year of the hurricane that brought down the mission churches and houses on both his islands. He retired to Sydney during the war and went on translating. In 1933 Synod congratulated him on the jubilee of his appointment. He died on a Sunday, 9 June 1935, at Roseville, Sydney, and was buried the next day.

Works used in this record
  • The Gospel in Futuna, with Chapters on Grammar and Native Customs. London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1914; written 1913. Two parts: the narrative of the mission, and a general account of the islands, their peoples, customs, religion, languages and folk-lore.
  • Heralds of Dawn. 1924. Portraits of the prominent Futunese of his time — unusual in the mission literature for being about the islanders rather than the missionaries.
  • Annual reports to Synod, printed in the Dayspring reports and the New Hebrides Magazine, 1883–1917.
  • The Futunese Scriptures, hymn-book, catechism and almanacs, printed at Futuna and in Sydney.
L IV 160–185, 191 · GF, throughout

Rev. Dr J. Graham Miller

historian of the Vanuatu churchAustralia & New Zealand
ChurchPresbyterian Church of Australia; later of Vanuatu
TongoaMissionary, 1941–1947
TangoaPrincipal, Teachers’ Training Institute, 1947–1952
Bible CollegeFirst principal, 1971–1973
Wrote from14 Franklin Street, Wangaratta, Victoria
WifeFlora Miller, his “inseparable helper”

Qualification

Miller wrote the history of a church he had helped to raise. He and his wife Flora were missionaries on Tongoa from 1941 to 1947, principal and staff of the Tangoa Training Institute from 1947 to 1952, and he returned as the first principal of the Bible College from 1971 to 1973. He watched the New Hebrides church reach self-government in 1948–49. The General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church of the New Hebrides encouraged him in 1973 to write the history, and the volumes were afterwards sponsored and published by the Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu.

K. M. Shing, headmaster of Onesua High School, wrote in the foreword to the first volume that no one was more qualified to read through the many books and journals of the early mission and set the story down in a form that could be understood by readers with limited English. The Moderator-General of the Presbyterian Church of Australia added that Miller wrote as a witness of these things, with a sharp mind, a rare gift of impartiality — painting the picture “warts and all” — and a great love for the people.

Method and intention

Miller called Live “a folk-history of, from and for the Ni-Vanuatu of today — and tomorrow”, written from the inside and from the standpoint of Ni-Vanuatu eager to know their own national history. He aimed to write the story not of the missions but of the churches that took root under them. He worked from the Synod minutes, the Dayspring reports, the New Hebrides Magazine, the Quarterly Jottings, and the diaries, letters and photographs of the pioneers’ descendants, and acknowledged the State Library of South Australia and the Hewitson Library at Knox College, Dunedin. He indexed the names of many hundreds of Ni-Vanuatu men and women deliberately, and wrote that he had done his best to fill out the details of their lives and labours: “They have drawn close to me as I have written of them.” He invited correspondence to correct the gaps and errors he expected.

The title puzzled his readers until the Rev. David Stewart, principal of the Bible College of New Zealand, identified its origin in Ezekiel 16:6 — God’s word to a child left weltering in its blood, to live and grow. Miller took it as the imperative verb, and as the history in biblical parable.

Family and place

His wife’s judgement and practical help in all checking and assessment of the material was, he wrote, decisive; at the time of Book Four they had travelled forty-five years together, and the tapestry of their years in Vanuatu formed the background of everything they wrote. Their sons and daughters were born in the islands. He wrote and sold the books from his home at 14 Franklin Street, Wangaratta, Victoria; they were printed by Mission Publications of Australia at Lawson, New South Wales, and sold through church bookrooms in Vanuatu, New Zealand, Australia, the United Kingdom and Canada.

The Live series
  • Live: A History of Church Planting in the New Hebrides to 1880, Book One. Sydney: Presbyterian Church of Australia. The first publication funded from the New Hebrides Educational Publications Fund, established with an anonymous donation of four thousand dollars. ISBN 0 909503 33 8. Used here for chapters 9 and 22.
  • Live … Book Four, 1881–1920. Port Vila: Presbyterian Church of Vanuatu, 1986. ISBN 0 949197 05 X. Medical services; church planting in the southern islands; Tanna. Chapter 12 is the conversion of Futuna.
  • Live … Book Six, The Northern Islands 1881–1948. Port Vila, 1989. Malekula, Ambrym, Paama and Lopevi. Used here for context and the glossary.
  • Books Two, Three, Five and a projected Seventh on Santo and Malo complete the series.
L I, foreword and preface · L IV, preface and colophon · L VI, preface
03

Authors of the earlier record

These five were missionaries first and writers second. Each left a book, a journal or a translation on which Gunn and Miller drew, and each appears in the genealogy itself as a participant.

Rev. Joseph Copeland

d. 1908Reformed Presbyterian Church
Joined the Mission1858
StationsTanna; Aneityum, Aname 1860–63; Futuna 1866–1881
Married1863, the widow of S. F. Johnston
WidowedFutuna, 20 January 1876
Later careerEditor, the weekly of the Presbyterian Church of NSW
DiedStrathfield, near Sydney, 1908

Copeland is an author of this record in two senses. He is the first resident missionary of Futuna and therefore a principal actor in it; and he is the compiler of the first Futunese Scriptures — the Harmony of the Gospels he placed in the people’s hands before leaving in 1881, together with a collection of hymns which Gunn afterwards absorbed into his own hymnal of 1898. Mrs Gunn’s young women’s class was still memorising a hundred pages of Copeland’s Harmony twenty years after he left the island.

He was a scholar and a missionary, careful and cautious but with the true evangelistic spirit, experienced in the ways of islanders and judicious with them. Baptising no one in fifteen years, he nonetheless broke the back of Futunese heathenism; Gunn judged that a few more years would have seen Christianity triumph. He also influenced the boy Habena during his charge of Aname, and that link with the first missionary of Futuna may well have kindled Habena’s own desire to serve there.

After resigning he served the Presbyterian Church of New South Wales for a number of years as editor of its weekly periodical — making him the only one of these authors whose principal writing was journalism. His interest in Futuna never waned; he revisited the group several times, and Gunn records receiving his help and advice with gratitude.

Works used in this record
  • The Harmony of the Gospels in Futunese, and a Futunese hymn collection.
  • Reports and letters quoted by Gunn, including his summary of the state of Futuna in 1875.
GF 14–30 · L I 31, 190 · L IV 161, 179

Rev. A. W. Murray

London Missionary Society
SocietyLondon Missionary Society
BasedSamoa, cruising to Melanesia
At FutunaMarch 1841; April 1845
Principal workMissions in Western Polynesia

Murray had a long association with the New Hebrides Mission and wrote the history of the LMS work in western Polynesia; he and Sunderland cruised regularly from Samoa to pioneer the Melanesian missions. He was aboard the Camden in March 1841 when Apela and Samuela were landed on Futuna, and aboard the John Williams in April 1845 when, with Dr Turner, he tried and failed to land and learn their fate. He was also present at Anelgauhat in May 1852, when Geddie consulted him and Sunderland about forming the first church in western Polynesia, and both strongly urged it.

He is therefore the eye-witness for the opening and the closing of the first Polynesian phase on Futuna. Gunn cites his book at page 23 for the part played by the chief Kautiama in getting teachers accepted on both Futuna and Aneityum.

Work used in this record
  • Missions in Western Polynesia, cited by Gunn, p. 23.
GF 6 n.1, 8 · L I 27–28, 81

Rev. Dr John Inglis

Aneityum
StationAname, Aneityum, 1852–1879
WifeMrs Jessie Inglis
AchievementCo-translator of the Aneityumese Bible
Principal workBible Illustrations from the New Hebrides

Inglis and Geddie between them made Aneityum the nursery of the Vanuatu church, and their translation — the New Testament of 1863, the Old Testament in two volumes in 1879 — was the first complete Bible in any language of Melanesia. Inglis retired in 1877–79, having maintained an outreach of twenty to thirty Aneityumese couples serving on other islands at any one time. He hoped Aneityum would be the Iona of the New Hebrides, and for a generation it was.

His book is quoted by Gunn twice on Futuna matters: at page 246 for the acceptance of teachers on both islands through Kautiama, and at page 223 for the 1856 tour of Christian Aneityum laid on for Waihit’s ten Futunese visitors. His most consequential sentence for this record is his statement of the mission’s policy of unhurried admission — “our first converts were always our best … they were the longest under instruction” — which is the reason Futuna waited fifty years for a baptism.

Work used in this record
  • Bible Illustrations from the New Hebrides, cited by Gunn, pp. 223 and 246.
  • The Aneityumese Scriptures, 1852–1879, with Geddie.
GF 6, 11–12 · L I 81–82, 189 · L IV 138–139

Rev. Dr John Geddie

Aneityum
OriginNova Scotia, Canada
StationAnelgauhat, Aneityum, from 1848
WifeMrs Charlotte Geddie, née McDonald
Principal workHis journal, published as Misi Gete

Geddie is the founder of the Presbyterian mission in these islands and the man whose diary supplies the most-quoted single paragraph in Miller’s first volume: his account of 13 May 1852, when thirteen Aneityumese were baptised and formed into the first church in western Polynesia. That church sent Waihit and Iosefa to Futuna eighteen months later. He also visited Futuna in 1851 and brought a chief and fourteen Futunese back to see what the gospel had done, and in January 1852 sheltered a Futuna refugee in the hope that it would reopen the way.

His caution about admitting converts — noting in 1850 that there were converts waiting for baptism but that delay was desirable — became the mission’s rule, with the consequences traced throughout the genealogy.

Work used in this record
  • Geddie’s journal, published as Misi Gete; quoted by Miller, p. 123.
GF 9–10 · L I 81–82, 93, 189

Dr George Turner

London Missionary Society
SocietyLondon Missionary Society
Tanna1842–43, with Nisbet
At FutunaApril 1845, with Murray
LaterSamoa

Turner and Nisbet were driven off Tanna in a whale-boat in February 1843, refusing to use their gun in self-defence, and were picked up by a Hobart whaler and carried to Samoa. Turner returned north on the John Williams in 1845 and was in the boat that tried to land on Futuna.

His contribution to this record is a single correction, and it is a good example of how Gunn worked. Gunn adds a footnote of his own to the 1845 episode: the missionaries were evidently unaware that the teachers had been settled at Imounga, because Dr Turner told him personally that they were stationed at what became the mission landing at Ipau. That is oral testimony from one participant, taken down decades later by another writer — and it is why the 1845 boat waited at the wrong end of the island.

Contribution to this record
  • Personal testimony to Gunn on the station of the Samoan teachers, recorded at The Gospel in Futuna, p. 8, note 1.
GF 8 n.1 · L I 34–35
04

Authors quoted at second hand

Four further writers appear in this record only through quotation inside Gunn or Miller. They are listed for completeness and so that a reader can trace any statement back to its origin.

Rev. John Williams

as a writerLondon Missionary Society
SocietyLondon Missionary Society, from 1817
Known asThe Apostle of the South Seas
KilledEromanga, 20 November 1839
SourceHis journal, in Prout’s Memoirs

Williams is an author of this record because his own journal supplies the account of the Futuna landfall. He wrote on the eve of it that the approaching week was to him the most important of his life, and afterwards that although he was not rich enough in teachers to spare two for the island, it would be occupied as soon as possible — and that they had given the Futunese to understand he would visit them again shortly. He was dead within three days. The pledge was remembered by the LMS leaders and honoured in 1841, and the whole subsequent history of the island turns on it.

Source of the quotations
  • Williams’ journal, quoted from Prout’s Memoirs, pp. 381–383.

06

Weighing the sources

A reader is entitled to know how far these authors can be trusted, and where they need reading against each other.

What Gunn is good for

Gunn is the only witness for the inner life of Futuna between 1883 and 1917 — the conversations, the names, the deathbeds, the exact wording of what people said. He knew the language, printed it, and preserved the speech of men and women who left no other trace. Heralds of Dawn is unusual in the whole mission literature for being a book about the islanders. He is also candid about failure: his own, and his converts’.

Where Gunn needs care

He writes as an advocate of a cause, in the vocabulary of his period, and calls the unconverted “heathen” and their culture “darkness” without qualification. His dates are sometimes loose — his introduction places Williams’ death in 1840 — and some estimates, notably Yaupa’s age of a hundred and thirty, are reasoned inferences rather than records. Where he is the only source for a spoken exchange, it is a recollection, often written decades later.

What Miller adds

Miller supplies the archive: dates, statistics, Synod decisions and the wider comparative frame across every island of the group. He corrects and completes Gunn at several points, and he preserves the one fact on which this entire genealogy hinges — that Konafia and Popoina saved the teacher Ru’s life, which Gunn does not report. Writing in the 1980s for a newly independent nation, he also names Ni-Vanuatu deliberately and at length, and treats them as the subject of the history rather than its object.

Where they disagree

The differences are small and are noted in the genealogy where they occur: the spelling of Futunese names, the exact circumstances of the death of Samuela’s daughter, the year of Williams’ death, and the precise population figure for 1893, which Gunn gives as a third of the island and Miller as a fall from 480 to 347. Neither author is contradicted by the other on any matter of substance.

A last note

Both principal authors were writing for the people of these islands rather than about them for others. Gunn dedicated his labour to a population of three hundred and went on translating for them from a Sydney suburb for eighteen years after he left. Miller wrote that his history was “of, from and for the Ni-Vanuatu of today — and tomorrow”. This compilation is made in the same spirit and for the same readers.
